cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

find_package(Threads REQUIRED)
# Game executable needs SFML+OpenGL; QUIET so the dev container can still
# configure CMake and build the core library + tests without them.
find_package(SFML 2.6 COMPONENTS graphics window system QUIET)
find_package(OpenGL QUIET)

# Core: SFML-free game logic shared with the unit tests.
add_library(llm_npc_core STATIC
    src/core/City.cpp
    src/core/Config.cpp
    src/core/DialogueSession.cpp
    src/core/KeyBindings.cpp
    src/core/LlmClient.cpp
    src/core/Npc.cpp
    src/core/PersonaLoader.cpp
    src/core/World.cpp
)
target_include_directories(llm_npc_core PUBLIC
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/core
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/external
)
target_link_libraries(llm_npc_core PUBLIC Threads::Threads)
if(WIN32)
    # httplib needs winsock when built with MinGW.
    target_link_libraries(llm_npc_core PUBLIC ws2_32)
endif()

if(SFML_FOUND AND OPENGL_FOUND)
    add_executable(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
        src/app/main.cpp
        src/app/DialogUI.cpp
        src/app/InputMap.cpp
        src/app/Menu.cpp
        src/app/Renderer3D.cpp
    )
    target_include_directories(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/app
    )
    target_link_libraries(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
        PRIVATE
            llm_npc_core
            sfml-graphics
            sfml-window
            sfml-system
            OpenGL::GL
    )
else()
    message(STATUS "SFML or OpenGL not found; building core library only "
                   "(use tests/Makefile for the test suite)")
endif()

# LLM NPC City

A small first-person 3D city where every inhabitant is a live LLM character.
Walk the streets, find the baker, the cop, the busker, the hot-dog vendor —
press `T` and talk to them about anything. Each NPC has their own personality,
their own knowledge of the city (and pointed ignorance of everything else),
and remembers your conversation.

Powered locally by [Ollama](https://ollama.com) — no cloud, no API key.

## Quick start (Windows)

1. **Install Ollama** from <https://ollama.com/download>, then pull the model:

   ```
   ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
   ```

2. **Install MSYS2** from <https://www.msys2.org> and, in the *UCRT64* shell:

   ```
   pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml
   ```

3. **Double-click `run.bat`** (or run `./run.ps1`). It checks Ollama is up,
   builds, and launches the game.

## Playing

- `WASD` to walk, mouse to look around.
- Walk up to anyone: `[T] Talk to <name>` appears — press `T`.
- Type, press `Enter`, and watch the reply stream in live. `Escape` to leave.
- `Escape` opens the pause menu: resume, quit, or **rebind every key with the
  mouse** (changes save instantly).

Full reference: [docs/CONTROLS.md](docs/CONTROLS.md).

## Meet the city

Ten residents, each with their own patch of downtown:

| Who | Where |
|-----|-------|
| Marge Holloway, baker | Marge's Bakery, north-west |
| Officer Dana Brooks | outside the police station |
| Theo Park, barista | Bean There Coffee |
| Ms. Adaeze Obi, librarian | the library steps |
| Hal Jensen, hardware man | Jensen Hardware |
| Gus Romano, hot-dog vendor | the cart, dead center of the plaza |
| Ray Okafor, taxi driver | idling by his cab, east of the plaza |
| Yuki Tanaka, tourist | photographing the fountain |
| Benny "Strings" Malone, busker | the park's street corner |
| Mr. Albert Whitfield, retired teacher | the park bench |

They know each other — ask Gus about the squeaky cart wheel and someone at
the hardware store may have opinions.

## Configuration

- `config/llm.cfg` — model, host/port, temperature, `keep_alive` (latency).
  Any model you have pulled in Ollama works; smaller = snappier.
- `config/keybindings.cfg` — key bindings (also editable in-game).
- `personas/*.persona` — the characters themselves. Edit freely; the file
  format is documented in [docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md).

## Development

Architecture, headless test workflow, and the latency playbook live in
[docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md). Short version:

```sh
make -C tests test      # full offline unit-test suite, no SFML required
```

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Linux launcher: verifies Ollama is reachable, builds, and runs the game.
# Run from anywhere; this script cds to its own directory.
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

HOST="${OLLAMA_HOST:-localhost}"
PORT="${OLLAMA_PORT:-11434}"

if ! curl -fsS --max-time 2 "http://${HOST}:${PORT}/api/tags" >/dev/null; then
    echo "Ollama not reachable at ${HOST}:${PORT}." >&2
    echo "Start it with:  ollama serve   (and pull a model: ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct)" >&2
    exit 1
fi

cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j

exec ./build/cpp_game_with_llm_npcs

Sudo credentials aren't cached, so the Homebrew installer needs you to type your password interactively. I'll walk you through each step — run these one at a time in the prompt using `!`:

**Step 1 — Install Homebrew:**
```
! /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
```

After it finishes, Homebrew on Apple Silicon puts itself at `/opt/homebrew/bin/brew`. You may need to add it to your PATH. If `brew` isn't found after install, run:
```
! echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile && eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
```

**Step 2 — Install dependencies (CMake, SFML, Ollama):**
```
! brew install cmake sfml && brew install --cask ollama
```

**Step 3 — Start Ollama and pull the model:**
```
! ollama serve &
```
Then in a new terminal (or after a few seconds):
```
! ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
```

**Step 4 — Build and run the game:**
```
! ./run.sh
```

---

Once you've run Step 1, paste the output here and I'll confirm what's installed and run the next steps for you where I can.

content.content:
# This is a basic version file for the Config-mode of find_package().
# It is used by write_basic_package_version_file() as input file for configure_file()
# to create a version-file which can be installed along a config.cmake file.
#
# The created file sets PACKAGE_VERSION_EXACT if the current version string and
# the requested version string are exactly the same and it sets
# PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE if the current version is >= requested version,
# but only if the requested major version is the same as the current one.
# The variable CVF_VERSION must be set before calling configure_file().


set(PACKAGE_VERSION "3.0.2")

if(PACKAGE_VERSION VERSION_LESS PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION)
  set(PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE FALSE)
else()

  if("3.0.2" MATCHES "^([0-9]+)\\.")
    set(CVF_VERSION_MAJOR "${CMAKE_MATCH_1}")
    if(NOT CVF_VERSION_MAJOR VERSION_EQUAL 0)
      string(REGEX REPLACE "^0+" "" CVF_VERSION_MAJOR "${CVF_VERSION_MAJOR}")
    endif()
  else()
    set(CVF_VERSION_MAJOR "3.0.2")
  endif()

  if(PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_RANGE)
    # both endpoints of the range must have the expected major version
    math (EXPR CVF_VERSION_MAJOR_NEXT "${CVF_VERSION_MAJOR} + 1")
    if (NOT PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_MIN_MAJOR STREQUAL CVF_VERSION_MAJOR
        OR ((PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_RANGE_MAX STREQUAL "INCLUDE" AND NOT PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_MAX_MAJOR STREQUAL CVF_VERSION_MAJOR)
          OR (PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_RANGE_MAX STREQUAL "EXCLUDE" AND NOT PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_MAX VERSION_LESS_EQUAL CVF_VERSION_MAJOR_NEXT)))
      set(PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE FALSE)
    elseif(PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_MIN_MAJOR STREQUAL CVF_VERSION_MAJOR
        AND ((PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_RANGE_MAX STREQUAL "INCLUDE" AND PACKAGE_VERSION VERSION_LESS_EQUAL PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_MAX)
        OR (PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_RANGE_MAX STREQUAL "EXCLUDE" AND PACKAGE_VERSION VERSION_LESS PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_MAX)))
      set(PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE TRUE)
    else()
      set(PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE FALSE)
    endif()
  else()
    if(PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION_MAJOR STREQUAL CVF_VERSION_MAJOR)
      set(PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE TRUE)
    else()
      set(PACKAGE_VERSION_COMPATIBLE FALSE)
    endif()

    if(PACKAGE_FIND_VERSION STREQUAL PACKAGE_VERSION)
      set(PACKAGE_VERSION_EXACT TRUE)
    endif()
  endif()
endif()


# if the installed or the using project don't have CMAKE_SIZEOF_VOID_P set, ignore it:
if("${CMAKE_SIZEOF_VOID_P}" STREQUAL "" OR "8" STREQUAL "")
  return()
endif()

# check that the installed version has the same 32/64bit-ness as the one which is currently searching:
if(NOT CMAKE_SIZEOF_VOID_P STREQUAL "8")
  math(EXPR installedBits "8 * 8")
  set(PACKAGE_VERSION "${PACKAGE_VERSION} (${installedBits}bit)")
  set(PACKAGE_VERSION_UNSUITABLE TRUE)
endif()

## Otherwise: match the shape, use the pattern

Pick the row closest to your project. Each example walks through
launch + first interaction; ignore any trailing "write the skill"
section — you're using the recipe, not authoring one.

| Project type | Handle | Example |
|---|---|---|
| CLI tool | direct invocation, exit code, stdin/stdout | [examples/cli.md](examples/cli.md) |
| Web server / API | background launch + `curl` smoke | [examples/server.md](examples/server.md) |
| TUI / interactive terminal | tmux `send-keys` / `capture-pane` | [examples/tui.md](examples/tui.md) |

| Library / SDK | import-and-call smoke script at the package boundary | [examples/library.md](examples/library.md) |

If nothing fits, start from the closest match and adapt. For a web
app, [examples/playwright.md](examples/playwright.md) — drive it with
`chromium-cli`, no custom driver needed. For a desktop app,
[examples/electron.md](examples/electron.md) — it has the `_electron`

## Drive it, don't just launch it

Launching with no interaction proves the entrypoint resolves. That's
not running the app — it's typechecking with extra steps. Drive it to
a point where a user would see something:

- CLI → type a representative command, check the exit code and output.
- Server → hit the route the diff touches with `curl`, read the body.

- GUI → click the button, screenshot the window. **Look at the

If the fallback pattern didn't work out of the box — you had to
install packages, set env vars, patch config, or write a driver —

content.text:
The game is running and focused on your screen now — give the mouse a try.

**What was wrong:** the camera spin was a macOS-specific bug in the mouse-look code. Every frame, the game re-centers the cursor and reads how far it moved. SFML 2.6 implements that re-centering on macOS by posting a synthetic mouse event, and my diagnostic showed it lands the cursor at the wrong coordinates entirely (off by a constant ~378×177 px). The cursor never actually returned to center, so the camera saw the same large delta every frame and spun continuously.

**The fix** (in `src/app/main.cpp` + a framework link in `CMakeLists.txt`): on macOS the game now bypasses SFML for this — it reads the true cursor position and warps it back to a fixed anchor using CoreGraphics directly (`CGWarpMouseCursorPosition`), all in one coordinate space, so the delta genuinely resets each frame. Linux/Windows keep the original code path.

Controls: `WASD` to walk, mouse to look, `T` to talk to an NPC, `Escape` for the pause menu.

Let me know if the camera is steady now — if anything still drifts, tell me what it does (constant spin vs. slow drift) and I'll dig further.

# Plan: Instruct NPCs to take in-world actions

## Context

The player can already *type* anything to an NPC, so an NPC will verbally
react to "follow me." What's missing is turning that intent into **world
behavior** — the NPC actually following, facing, gesturing, or chasing. Today
NPCs are completely static: `Npc` stores `position_`/`facingDeg_` set once via
`setPlacement()` and never updated, and the main loop has no per-frame NPC
behavior tick. This feature lets instructions like *"follow me"*, *"raise your
right hand"*, *"wave"*, *"stop"*, and *"arrest me if you can"* drive real
behavior, while keeping compliance **in character** (the LLM decides whether to
obey) and rendering gestures with **real arm poses**.

## Approach

Have the LLM emit a machine-readable action tag at the end of its reply *only
when its character would actually comply*. The game parses the tag out of the
reply text (so it's never shown), sets the NPC's behavior, and ticks behavior
each frame. This reuses the existing LLM round-trip — no new networking.

### Action vocabulary
`follow`, `stop`, `face`, `raise_hand`, `wave`, `arrest`. Tag format, one per
reply on its own line: `[[ACTION: follow]]`.

Two independent state axes on an NPC:
- **Movement behavior** (persistent until changed): `None | Follow | Arrest`,
  plus `Stop`/`Face` which set facing but no movement.
- **Gesture pose** (transient, timed overlay): `None | RaiseHand | Wave`.

## Changes

### 1. `src/core/NpcAction.hpp` (new, header-only — no CMake/Make change)
- `enum class NpcAction { None, Follow, Stop, Face, RaiseHand, Wave, Arrest };`
- `inline NpcAction parseActionTag(std::string& reply)`: case-insensitive scan
  for `[[ACTION: <kw>]]`, map keyword→enum, **erase the tag from `reply`** (and
  trailing whitespace) so it never displays, return `None` when absent/unknown.
- Header-only keeps it out of `CMakeLists.txt`; `tests/` includes it directly.

### 2. `src/core/Persona.hpp` — `renderSystemPrompt()`
Append a shared "Action protocol" block: list the tags, instruct the model to
end its reply with exactly one tag **only if the character would truly do it**
(otherwise none), and never speak the tag aloud. This is what makes compliance
in-character (a cop may `arrest`; a tourist refuses → no tag).

### 3. `src/core/Npc.hpp` / `Npc.cpp`
- New fields: `NpcAction behavior_ = None`, `NpcAction pose_ = None`,
  `float poseTimer_ = 0.f`.
- In `onReplyArrived()`: call `parseActionTag()` on the reply content before
  returning it; route movement verbs → `behavior_`, gesture verbs → `pose_` +
  `poseTimer_` (e.g. 4s hold / wave duration). Return the cleaned text so the
  tag is stripped from the transcript.
- New `void update(float dt, const Vec3& playerPos, const City& city)`:
  - `Follow`: if `distanceXZ(pos, player) > kFollowStop (~2.5)`, step toward
    player via `city.resolveMovement(position_, target, kNpcRadius)` at
    `kNpcWalk (~3.8)`; always face player.
  - `Arrest`: same but faster (`kNpcRun ~6.0`); within `kCatch (~1.6)` switch to
    `Stop` (caught) and face player.
  - `Stop`/`Face`: face player, no movement.
  - Gesture timer counts down; `pose_`→`None` at zero (independent of movement).
  - Facing toward player: `facingDeg_ = atan2(dx, dz) * 180/π` (matches the
    `(sin,0,cos)` yaw convention in `flatForward`/`forwardFromAngles`).
- Accessors: `NpcAction pose() const`, `float poseTimer() const`.
- Reuses `distanceXZ`, `normalize`, `City::resolveMovement` (no new math).

### 4. `src/app/Renderer3D.hpp` / `Renderer3D.cpp` — `NpcVisual` + `drawNpc`
- Extend `NpcVisual` with `pose` (None/RaiseHand/Wave) and `gesturePhase`
  (float seconds, for wave oscillation).
- `drawNpc`: add two arms (thin `drawTexturedBox`/cylinder at shoulder height,
  ~1.35 y). Default: arms at sides. `RaiseHand`: right arm rotated up. `Wave`:
  right arm up, oscillate with `sin(gesturePhase * speed)`. Left arm static.

### 5. `src/app/main.cpp` — wiring
- After resolving player movement (after line ~319), loop NPCs and call
  `npc.update(dt, camera.position, world.city())`.
- In the existing `drawNpc` call (~359), pass `npc.pose()` and a running phase
  (reuse `frameClock`/accumulated time) into `NpcVisual`.
- Optional flourish: brief HUD line when caught by an `arrest` NPC.

### 6. Tests (CLAUDE.md requires tests for new business logic)
- `tests/test_npc_action.cpp` (new, auto-globbed): `parseActionTag` extracts
  each keyword, strips the tag, is case-insensitive, returns `None` for
  missing/unknown, and leaves surrounding prose intact.
- Extend NPC tests (pattern from `tests/test_npc_history.cpp` + `FakeOllama.hpp`):
  feed a reply containing `[[ACTION: follow]]`, assert behavior set and tag
  stripped; then `update()` over several ticks moves the NPC closer and halts
  within stop radius; `face` sets facing; `arrest` moves faster. Pure logic,
  SFML-free.

## Out of scope / notes
- No pathfinding around buildings beyond `resolveMovement`'s slide (NPCs can
  bump a corner); fine for the open plaza. Can revisit if needed.
- `stop` leaves the NPC wherever it is (no "return home").

## Verification
- `make -C tests test` — full offline suite incl. new action/behavior tests.
- `cmake --build build -j` then run the game (Ollama already up). Walk to
  Officer Brooks, say "follow me" → she trails you; "stop" → she halts; "raise
  your right hand" → arm raises; "arrest me if you can" → she chases and stops
  on catch. Ask the baker to arrest you → expect a verbal refusal, no movement
  (in-character). Confirm action tags never appear in the transcript.

## Branch & commits
This is the `be_able_to_instruct_npcs` work. Recommend first committing the
already-approved mouse/strafe fixes on the current branch (two `fix(app):`
commits), then branching `be_able_to_instruct_npcs` for this feature. Per
CLAUDE.md I'll run `/code-review` before committing the feature and won't push
unless asked.

obey) and rendering gestures with **real arm poses**.

Have the LLM emit a machine-readable action tag at the end of its reply *only
when its character would actually comply*. The game parses the tag out of the
reply text (so it's never shown), sets the NPC's behavior, and ticks behavior
each frame. This reuses the existing LLM round-trip — no new networking.

### Action vocabulary
`follow`, `stop`, `face`, `raise_hand`, `wave`, `arrest`. Tag format, one per
reply on its own line: `[[ACTION: follow]]`.

content.text:
The mechanism works end-to-end, but two LLM-quality issues surfaced with the 3B model:
1. The clipped-persona cop returns **only the tag, no spoken line** (→ empty transcript line).
2. The baker correctly *refused* to arrest but tacked on a **spurious `[[ACTION: raise_hand]]`**.

Both are prompt-adherence quirks, not code bugs. Let me tighten the protocol wording to require a spoken line first and to only tag the action actually being performed, then re-test the worst cases.

content.text:
`high effort → 3+4 angles × 6 candidates → 1-vote verify (recall-biased) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle, up to 6 each)

Run **7 independent finder angles** via the Agent tool. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

Cleanup and altitude candidates use the same `file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in
`failure_scenario`, state the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank
cleanup and altitude findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates bypass the verify step and are the
dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Verify (1-vote, recall-biased)

Dedup near-duplicates (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). For
each remaining candidate, run **one verifier** via the Agent tool:
give it the diff, the relevant file(s), and the candidate; it returns exactly
one of **CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE / REFUTED**.

**PLAUSIBLE by default** — do not refute a candidate for being "speculative" or
"depends on runtime state" when the state is realistic: concurrency races,
nil/undefined on a rare-but-reachable path (error handler, cold cache, missing
optional field), falsy-zero treated as missing, off-by-one on a boundary the
code does not exclude, retry storms / partial failures, regex/allowlist that
lost an anchor. These are PLAUSIBLE.

**REFUTED** only when constructible from the code: factually wrong (quote the
actual line); provably impossible (type/constant/invariant — show it); already
handled in this diff (cite the guard); or pure style with no observable effect.

Keep **CONFIRMED and PLAUSIBLE**. Drop REFUTED.

## Output

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives verification, return `[]`.

The code-review skill is designed to fan out across many cold subagents, but I have full context on every line I just wrote, and my standing guidance is to avoid spawning agents unless you explicitly ask. So I'll run the review inline at high recall — same angles, same bar — rather than spinning up 7+ cold agents. Let me pull the full diff and scan it.

content.text:
The game is up and focused. Here's what I found and fixed — the actions *were* working internally; you just couldn't see them.

**Diagnosis** (I ran the exact runtime pipeline headlessly — real persona prompt + real Ollama + the game's parser): the model emits valid tags and the NPC's `behavior` correctly becomes `Follow`, `pose` becomes `RaiseHand`, etc. The problem was purely visibility:

1. **The NPC often said nothing.** Clipped personas (like the cop) reply with *only* the action tag, which gets stripped → an empty transcript line. So it looked like nothing happened.
2. **Gestures expired in 4 seconds**, and that timer started the moment the reply arrived — while you were still reading the dialog. By the time you exited and turned to look, the hand was already back down.

**Fixes:**
- NPCs now show a **stage direction** in the transcript whenever they act — e.g. *"Officer Dana Brooks falls into step with you."* or *"…raises their right hand."* — even when they speak no words. (And "(… says nothing.)" if they truly did nothing.)
- **Gestures now hold 15s** instead of 4, so they're still playing when you leave the dialog to look.
- (From the earlier review: the pause menu now freezes NPC movement.)

**How to test:** Walk up to Officer Dana Brooks (outside the police station), press `T`, type **"raise your right hand"**, Enter, wait for the reply, press `Escape`, and look at her — arm should be up. Then try **"follow me"** and walk away. Note: compliance is in-character, so some NPCs will refuse or reinterpret (the cop sometimes "keeps an eye on you" = faces you instead of leaving her post) — that's the intended emergent behavior, not a bug.

One known cosmetic nit: while the reply streams, the raw `[[ACTION: …]]` tag may flicker briefly before the line finalizes clean. I left that alone since it's transient; I can filter it from the live stream if it bugs you.

Does it work now when you test it?

# Plan: Police-only arrests, facing fix, moods + expressive faces

## Context

The NPC instruction feature (committed as `1b15976`) works, and play-testing
surfaced the next round of requests:
1. **Anyone can "arrest"** — only police should; civilians should instead
   summon the police to come arrest you.
2. **"Face me" turns NPCs the wrong way** — they mirror the player's movement
   instead of tracking it.
3. **NPCs aren't emotionally reactive** — "I love you" should fluster them,
   "you suck" should anger them, "I like your hat" should flatter them.
4. **No faces** — heads are blank skin boxes; expressions should be visible.

Items 3+4 unify naturally: the LLM emits a mood tag each reply, and the mood
renders as a facial expression on the model.

## Verified groundwork (done during planning)

- **Facing bug root cause**: `Renderer3D::drawNpc` rotates by `-facingDeg`,
  but rotation by `+f` about Y maps local +Z (the visor/front) to
  `(sin f, 0, cos f)` = `flatForward(f)`. The `-f` mirrors every NPC in X.
  Persona files are authored to the *documented* convention (librarian at
  (-36,0), library west, plaza east, `facing = 90` = +X toward plaza ✓), so
  the renderer sign is the bug and persona files stay untouched.
- **Model behavior with two tags** (tested against live qwen2.5:3b): emits
  mood tags reliably but sloppily — duplicates, tags at start/middle, unknown
  words ("annoyed"), occasional single brackets `[ACTION: wave]`, spurious
  actions. The parser must scan the whole reply, strip every directive
  wherever it appears, map synonyms, and take the **last** mood as final.

## Changes

### 1. `src/core/NpcAction.hpp` — generalize the tag parser
- Add `enum class NpcMood { Neutral, Happy, Angry, Sad, Embarrassed, Surprised }`.
- Add `NpcAction::CallPolice` to the action enum.
- New `struct Directives { NpcAction action; NpcMood mood; bool hasMood; }` and
  `Directives parseDirectives(std::string& reply)`:
  - Scans for every `[[KIND: keyword]]` **and** single-bracket `[KIND: keyword]`
    where KIND is `action`/`mood` (case-insensitive, whitespace-tolerant).
  - Strips **all** matched tags from the reply wherever they appear (start,
    middle, end — the model doesn't follow placement rules), collapsing
    doubled whitespace at the seams; unknown keywords are also stripped (so
    brackets never leak to the transcript) but map to None/no-mood.
  - Last mood tag wins. Synonym map: annoyed/irritated/frustrated→angry;
    flattered/pleased/excited/joyful→happy; flustered/awkward/shy→embarrassed;
    shocked/startled→surprised; upset/hurt→sad.
  - Action keyword `call_police` (also `call police`, `police`) → CallPolice.
- Keep `parseActionTag` as a thin wrapper (returns `.action`) so existing
  callers/tests survive; update the one test that expects unknown tags to be
  left in the text (they're now stripped — a display improvement).

### 2. Persona: police flag + persona-aware protocol + mood protocol
- `Persona` (src/core/Persona.hpp) gains `bool police = false`.
- `renderActionProtocol()` becomes non-static / takes the flag: police get the
  `[[ACTION: arrest]]` line; civilians instead get
  `[[ACTION: call_police]] - you call out for the police to come arrest the player`.
- Append a MOOD block: react like a real person (compliments flatter,
  insults sting, love declarations fluster, surprises startle — show it in
  your words), and ALWAYS end with exactly one `[[MOOD: …]]` tag from the
  six. Tighten ACTION wording: "most replies need NO action directive".
- `PersonaLoader.cpp`: parse new header key `police = true` (accept
  true/yes/1; loader errors on unknown keys today, so this is required).
- `personas/cop.persona`: add `police = true`.

### 3. `src/core/Npc.hpp` / `Npc.cpp` — moods, summoning, lookAt
- `onReplyArrived`: use `parseDirectives`; route action via `applyAction` as
  today; set `mood_` + `moodTimer_` (~25 s decay back to Neutral, ticked in
  `update()` like the gesture timer).
- `applyAction`: if `action == Arrest && !persona_.police` convert to
  CallPolice (the model sometimes disobeys). CallPolice sets `lastAction_`
  and triggers a Wave pose (visually flagging someone down); no movement
  behavior change for the caller.
- New public `void commandArrest()` (sets behavior to Arrest, clears catch
  latch) so the main loop can order police around, and
  `void lookAt(const Vec3&)` (public wrapper over `faceToward`).
- Accessor `NpcMood mood() const`.

### 4. Renderer — facing sign fix + faces
- `drawNpc`: `glRotatef(-npc.facingDeg, …)` → `glRotatef(npc.facingDeg, …)`.
  (One character; fixes "face me" mirroring AND every NPC's authored facing.)
- `NpcVisual` gains renderer-local `NpcFace` enum (mirrors NpcMood, same
  pattern as the existing NpcPose) — main.cpp maps mood→face.
- New private `drawFace(NpcFace)` called from `drawNpc` in the local frame:
  small `drawTexturedBox` quads proud of the head's front (+Z) face —
  - eyes: two dark boxes (bigger when Surprised),
  - brows: thin boxes, rotated inward for Angry / outward for Sad
    (glPushMatrix + glRotatef about Z, same pattern as drawArm),
  - mouth: thin box; raised corner boxes for Happy, lowered for Sad,
    small open square for Surprised,
  - blush: two pink boxes on the cheeks when Embarrassed.

### 5. `src/app/main.cpp` — wiring
- Reply-arrival block: stage directions for CallPolice ("calls for the
  police!"); after applying, if `npc.lastAction() == CallPolice`, loop the
  world's NPCs and `commandArrest()` every `persona().police` NPC (the cop
  visibly sprints over; the existing catch latch shows "caught you!").
- T-key talk handler: `npc.lookAt(camera.position)` so an NPC turns to you
  the moment you start talking ("they should face you if they aren't
  already").
- NPC draw loop: map `npc.mood()` → `NpcFace`, pass into `NpcVisual`.

### 6. Tests (auto-globbed by tests/Makefile)
- Extend `tests/test_npc_action.cpp`: parseDirectives strips tags anywhere
  (start/middle/adjacent), single-bracket form, last-mood-wins, synonym map,
  unknown keyword stripped → no mood/None action, call_police keyword.
- Extend `tests/test_npc_behavior.cpp`: civilian `arrest` converts to
  CallPolice (no chase) while a `police = true` persona keeps Arrest; mood set
  by reply and decays to Neutral via `update()`; `commandArrest()` makes a cop
  chase; `lookAt` turns without moving.
- Extend `tests/test_persona.cpp` / `test_persona_roster.cpp` patterns:
  loader parses `police = true`; prompt contains the arrest directive only
  for police personas, and always contains the MOOD block.

## Out of scope
- The pedestrian doesn't pathfind to the cop; the cop comes to you.
- Moods don't alter movement/voice — facial expression + prose only.
- The transient raw-tag flicker during streaming (pre-existing cosmetic nit).

## Verification
- `make -C tests test` — full offline suite.
- `cmake --build build -j`; relaunch the game (Ollama already up):
  - "face me" to a side-on NPC → turns *toward* you and tracks correctly.
  - Walk up + `T` → NPC turns to face you immediately.
  - To the baker: "arrest me!" → she refuses/calls police; the cop sprints
    over and "caught you!" appears. To the cop: "arrest me" → she chases.
  - "I love you" → embarrassed face (blush); "you suck" → angry brows;
    "I like your hat" → happy face. Watch the face change after each reply.
- Headless spot-check (same harness as /tmp/instr_check.cpp) to confirm tag
  hygiene with the real persona prompts before in-game testing.

## Commit
Single commit on `be_able_to_instruct_npcs` after /code-review:
`feat(npc): police-only arrests, moods with facial expressions, facing fix`
(no push, per repo rules).

# Plan: Instruct NPCs to take in-world actions

## Context

The player can already *type* anything to an NPC, so an NPC will verbally
react to "follow me." What's missing is turning that intent into **world
behavior** — the NPC actually following, facing, gesturing, or chasing. Today
NPCs are completely static: `Npc` stores `position_`/`facingDeg_` set once via
`setPlacement()` and never updated, and the main loop has no per-frame NPC
behavior tick. This feature lets instructions like *"follow me"*, *"raise your
right hand"*, *"wave"*, *"stop"*, and *"arrest me if you can"* drive real
behavior, while keeping compliance **in character** (the LLM decides whether to
obey) and rendering gestures with **real arm poses**.

## Approach

Have the LLM emit a machine-readable action tag at the end of its reply *only
when its character would actually comply*. The game parses the tag out of the
reply text (so it's never shown), sets the NPC's behavior, and ticks behavior
each frame. This reuses the existing LLM round-trip — no new networking.

### Action vocabulary
`follow`, `stop`, `face`, `raise_hand`, `wave`, `arrest`. Tag format, one per
reply on its own line: `[[ACTION: follow]]`.

Two independent state axes on an NPC:
- **Movement behavior** (persistent until changed): `None | Follow | Arrest`,
  plus `Stop`/`Face` which set facing but no movement.
- **Gesture pose** (transient, timed overlay): `None | RaiseHand | Wave`.

## Changes

### 1. `src/core/NpcAction.hpp` (new, header-only — no CMake/Make change)
- `enum class NpcAction { None, Follow, Stop, Face, RaiseHand, Wave, Arrest };`
- `inline NpcAction parseActionTag(std::string& reply)`: case-insensitive scan
  for `[[ACTION: <kw>]]`, map keyword→enum, **erase the tag from `reply`** (and
  trailing whitespace) so it never displays, return `None` when absent/unknown.
- Header-only keeps it out of `CMakeLists.txt`; `tests/` includes it directly.

### 2. `src/core/Persona.hpp` — `renderSystemPrompt()`
Append a shared "Action protocol" block: list the tags, instruct the model to
end its reply with exactly one tag **only if the character would truly do it**
(otherwise none), and never speak the tag aloud. This is what makes compliance
in-character (a cop may `arrest`; a tourist refuses → no tag).

### 3. `src/core/Npc.hpp` / `Npc.cpp`
- New fields: `NpcAction behavior_ = None`, `NpcAction pose_ = None`,
  `float poseTimer_ = 0.f`.
- In `onReplyArrived()`: call `parseActionTag()` on the reply content before
  returning it; route movement verbs → `behavior_`, gesture verbs → `pose_` +
  `poseTimer_` (e.g. 4s hold / wave duration). Return the cleaned text so the
  tag is stripped from the transcript.
- New `void update(float dt, const Vec3& playerPos, const City& city)`:
  - `Follow`: if `distanceXZ(pos, player) > kFollowStop (~2.5)`, step toward
    player via `city.resolveMovement(position_, target, kNpcRadius)` at
    `kNpcWalk (~3.8)`; always face player.
  - `Arrest`: same but faster (`kNpcRun ~6.0`); within `kCatch (~1.6)` switch to
    `Stop` (caught) and face player.
  - `Stop`/`Face`: face player, no movement.
  - Gesture timer counts down; `pose_`→`None` at zero (independent of movement).
  - Facing toward player: `facingDeg_ = atan2(dx, dz) * 180/π` (matches the
    `(sin,0,cos)` yaw convention in `flatForward`/`forwardFromAngles`).
- Accessors: `NpcAction pose() const`, `float poseTimer() const`.
- Reuses `distanceXZ`, `normalize`, `City::resolveMovement` (no new math).

### 4. `src/app/Renderer3D.hpp` / `Renderer3D.cpp` — `NpcVisual` + `drawNpc`
- Extend `NpcVisual` with `pose` (None/RaiseHand/Wave) and `gesturePhase`
  (float seconds, for wave oscillation).
- `drawNpc`: add two arms (thin `drawTexturedBox`/cylinder at shoulder height,
  ~1.35 y). Default: arms at sides. `RaiseHand`: right arm rotated up. `Wave`:
  right arm up, oscillate with `sin(gesturePhase * speed)`. Left arm static.

### 5. `src/app/main.cpp` — wiring
- After resolving player movement (after line ~319), loop NPCs and call
  `npc.update(dt, camera.position, world.city())`.
- In the existing `drawNpc` call (~359), pass `npc.pose()` and a running phase
  (reuse `frameClock`/accumulated time) into `NpcVisual`.
- Optional flourish: brief HUD line when caught by an `arrest` NPC.

### 6. Tests (CLAUDE.md requires tests for new business logic)
- `tests/test_npc_action.cpp` (new, auto-globbed): `parseActionTag` extracts
  each keyword, strips the tag, is case-insensitive, returns `None` for
  missing/unknown, and leaves surrounding prose intact.
- Extend NPC tests (pattern from `tests/test_npc_history.cpp` + `FakeOllama.hpp`):
  feed a reply containing `[[ACTION: follow]]`, assert behavior set and tag
  stripped; then `update()` over several ticks moves the NPC closer and halts
  within stop radius; `face` sets facing; `arrest` moves faster. Pure logic,
  SFML-free.

## Out of scope / notes
- No pathfinding around buildings beyond `resolveMovement`'s slide (NPCs can
  bump a corner); fine for the open plaza. Can revisit if needed.
- `stop` leaves the NPC wherever it is (no "return home").

## Verification
- `make -C tests test` — full offline suite incl. new action/behavior tests.
- `cmake --build build -j` then run the game (Ollama already up). Walk to
  Officer Brooks, say "follow me" → she trails you; "stop" → she halts; "raise
  your right hand" → arm raises; "arrest me if you can" → she chases and stops
  on catch. Ask the baker to arrest you → expect a verbal refusal, no movement
  (in-character). Confirm action tags never appear in the transcript.

## Branch & commits
This is the `be_able_to_instruct_npcs` work. Recommend first committing the
already-approved mouse/strafe fixes on the current branch (two `fix(app):`
commits), then branching `be_able_to_instruct_npcs` for this feature. Per
CLAUDE.md I'll run `/code-review` before committing the feature and won't push
unless asked.

# Plan: Police-only arrests, facing fix, moods + expressive faces

## Context

The NPC instruction feature (committed as `1b15976`) works, and play-testing
surfaced the next round of requests:
1. **Anyone can "arrest"** — only police should; civilians should instead
   summon the police to come arrest you.
2. **"Face me" turns NPCs the wrong way** — they mirror the player's movement
   instead of tracking it.
3. **NPCs aren't emotionally reactive** — "I love you" should fluster them,
   "you suck" should anger them, "I like your hat" should flatter them.
4. **No faces** — heads are blank skin boxes; expressions should be visible.

Items 3+4 unify naturally: the LLM emits a mood tag each reply, and the mood
renders as a facial expression on the model.

## Verified groundwork (done during planning)

- **Facing bug root cause**: `Renderer3D::drawNpc` rotates by `-facingDeg`,
  but rotation by `+f` about Y maps local +Z (the visor/front) to
  `(sin f, 0, cos f)` = `flatForward(f)`. The `-f` mirrors every NPC in X.
  Persona files are authored to the *documented* convention (librarian at
  (-36,0), library west, plaza east, `facing = 90` = +X toward plaza ✓), so
  the renderer sign is the bug and persona files stay untouched.
- **Model behavior with two tags** (tested against live qwen2.5:3b): emits
  mood tags reliably but sloppily — duplicates, tags at start/middle, unknown
  words ("annoyed"), occasional single brackets `[ACTION: wave]`, spurious
  actions. The parser must scan the whole reply, strip every directive
  wherever it appears, map synonyms, and take the **last** mood as final.

## Changes

### 1. `src/core/NpcAction.hpp` — generalize the tag parser
- Add `enum class NpcMood { Neutral, Happy, Angry, Sad, Embarrassed, Surprised }`.
- Add `NpcAction::CallPolice` to the action enum.
- New `struct Directives { NpcAction action; NpcMood mood; bool hasMood; }` and
  `Directives parseDirectives(std::string& reply)`:
  - Scans for every `[[KIND: keyword]]` **and** single-bracket `[KIND: keyword]`
    where KIND is `action`/`mood` (case-insensitive, whitespace-tolerant).
  - Strips **all** matched tags from the reply wherever they appear (start,
    middle, end — the model doesn't follow placement rules), collapsing
    doubled whitespace at the seams; unknown keywords are also stripped (so
    brackets never leak to the transcript) but map to None/no-mood.
  - Last mood tag wins. Synonym map: annoyed/irritated/frustrated→angry;
    flattered/pleased/excited/joyful→happy; flustered/awkward/shy→embarrassed;
    shocked/startled→surprised; upset/hurt→sad.
  - Action keyword `call_police` (also `call police`, `police`) → CallPolice.
- Keep `parseActionTag` as a thin wrapper (returns `.action`) so existing
  callers/tests survive; update the one test that expects unknown tags to be
  left in the text (they're now stripped — a display improvement).

### 2. Persona: police flag + persona-aware protocol + mood protocol
- `Persona` (src/core/Persona.hpp) gains `bool police = false`.
- `renderActionProtocol()` becomes non-static / takes the flag: police get the
  `[[ACTION: arrest]]` line; civilians instead get
  `[[ACTION: call_police]] - you call out for the police to come arrest the player`.
- Append a MOOD block: react like a real person (compliments flatter,
  insults sting, love declarations fluster, surprises startle — show it in
  your words), and ALWAYS end with exactly one `[[MOOD: …]]` tag from the
  six. Tighten ACTION wording: "most replies need NO action directive".
- `PersonaLoader.cpp`: parse new header key `police = true` (accept
  true/yes/1; loader errors on unknown keys today, so this is required).
- `personas/cop.persona`: add `police = true`.

### 3. `src/core/Npc.hpp` / `Npc.cpp` — moods, summoning, lookAt
- `onReplyArrived`: use `parseDirectives`; route action via `applyAction` as
  today; set `mood_` + `moodTimer_` (~25 s decay back to Neutral, ticked in
  `update()` like the gesture timer).
- `applyAction`: if `action == Arrest && !persona_.police` convert to
  CallPolice (the model sometimes disobeys). CallPolice sets `lastAction_`
  and triggers a Wave pose (visually flagging someone down); no movement
  behavior change for the caller.
- New public `void commandArrest()` (sets behavior to Arrest, clears catch
  latch) so the main loop can order police around, and
  `void lookAt(const Vec3&)` (public wrapper over `faceToward`).
- Accessor `NpcMood mood() const`.

### 4. Renderer — facing sign fix + faces
- `drawNpc`: `glRotatef(-npc.facingDeg, …)` → `glRotatef(npc.facingDeg, …)`.
  (One character; fixes "face me" mirroring AND every NPC's authored facing.)
- `NpcVisual` gains renderer-local `NpcFace` enum (mirrors NpcMood, same
  pattern as the existing NpcPose) — main.cpp maps mood→face.
- New private `drawFace(NpcFace)` called from `drawNpc` in the local frame:
  small `drawTexturedBox` quads proud of the head's front (+Z) face —
  - eyes: two dark boxes (bigger when Surprised),
  - brows: thin boxes, rotated inward for Angry / outward for Sad
    (glPushMatrix + glRotatef about Z, same pattern as drawArm),
  - mouth: thin box; raised corner boxes for Happy, lowered for Sad,
    small open square for Surprised,
  - blush: two pink boxes on the cheeks when Embarrassed.

### 5. `src/app/main.cpp` — wiring
- Reply-arrival block: stage directions for CallPolice ("calls for the
  police!"); after applying, if `npc.lastAction() == CallPolice`, loop the
  world's NPCs and `commandArrest()` every `persona().police` NPC (the cop
  visibly sprints over; the existing catch latch shows "caught you!").
- T-key talk handler: `npc.lookAt(camera.position)` so an NPC turns to you
  the moment you start talking ("they should face you if they aren't
  already").
- NPC draw loop: map `npc.mood()` → `NpcFace`, pass into `NpcVisual`.

### 6. Tests (auto-globbed by tests/Makefile)
- Extend `tests/test_npc_action.cpp`: parseDirectives strips tags anywhere
  (start/middle/adjacent), single-bracket form, last-mood-wins, synonym map,
  unknown keyword stripped → no mood/None action, call_police keyword.
- Extend `tests/test_npc_behavior.cpp`: civilian `arrest` converts to
  CallPolice (no chase) while a `police = true` persona keeps Arrest; mood set
  by reply and decays to Neutral via `update()`; `commandArrest()` makes a cop
  chase; `lookAt` turns without moving.
- Extend `tests/test_persona.cpp` / `test_persona_roster.cpp` patterns:
  loader parses `police = true`; prompt contains the arrest directive only
  for police personas, and always contains the MOOD block.

## Out of scope
- The pedestrian doesn't pathfind to the cop; the cop comes to you.
- Moods don't alter movement/voice — facial expression + prose only.
- The transient raw-tag flicker during streaming (pre-existing cosmetic nit).

## Verification
- `make -C tests test` — full offline suite.
- `cmake --build build -j`; relaunch the game (Ollama already up):
  - "face me" to a side-on NPC → turns *toward* you and tracks correctly.
  - Walk up + `T` → NPC turns to face you immediately.
  - To the baker: "arrest me!" → she refuses/calls police; the cop sprints
    over and "caught you!" appears. To the cop: "arrest me" → she chases.
  - "I love you" → embarrassed face (blush); "you suck" → angry brows;
    "I like your hat" → happy face. Watch the face change after each reply.
- Headless spot-check (same harness as /tmp/instr_check.cpp) to confirm tag
  hygiene with the real persona prompts before in-game testing.

## Commit
Single commit on `be_able_to_instruct_npcs` after /code-review:
`feat(npc): police-only arrests, moods with facial expressions, facing fix`
(no push, per repo rules).

# Plan: Police-only arrests, facing fix, moods + expressive faces

## Context

The NPC instruction feature (committed as `1b15976`) works, and play-testing
surfaced the next round of requests:
1. **Anyone can "arrest"** — only police should; civilians should instead
   summon the police to come arrest you.
2. **"Face me" turns NPCs the wrong way** — When they face me, they stay still and when I turn left, they turn right. they mirror the player's movement
   instead of tracking it.
3. **NPCs aren't emotionally reactive** — "I love you" should fluster them,
   "you suck" should anger them, "I like your hat" should flatter them.
4. **No faces** — heads are blank skin boxes; expressions should be visible.

Items 3+4 unify naturally: the LLM emits a mood tag each reply, and the mood
renders as a facial expression on the model.

## Verified groundwork (done during planning)

- **Facing bug root cause**: `Renderer3D::drawNpc` rotates by `-facingDeg`,
  but rotation by `+f` about Y maps local +Z (the visor/front) to
  `(sin f, 0, cos f)` = `flatForward(f)`. The `-f` mirrors every NPC in X.
  Persona files are authored to the *documented* convention (librarian at
  (-36,0), library west, plaza east, `facing = 90` = +X toward plaza ✓), so
  the renderer sign is the bug and persona files stay untouched.
- **Model behavior with two tags** (tested against live qwen2.5:3b): emits
  mood tags reliably but sloppily — duplicates, tags at start/middle, unknown
  words ("annoyed"), occasional single brackets `[ACTION: wave]`, spurious
  actions. The parser must scan the whole reply, strip every directive
  wherever it appears, map synonyms, and take the **last** mood as final.

## Changes

### 1. `src/core/NpcAction.hpp` — generalize the tag parser
- Add `enum class NpcMood { Neutral, Happy, Angry, Sad, Embarrassed, Surprised }`.
- Add `NpcAction::CallPolice` to the action enum.
- New `struct Directives { NpcAction action; NpcMood mood; bool hasMood; }` and
  `Directives parseDirectives(std::string& reply)`:
  - Scans for every `[[KIND: keyword]]` **and** single-bracket `[KIND: keyword]`
    where KIND is `action`/`mood` (case-insensitive, whitespace-tolerant).
  - Strips **all** matched tags from the reply wherever they appear (start,
    middle, end — the model doesn't follow placement rules), collapsing
    doubled whitespace at the seams; unknown keywords are also stripped (so
    brackets never leak to the transcript) but map to None/no-mood.
  - Last mood tag wins. Synonym map: annoyed/irritated/frustrated→angry;
    flattered/pleased/excited/joyful→happy; flustered/awkward/shy→embarrassed;
    shocked/startled→surprised; upset/hurt→sad.
  - Action keyword `call_police` (also `call police`, `police`) → CallPolice.
- Keep `parseActionTag` as a thin wrapper (returns `.action`) so existing
  callers/tests survive; update the one test that expects unknown tags to be
  left in the text (they're now stripped — a display improvement).

### 2. Persona: police flag + persona-aware protocol + mood protocol
- `Persona` (src/core/Persona.hpp) gains `bool police = false`.
- `renderActionProtocol()` becomes non-static / takes the flag: police get the
  `[[ACTION: arrest]]` line; civilians instead get
  `[[ACTION: call_police]] - you call out for the police to come arrest the player`.
- Append a MOOD block: react like a real person (compliments flatter,
  insults sting, love declarations fluster, surprises startle — show it in
  your words), and ALWAYS end with exactly one `[[MOOD: …]]` tag from the
  six. Tighten ACTION wording: "most replies need NO action directive".
- `PersonaLoader.cpp`: parse new header key `police = true` (accept
  true/yes/1; loader errors on unknown keys today, so this is required).
- `personas/cop.persona`: add `police = true`.

### 3. `src/core/Npc.hpp` / `Npc.cpp` — moods, summoning, lookAt

  today; set `mood_` + `moodTimer_` (~25 s decay back to Neutral, ticked in

# Plain-make test runner for the SFML-free core library.
#
# The dev container has g++/make but no cmake or SFML, so this Makefile is the
# primary way to build and run unit tests there. It compiles every
# src/core/*.cpp plus every tests/test_*.cpp into one doctest binary.
#
#   make -C tests test     # build + run all tests
#   make -C tests clean    # remove build artifacts

CXX      ?= g++
CXXFLAGS ?= -std=c++17 -g -O0 -pthread -Wall -Wextra
INCLUDES := -I../src/core -I../external -I.

BUILD  := build
TARGET := $(BUILD)/run_tests

CORE_SRCS := $(wildcard ../src/core/*.cpp)
TEST_SRCS := $(wildcard test_*.cpp)

CORE_OBJS := $(patsubst ../src/core/%.cpp,$(BUILD)/core_%.o,$(CORE_SRCS))
TEST_OBJS := $(patsubst %.cpp,$(BUILD)/%.o,$(TEST_SRCS))

.PHONY: test build clean

test: $(TARGET)
	./$(TARGET)

build: $(TARGET)

$(TARGET): $(CORE_OBJS) $(TEST_OBJS)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $^ -o $@

$(BUILD)/core_%.o: ../src/core/%.cpp | $(BUILD)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(INCLUDES) -c $< -o $@

$(BUILD)/%.o: %.cpp | $(BUILD)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(INCLUDES) -c $< -o $@

$(BUILD):
	mkdir -p $(BUILD)

clean:
	rm -rf $(BUILD)

content.text:
The game is up and focused — everything's in, across six commits, 75 tests passing, and the LLM behavior verified headlessly against the real prompts.

**What's new:**

1. **Faces** — every NPC has eyes, brows, and a mouth, and the expression follows their mood from the conversation: happy (raised mouth corners), angry (slanted brows), sad, embarrassed (cheek blush), surprised (wide eyes, open mouth). Moods fade back to neutral after ~25s.
2. **Emotional reactivity** — verified headlessly: *"I love you"* → flustered + embarrassed face; *"you suck"* → angry; *"I like your hat"* → happy. The prompt also teaches `*asterisk*` emotes — `*shouts loudly*` got an in-character warning from the baker.
3. **Police-only arrests** — only Officer Brooks (persona file says `police = true`) can arrest. Civilians who *would* arrest you instead **call for the police**: they wave for attention and every officer in the city sprints toward you. Enforced both in the prompt and in core code, so even if the model disobeys, a civilian can't chase you.
4. **Jail** — when an officer catches you, you're hauled to the police station and held 10 seconds (movement locked, countdown on screen, "disturbing the peace"); the officer walks back to their post afterward. Keep harassing a shopkeeper after a warning and this is where you end up.
5. **Facing fixed** — the renderer was mirroring all NPCs in X (one sign flip); "face me" now tracks you correctly, and NPCs turn to you the instant you press `T`.

**Try:** insult the baker and watch her face; shout at her twice and watch the cop come for you; then tell the cop "arrest me if you can" and lead her on a chase.

One quirk to expect from the 3B model: occasional stray bracketed text (like `[Moores]`) in replies — that's model noise, not the action system; the directive tags themselves are stripped reliably. Tell me how it plays!

Produce a Merge Request description for the current branch, comparing it to
its base branch. The output should be ready to paste directly into GitHub,
GitLab, or wherever I open the MR.

## Step 1 — Identify the Base
- Determine the base branch. Priority order:
  1. Use "" if given (e.g. `/mr-description develop`)
  2. Otherwise detect: `git merge-base` against `main`, `master`, or `develop`
     — whichever exists and gives a sensible diff
  3. If ambiguous, ask which base I want before continuing
- State which base you chose and which commit hash it resolves to.

## Step 2 — Gather the Facts
Run these and use their output (don't show me the raw output):
- `git log <base>..HEAD --pretty=format:"%h %s"`  (commit list)
- `git diff <base>..HEAD --stat`                   (file change summary)
- `git diff <base>..HEAD`                          (actual changes, for the why)
- Read the meaningfully-changed files yourself to understand purpose, not
  just lines moved.

## Step 3 — Produce the Description
Output exactly this structure, in Markdown, ready to paste:

```markdown
## Summary
[2-3 sentences: what this change accomplishes and why it exists.
Plain language, no jargon dump. Lead with the user-visible impact
or the problem being solved, not the implementation detail.]

## Changes by File

[For each meaningfully-changed file, a short section: the file path as a
bold heading with its change type, then a sentence or two underneath
explaining why it changed and what the change does.]

**`path/to/file.py`** — modified
Explanation of why this file changed and what the change accomplishes.
Can run to a second sentence if the change warrants it.

**`path/to/other.py`** — added
What this new file is for and why it was needed.

[Group trivial changes — formatting-only, generated files, lockfile updates
— at the end under a single heading like "**Minor / generated**" with a
one-line summary rather than a section each.]

## Why
[A short section explaining the reasoning behind the change. What problem
prompted it? What alternative approaches were considered or rejected?
What tradeoffs were accepted? This is the part future-you and reviewers
care about most. 1-2 short paragraphs.]

## Testing
[How was this verified? Tests added, tests run, manual checks, edge cases
exercised. If a test suite was run, give pass/fail numbers.]

## Risk and Rollback
[What's the blast radius if this breaks? How to revert?
Skip this section entirely for trivial changes — only include for changes
touching shared infrastructure, data models, auth, public APIs, or
anything else with meaningful blast radius.]

## Diagram
[INCLUDE ONLY WHEN IT GENUINELY HELPS. Apply this test:
- Does the change reorganize architecture, add a new flow between modules,
  introduce a state machine, or change how components communicate? → diagram
- Is it a bug fix, small refactor, doc update, config tweak, or single-file
  change? → no diagram, omit this section entirely

When included, use Mermaid. Pick the right type:
- flowchart  → for data or call flow between components
- sequenceDiagram  → for ordered interactions over time
- stateDiagram-v2  → for state transitions
- classDiagram  → for new type hierarchies

Show the "after" state, optionally with a brief "before" if the contrast
is the point of the change.]

## Checklist
- [ ] Tests pass locally
- [ ] No new linter or type-check errors
- [ ] Documentation updated (if user-facing)
- [ ] Breaking changes noted in description (if any)
[Add or remove items based on what this project actually cares about —
infer from CLAUDE.md and the repo's existing PR template if one exists
at .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md or similar.]
```

## Step 4 — Tone and Quality Rules
- Write for a reviewer who hasn't been in your head. They need to understand
  what changed and why, fast.
- Each file's explanation should answer "why this file?" not just restate
  the filename. "Updated parser.py" is useless. "Added short-form SCPI
  command support so MEAS works in addition to MEASure" is useful.
- The Summary should let someone decide in 10 seconds whether to keep reading.
- The Why section is where reviewers form opinions — be honest about
  tradeoffs. If you cut a corner, say so.
- Don't pad. If a section would be empty or trivial, omit it (except Summary,
  Changes by File, and Why, which are always required).
- If commit messages are good, draw on them; if they're sparse, infer purpose
  from the actual diff.

## Step 5 — Output
Print the description as a single fenced markdown block so I can copy it
cleanly. Don't print anything else after it — no "here's what I generated"
preamble or postamble — just the description, ready to paste.

Also save a copy to docs/walkthroughs/mr-<branch-name>-<date>.md as a record.

input.content:
## Summary

NPCs can now be *instructed* and *react emotionally*. Tell any resident to
follow you, wave, raise a hand, or face you and they'll actually do it; insult,
compliment, or surprise them and their words and face respond. Only police can
arrest — civilians instead flag down an officer, who chases you and hauls you
to the station for a short sentence. The character models gained arms and
expressive faces so all of this is visible in the world, and a long-standing
bug that mirrored every NPC's facing direction is fixed.

## Changes by File

**`src/core/NpcAction.hpp`** — added
The heart of the feature: defines the `NpcAction` vocabulary (follow, stop,
face, raise_hand, wave, arrest, call_police, plus internal return_home) and the
`NpcMood` set, and implements `parseDirectives()` — a tolerant parser that pulls
`[[ACTION: x]]` / `[[MOOD: y]]` tags out of an LLM reply. It copes with the mess
a small model actually emits: tags anywhere in the text, single- or
double-bracket forms, duplicates (last mood wins), and synonym words
(`annoyed`→angry, `flattered`→happy, …). All recognized-looking tags are
stripped so brackets never reach the on-screen transcript.

**`src/core/Persona.hpp`** — modified
Adds a `police` flag and rewrites the appended system-prompt protocol. The
prompt is now persona-aware (police get the `arrest` directive; everyone else
gets `call_police`), teaches the model to treat `*asterisk*` text as player
emotes, instructs warn-then-escalate handling of disruptive players, and
mandates a mood tag on every reply.

**`src/core/Npc.hpp` / `src/core/Npc.cpp`** — modified
NPCs gained world behavior. `onReplyArrived()` now parses directives and sets
movement behavior, a timed gesture pose, and a decaying mood. `update(dt,
playerPos, city)` ticks that behavior each frame — following/chasing via the
existing `City::resolveMovement` collision slide, facing the player, returning
home, and expiring gestures/moods. Adds `commandArrest()`, `commandReturnHome()`,
and `lookAt()` so the main loop can drive police, plus the police-gating rule
that converts a civilian's `arrest` into `call_police`.

**`src/core/PersonaLoader.cpp`** — modified
Parses the new `police = true` header key (required, since the loader rejects
unknown keys).

**`personas/cop.persona`** — modified
Marks Officer Dana Brooks as `police = true` — the only resident who can arrest.

**`src/app/Renderer3D.hpp` / `src/app/Renderer3D.cpp`** — modified
Fixes the facing bug (`glRotatef(-facing…)` → `glRotatef(facing…)`, which had
mirrored every NPC in X) and adds two new bits of geometry: arms that pivot at
the shoulder for raise-hand/wave poses, and a face (eyes, brows, mouth, blush)
whose shape follows the NPC's mood. `NpcVisual` carries the new pose and face
inputs.

**`src/app/main.cpp`** — modified
Wires it together: ticks every NPC each frame (frozen by the pause menu),
narrates actions as transcript stage directions (so a wordless tag-only reply
still reads), turns an NPC to face you when a chat opens, routes a `call_police`
summons to every officer, maps mood→face for rendering, and implements the
jail — on capture the player is teleported to the station, movement locks for
10s with an on-screen countdown, and the arresting officer walks back to post.

**`tests/test_npc_action.cpp` / `test_npc_behavior.cpp` / `test_persona.cpp`** — modified
Cover the new business logic: directive parsing (placement, bracket forms,
synonyms, stripping), follow/arrest/face/return-home movement convergence, mood
decay, civilian→call_police conversion, and the police-gated prompt.

### Minor / build
**`tests/Makefile`** — added `-MMD -MP` header-dependency tracking; an `Npc`
layout change had previously left stale objects that failed with ABI
mismatches.

## Why

The game's premise is live LLM characters, but until now they could only *talk*
— they were static props. Letting the model emit structured action/mood tags
turns conversation into behavior and expression without any new I/O: it rides
the existing chat round-trip. Tags are the right altitude because the model
already produces text; the work is making the parser robust to a 3B model's
sloppiness rather than assuming clean output.

Compliance is intentionally left to the model (a cop may arrest, a baker
refuses) so behavior stays in-character and emergent. The one place we *don't*
trust the model is authority: arrest is gated in code, not just in the prompt,
so a civilian can never chase the player even if the model emits the wrong tag —
they call the police instead. Faces and arms are deliberately simple textured
boxes (no asset pipeline, matching the existing procedural-geometry style)
because the goal is legible expression at a distance, not fidelity.

The facing fix shipped here because it was the same renderer code the gestures
touched, and the bug (every NPC mirrored in X) made "face me" turn the wrong
way — it was one sign flip against the documented coordinate convention.

## Testing

- `make -C tests test` — full offline suite: **75 test cases, 511 assertions,
  all passing** (1 skipped: the live-Ollama test). 22 of these are new.
- `cmake --build build -j` — clean build of the SFML/OpenGL game target.
- Headless end-to-end checks against the real local Ollama (qwen2.5:3b-instruct)
  with the real persona prompts confirmed in-character tag emission: "I love
  you"→embarrassed, "you suck"→angry, "I like your hat"→happy, `*shouts*`→an
  in-character warning, and police arrest gating.
- Manual in-game runs for the facing fix, gestures, faces, and the
  call-police→chase→jail flow.

## Risk and Rollback

Blast radius is contained to the NPC/dialogue/render layer; no save format,
network protocol, or build-system contract changes (the `tests/Makefile` tweak
is additive). The persona file format gained one optional key. The 7 commits
are independent and revert cleanly; the lowest-level dependency is
`NpcAction.hpp`, so reverting the whole branch is `git revert 1b15976..HEAD` or
simply not merging.

## Diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant M as main loop
    participant N as Npc
    participant L as LlmClient/Ollama
    P->>M: types "follow me" / "arrest me"
    M->>N: ask()
    N->>L: chat (persona prompt + protocol)
    L-->>N: reply with [[ACTION/MOOD]] tags
    N->>N: parseDirectives() → behavior, pose, mood
    Note over M,N: each frame: npc.update(dt, playerPos, city)
    N-->>M: position / facing / pose / mood
    M->>M: render arms + face; narrate stage direction
    alt civilian summons police
        M->>N: commandArrest() on every police NPC
        N-->>M: hasCaughtPlayer()
        M->>P: teleport to station, lock 10s, officer returns home
    end
```

## Checklist
- [x] Tests pass locally (75 cases / 511 assertions)

## Summary

NPCs can now be *instructed* and *react emotionally*. Tell any resident to
follow you, wave, raise a hand, or face you and they'll actually do it; insult,
compliment, or surprise them and their words and face respond. Only police can
arrest — civilians instead flag down an officer, who chases you and hauls you
to the station for a short sentence. The character models gained arms and
expressive faces so all of this is visible in the world, and a long-standing
bug that mirrored every NPC's facing direction is fixed.

## Changes by File

**`src/core/NpcAction.hpp`** — added
The heart of the feature: defines the `NpcAction` vocabulary (follow, stop,
face, raise_hand, wave, arrest, call_police, plus internal return_home) and the
`NpcMood` set, and implements `parseDirectives()` — a tolerant parser that pulls
`[[ACTION: x]]` / `[[MOOD: y]]` tags out of an LLM reply. It copes with the mess
a small model actually emits: tags anywhere in the text, single- or
double-bracket forms, duplicates (last mood wins), and synonym words
(`annoyed`→angry, `flattered`→happy, …). All recognized-looking tags are
stripped so brackets never reach the on-screen transcript.

**`src/core/Persona.hpp`** — modified
Adds a `police` flag and rewrites the appended system-prompt protocol. The
prompt is now persona-aware (police get the `arrest` directive; everyone else
gets `call_police`), teaches the model to treat `*asterisk*` text as player
emotes, instructs warn-then-escalate handling of disruptive players, and
mandates a mood tag on every reply.

**`src/core/Npc.hpp` / `src/core/Npc.cpp`** — modified
NPCs gained world behavior. `onReplyArrived()` now parses directives and sets
movement behavior, a timed gesture pose, and a decaying mood. `update(dt,
playerPos, city)` ticks that behavior each frame — following/chasing via the
existing `City::resolveMovement` collision slide, facing the player, returning
home, and expiring gestures/moods. Adds `commandArrest()`, `commandReturnHome()`,
and `lookAt()` so the main loop can drive police, plus the police-gating rule
that converts a civilian's `arrest` into `call_police`.

**`src/core/PersonaLoader.cpp`** — modified
Parses the new `police = true` header key (required, since the loader rejects
unknown keys).

**`personas/cop.persona`** — modified
Marks Officer Dana Brooks as `police = true` — the only resident who can arrest.

**`src/app/Renderer3D.hpp` / `src/app/Renderer3D.cpp`** — modified
Fixes the facing bug (`glRotatef(-facing…)` → `glRotatef(facing…)`, which had
mirrored every NPC in X) and adds two new bits of geometry: arms that pivot at
the shoulder for raise-hand/wave poses, and a face (eyes, brows, mouth, blush)
whose shape follows the NPC's mood. `NpcVisual` carries the new pose and face
inputs.

**`src/app/main.cpp`** — modified
Wires it together: ticks every NPC each frame (frozen by the pause menu),
narrates actions as transcript stage directions (so a wordless tag-only reply
still reads), turns an NPC to face you when a chat opens, routes a `call_police`
summons to every officer, maps mood→face for rendering, and implements the
jail — on capture the player is teleported to the station, movement locks for
10s with an on-screen countdown, and the arresting officer walks back to post.

**`tests/test_npc_action.cpp` / `test_npc_behavior.cpp` / `test_persona.cpp`** — modified
Cover the new business logic: directive parsing (placement, bracket forms,
synonyms, stripping), follow/arrest/face/return-home movement convergence, mood
decay, civilian→call_police conversion, and the police-gated prompt.

### Minor / build
**`tests/Makefile`** — added `-MMD -MP` header-dependency tracking; an `Npc`
layout change had previously left stale objects that failed with ABI
mismatches.

## Why

The game's premise is live LLM characters, but until now they could only *talk*
— they were static props. Letting the model emit structured action/mood tags
turns conversation into behavior and expression without any new I/O: it rides
the existing chat round-trip. Tags are the right altitude because the model
already produces text; the work is making the parser robust to a 3B model's
sloppiness rather than assuming clean output.

Compliance is intentionally left to the model (a cop may arrest, a baker
refuses) so behavior stays in-character and emergent. The one place we *don't*
trust the model is authority: arrest is gated in code, not just in the prompt,
so a civilian can never chase the player even if the model emits the wrong tag —
they call the police instead. Faces and arms are deliberately simple textured
boxes (no asset pipeline, matching the existing procedural-geometry style)
because the goal is legible expression at a distance, not fidelity.

The facing fix shipped here because it was the same renderer code the gestures
touched, and the bug (every NPC mirrored in X) made "face me" turn the wrong
way — it was one sign flip against the documented coordinate convention.

## Testing

- `make -C tests test` — full offline suite: **75 test cases, 511 assertions,
  all passing** (1 skipped: the live-Ollama test). 22 of these are new.
- `cmake --build build -j` — clean build of the SFML/OpenGL game target.
- Headless end-to-end checks against the real local Ollama (qwen2.5:3b-instruct)
  with the real persona prompts confirmed in-character tag emission: "I love
  you"→embarrassed, "you suck"→angry, "I like your hat"→happy, `*shouts*`→an
  in-character warning, and police arrest gating.
- Manual in-game runs for the facing fix, gestures, faces, and the
  call-police→chase→jail flow.

## Risk and Rollback

Blast radius is contained to the NPC/dialogue/render layer; no save format,
network protocol, or build-system contract changes (the `tests/Makefile` tweak
is additive). The persona file format gained one optional key. The 7 commits
are independent and revert cleanly; the lowest-level dependency is
`NpcAction.hpp`, so reverting the whole branch is `git revert 1b15976..HEAD` or
simply not merging.

## Diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant M as main loop
    participant N as Npc
    participant L as LlmClient/Ollama
    P->>M: types "follow me" / "arrest me"
    M->>N: ask()
    N->>L: chat (persona prompt + protocol)
    L-->>N: reply with [[ACTION/MOOD]] tags
    N->>N: parseDirectives() → behavior, pose, mood
    Note over M,N: each frame: npc.update(dt, playerPos, city)
    N-->>M: position / facing / pose / mood
    M->>M: render arms + face; narrate stage direction
    alt civilian summons police
        M->>N: commandArrest() on every police NPC
        N-->>M: hasCaughtPlayer()
        M->>P: teleport to station, lock 10s, officer returns home
    end
```

## Checklist
- [x] Tests pass locally (75 cases / 511 assertions)
- [x] No new compiler errors (clean cmake build)
- [x] Player-facing behavior documented in this description
- [ ] No breaking changes (persona format gained one optional key — non-breaking)

## Summary

NPCs can now be *instructed* and *react emotionally*. Tell any resident to
follow you, wave, raise a hand, or face you and they'll actually do it; insult,
compliment, or surprise them and their words and face respond. Only police can
arrest — civilians instead flag down an officer, who chases you and hauls you
to the station for a short sentence. The character models gained arms and
expressive faces so all of this is visible in the world, and a long-standing
bug that mirrored every NPC's facing direction is fixed.

## Changes by File

**`src/core/NpcAction.hpp`** — added
The heart of the feature: defines the `NpcAction` vocabulary (follow, stop,
face, raise_hand, wave, arrest, call_police, plus internal return_home) and the
`NpcMood` set, and implements `parseDirectives()` — a tolerant parser that pulls
`[[ACTION: x]]` / `[[MOOD: y]]` tags out of an LLM reply. It copes with the mess
a small model actually emits: tags anywhere in the text, single- or
double-bracket forms, duplicates (last mood wins), and synonym words
(`annoyed`→angry, `flattered`→happy, …). All recognized-looking tags are
stripped so brackets never reach the on-screen transcript.

**`src/core/Persona.hpp`** — modified
Adds a `police` flag and rewrites the appended system-prompt protocol. The
prompt is now persona-aware (police get the `arrest` directive; everyone else
gets `call_police`), teaches the model to treat `*asterisk*` text as player
emotes, instructs warn-then-escalate handling of disruptive players, and
mandates a mood tag on every reply.

**`src/core/Npc.hpp` / `src/core/Npc.cpp`** — modified
NPCs gained world behavior. `onReplyArrived()` now parses directives and sets
movement behavior, a timed gesture pose, and a decaying mood. `update(dt,
playerPos, city)` ticks that behavior each frame — following/chasing via the
existing `City::resolveMovement` collision slide, facing the player, returning
home, and expiring gestures/moods. Adds `commandArrest()`, `commandReturnHome()`,
and `lookAt()` so the main loop can drive police, plus the police-gating rule
that converts a civilian's `arrest` into `call_police`.

**`src/core/PersonaLoader.cpp`** — modified
Parses the new `police = true` header key (required, since the loader rejects
unknown keys).

**`personas/cop.persona`** — modified
Marks Officer Dana Brooks as `police = true` — the only resident who can arrest.

**`src/app/Renderer3D.hpp` / `src/app/Renderer3D.cpp`** — modified
Fixes the facing bug (`glRotatef(-facing…)` → `glRotatef(facing…)`, which had
mirrored every NPC in X) and adds two new bits of geometry: arms that pivot at
the shoulder for raise-hand/wave poses, and a face (eyes, brows, mouth, blush)
whose shape follows the NPC's mood. `NpcVisual` carries the new pose and face
inputs.

**`src/app/main.cpp`** — modified
Wires it together: ticks every NPC each frame (frozen by the pause menu),
narrates actions as transcript stage directions (so a wordless tag-only reply
still reads), turns an NPC to face you when a chat opens, routes a `call_police`
summons to every officer, maps mood→face for rendering, and implements the
jail — on capture the player is teleported to the station, movement locks for
10s with an on-screen countdown, and the arresting officer walks back to post.

**`tests/test_npc_action.cpp` / `test_npc_behavior.cpp` / `test_persona.cpp`** — modified
Cover the new business logic: directive parsing (placement, bracket forms,
synonyms, stripping), follow/arrest/face/return-home movement convergence, mood
decay, civilian→call_police conversion, and the police-gated prompt.

### Minor / build
**`tests/Makefile`** — added `-MMD -MP` header-dependency tracking; an `Npc`
layout change had previously left stale objects that failed with ABI
mismatches.

## Why

The game's premise is live LLM characters, but until now they could only *talk*
— they were static props. Letting the model emit structured action/mood tags
turns conversation into behavior and expression without any new I/O: it rides
the existing chat round-trip. Tags are the right altitude because the model
already produces text; the work is making the parser robust to a 3B model's
sloppiness rather than assuming clean output.

Compliance is intentionally left to the model (a cop may arrest, a baker
refuses) so behavior stays in-character and emergent. The one place we *don't*
trust the model is authority: arrest is gated in code, not just in the prompt,
so a civilian can never chase the player even if the model emits the wrong tag —
they call the police instead. Faces and arms are deliberately simple textured
boxes (no asset pipeline, matching the existing procedural-geometry style)
because the goal is legible expression at a distance, not fidelity.

The facing fix shipped here because it was the same renderer code the gestures
touched, and the bug (every NPC mirrored in X) made "face me" turn the wrong
way — it was one sign flip against the documented coordinate convention.

## Testing

- `make -C tests test` — full offline suite: **75 test cases, 511 assertions,
  all passing** (1 skipped: the live-Ollama test). 22 of these are new.
- `cmake --build build -j` — clean build of the SFML/OpenGL game target.
- Headless end-to-end checks against the real local Ollama (qwen2.5:3b-instruct)
  with the real persona prompts confirmed in-character tag emission: "I love
  you"→embarrassed, "you suck"→angry, "I like your hat"→happy, `*shouts*`→an
  in-character warning, and police arrest gating.
- Manual in-game runs for the facing fix, gestures, faces, and the
  call-police→chase→jail flow.

## Risk and Rollback

Blast radius is contained to the NPC/dialogue/render layer; no save format,
network protocol, or build-system contract changes (the `tests/Makefile` tweak
is additive). The persona file format gained one optional key. The 7 commits
are independent and revert cleanly; the lowest-level dependency is
`NpcAction.hpp`, so reverting the whole branch is `git revert 1b15976..HEAD` or
simply not merging.

    participant N as Npc
    participant L as LlmClient/Ollama
    P->>M: types "follow me" / "arrest me"

        M->>P: teleport to station, lock 10s, officer returns home
    end
```
