# Plan: A bigger, livelier city — better characters, traffic, crowds, real punishments

## Context

The player wants the world to feel less blocky and more alive. Five asks,
scoped against the engine's hard ceiling (legacy **OpenGL 2.1 fixed-function**,
100% procedural geometry, no asset/shader pipeline — so literal Fortnite/GTA
fidelity is out; the agreed target is a strong *stylized procedural* step up):

1. **Better characters** — push procedural humanoids hard (no new deps).
2. **Graduated punishments** — `*shoots someone*` must be punished harder than
   "disturbing the peace"; several tiers, not one flat 10s jail.
3. **Bigger map + more buildings** and **cars**.
4. **More people** — a larger crowd that wanders (chosen over streaming
   spawn/despawn, so NPC lifetimes stay stable and simple).
5. **Cars** — **full driving traffic** (chosen): cars follow the street grid,
   stop/turn, and the player collides with them.

Locked decisions (from clarifying Q&A):
- Characters: **procedural overhaul, no new dependencies.**
- Crowd: **fixed larger wandering crowd at startup** (not streaming).
- Cars: **full driving traffic** (lane-following + intersection stops +
  look-ahead braking + player collision — not free-form A* pathfinding).

Constraints (CLAUDE.md): no placeholders/TODOs; comment every public function;
match naming; **tests required for new business logic** (all new core logic is
SFML-free and unit-tested with doctest; the renderer stays untested as before).
Work on a feature branch, incremental `type(scope): description` commits, build
+ `make -C tests test` green after each, inline review before each commit. No
push (user handles pushes).

Suggested branch: `6-bigger-livelier-city` (current branch `5-detail-the-town`
holds the finished visual pass).

---

## Phase 1 — Procedural character overhaul  `feat(render): articulated characters with per-NPC variety`

Goal: replace today's capsule figure (`Renderer3D::drawNpc`, src/app/Renderer3D.cpp:747)
with an articulated, varied humanoid.

- **Per-NPC appearance.** Add a small `NpcAppearance` struct (skin tone, hair
  color/style id, shirt + pants colors, height/build scale) to
  `Renderer3D.hpp`'s `NpcVisual`. Derive it deterministically from a per-NPC
  seed so a given NPC always looks the same. Source the seed from the NPC
  (add `std::uint32_t appearanceSeed()` to `Npc`, set at construction); the
  fixed shopkeeper palettes (`kNpcPalettes`) remain available so police read
  blue and named shops keep recognizable colors.
- **Articulated body in `drawNpc`.** Rebuild from smooth parts: pelvis, two
  upper+lower legs with a knee bend and simple **shoes**, a tapered torso,
  chest/collar accent, neck, sphere head + varied hair cap, and arms rebuilt in
  `drawArm` as upper arm + forearm (elbow) + a small **hand**. Reuse existing
  `drawSphere`/`drawTaperedCylinder`/`drawBlobShadow` (Renderer3D.cpp:182-260).
- **Walk cycle.** Add an optional `locomotionPhase` to `NpcVisual`; swing
  legs/arms when the NPC is moving. Feed it from a phase the `Npc` accumulates
  while its position changes (so wanderers and followers visibly walk). Keep
  the existing raise/wave pose logic.
- **LOD + culling** (also serves Phases 4-5): skip `drawNpc` beyond a cull
  radius, and drop sphere/cylinder segment counts for distant NPCs so a crowd
  stays cheap. Add the cull check in the render loop (main.cpp:458).

Files: `src/app/Renderer3D.cpp`, `src/app/Renderer3D.hpp`, `src/app/main.cpp`,
`src/core/Npc.hpp/.cpp` (seed + locomotion phase accessor).
Tests: none for geometry (renderer is untested by design); the seed/phase
accessors are trivial.

## Phase 2 — Graduated punishments  `feat(law): offense severity tiers and sentences`

Goal: the punishment scales with the crime; `*shoots*` ≫ shouting.

- **New core `Offense.hpp/.cpp`** (SFML-free, unit-tested): a `Charge` enum
  (e.g. `None, DisturbingPeace, Theft, Assault, ArmedViolence`), a table mapping
  each to a sentence (jail seconds + HUD label + whether it triggers a
  city-wide manhunt), and `classifyPlayerAction(const std::string& text)` that
  scans the player's line/`*action*` for keywords (gun/shoot/kill → ArmedViolence;
  hit/punch/stab/attack → Assault; steal/rob/loot → Theft; shout/threaten/curse
  → DisturbingPeace; else None). This is the deterministic floor.
- **LLM may escalate, never invent silently.** Officers already decide arrests
  in-character via `[[ACTION: arrest]]`. Add an optional `[[CHARGE: x]]` tag the
  officer can emit, parsed in `parseDirectives` (NpcAction.hpp) into
  `Directives.charge`. Final charge = max(classifier floor, LLM charge) — same
  defense-in-depth shape as the existing civilian-arrest→call_police guard
  (Npc.cpp:69). Update `Persona::renderActionProtocol` to mention serious crimes
  warrant immediate arrest + a charge.
- **Wire into main.cpp.** Track the player's current charge (max severity since
  last release), updated when they submit a line. On catch (`hasCaughtPlayer`,
  main.cpp:388), set `jailSecondsLeft` from the charge's sentence and show the
  charge-specific HUD message (replaces the hardcoded "disturbing the peace",
  main.cpp:494). ArmedViolence → **manhunt**: every officer `commandArrest()`s
  (reuse main.cpp:441-444), and a longer sentence.
- **Punishment variety:** warning (no detention) for None; escalating jail by
  tier; manhunt for the top tier.

Files: new `src/core/Offense.hpp/.cpp`, `src/core/NpcAction.hpp` (charge tag),
`src/core/Persona.hpp`, `src/app/main.cpp`, `CMakeLists.txt` + `tests/Makefile`
pick up the new core file automatically (globbed).
Tests: new `tests/test_offense.cpp` — classifier keywords, max-severity merge,
sentence table, manhunt flag.

## Phase 3 — Bigger map + more buildings  `feat(city): larger downtown grid with more blocks`

Goal: more world, denser detail, and the lane skeleton traffic needs.

- Grow `City::makeDowntown` (src/core/City.cpp:69) from 3×3 to ~**5×5 blocks**
  on the same 64-unit pitch; raise `halfSize_` accordingly (~170-200). Keep the
  plaza center and park; add residential/office/mixed filler with varied
  heights and a few new enterable shops if cheap, plus more street props
  (lamps/trees/benches/parked cars as scenery).
- Record the **street grid** (the 16-unit gaps between blocks) as data the
  traffic system reads in Phase 5 — expose lane centerlines from the block
  pitch rather than hand-listing them.
- Keep collision correct: `rebuildCollision` already handles solid vs. hollow.

Files: `src/core/City.cpp`, possibly `src/core/City.hpp` (a helper exposing the
block grid / street centerlines).
Tests: extend `tests/test_city.cpp` — new bounds, shops still enterable/hollow,
holding cell intact, world-bounds invariant for the larger map.

## Phase 4 — Wandering crowd  `feat(npc): procedural pedestrians that wander`

Goal: many more talkable people, some of them arrestable cops.

- **New core `PersonaFactory.hpp/.cpp`** (SFML-free, unit-tested): builds a
  `Persona` from seeded pools (first/last name, role like jogger/tourist/student/
  commuter, 2-3 traits, speaking style, knowledge boundary) with a configurable
  probability of `police = true`. Returns the same `Persona` struct the loader
  produces, so `Npc` is unchanged.
- **Wander behavior.** Add `NpcAction::Wander` (not LLM-emittable; an ambient
  default). In `Npc::update` (Npc.cpp:109): pick a random nearby reachable goal,
  walk via `city.resolveMovement`, pause, repeat; turn to face travel. Talking/
  instructing overrides it (Follow/Stop/Face/Arrest); reuse existing routing.
- **Spawn at startup** in main.cpp after the file roster (main.cpp:224-231):
  generate N pedestrians (start ~25-40, tunable) at valid non-colliding
  positions spread across the bigger map, `behavior_ = Wander`. They share the
  one `LlmClient` (LLM only fires when talked to). Crowd count is fixed → NPC
  indices stay stable, so `pendingRoutes`/`wasCaught`/`session.npcIndex()` keep
  working unchanged.
- Relies on Phase 1 culling/LOD for framerate.

Files: new `src/core/PersonaFactory.hpp/.cpp`, `src/core/NpcAction.hpp`
(Wander), `src/core/Npc.cpp` (wander update), `src/app/main.cpp` (spawn loop).
Tests: new `tests/test_persona_factory.cpp` (determinism, police probability
bounds, required fields); extend `tests/test_npc_behavior.cpp` (wander stays in
bounds, avoids obstacles, instructions override and the NPC doesn't auto-resume
into walls).

## Phase 5 — Driving traffic  `feat(traffic): cars that drive the street grid`

Goal: cars that actually drive, stop, turn, and block the player.

- **New core `Traffic.hpp/.cpp`** (SFML-free, unit-tested): a road network of
  lane centerlines built from the Phase-3 block grid; `Vehicle{pos, headingDeg,
  speed, lane, t}`; `Traffic::update(dt, playerPos)` advances each car along its
  lane, **brakes** when a player/another car is within a look-ahead box,
  **stops** at intersections to avoid cross-traffic, and **turns** by choosing a
  connected lane at the end of a segment. Deterministic, seedable.
- **Player ↔ car collision** in main.cpp: after the static-city movement
  resolve, reject the step if it lands in a car footprint (cars are solid moving
  obstacles); cars brake for the player rather than shoving them. Keep simple
  and safe (no ragdoll/damage).
- **Render** `drawCar` in Renderer3D (rounded body, cabin, wheels, headlights/
  taillights, blob shadow) and a render+update call in the main loop. A few
  parked cars from Phase 3 stay as static scenery.

Files: new `src/core/Traffic.hpp/.cpp`, `src/app/Renderer3D.cpp/.hpp`
(`drawCar`), `src/app/main.cpp` (update + render + player collision).
Tests: new `tests/test_traffic.cpp` — cars stay on lanes/in bounds, brake when
something is ahead, stop at intersections, don't overlap the player.

---

## Performance
Immediate-mode draw cost scales with NPC + car count. Mitigations: distance
cull + segment-count LOD for NPCs (Phase 1), cap crowd/car counts (tunable
constants), and keep per-frame core updates O(n) with small n. Target: smooth
on the bigger map with the full crowd + traffic.

## Risks / honest notes
- **Look ceiling:** this is stylized-procedural, a clear step up from capsules —
  not Fortnite-quality authored characters. Stated up front.
- **Traffic is the riskiest piece** (most moving parts, easiest to look buggy);
  kept tractable as lane-follow + look-ahead brake + intersection stop, not full
  pathfinding. Built core-first and unit-tested so behavior is verifiable
  headlessly before it's ever rendered.
- All new logic is SFML-free core → unit-tested; only geometry/rendering is
  eyeballed (as today — I can't screenshot the GL window here, so you verify
  visuals and I tune the named constants).

## Out of scope
No shaders/asset pipeline/authored models; no streaming chunk spawn/despawn
(fixed crowd chosen); no vehicle damage/driving-by-player; no new third-party
dependencies.

## Verification (each phase)
- `cmake --build build -j` clean; `make -C tests test` green (suite grows with
  the new core tests).
- Launch and check that phase live: articulated varied people who walk;
  `*shoots a civilian*` → manhunt + a long, correctly-labeled sentence while a
  `*shouts*` → short/none; a visibly bigger city; a wandering crowd you can walk
  up to and talk to (some are cops who can arrest you); cars driving the grid,
  stopping/turning, and blocking you.
- Inline syntax/perf review before each commit; `/code-review` at the end.

# Plain-make test runner for the SFML-free core library.
#
# The dev container has g++/make but no cmake or SFML, so this Makefile is the
# primary way to build and run unit tests there. It compiles every
# src/core/*.cpp plus every tests/test_*.cpp into one doctest binary.
#
#   make -C tests test     # build + run all tests
#   make -C tests clean    # remove build artifacts

CXX      ?= g++
CXXFLAGS ?= -std=c++17 -g -O0 -pthread -Wall -Wextra
INCLUDES := -I../src/core -I../external -I.

BUILD  := build
TARGET := $(BUILD)/run_tests

CORE_SRCS := $(wildcard ../src/core/*.cpp)
TEST_SRCS := $(wildcard test_*.cpp)

CORE_OBJS := $(patsubst ../src/core/%.cpp,$(BUILD)/core_%.o,$(CORE_SRCS))
TEST_OBJS := $(patsubst %.cpp,$(BUILD)/%.o,$(TEST_SRCS))

.PHONY: test build clean

test: $(TARGET)
	./$(TARGET)

build: $(TARGET)

$(TARGET): $(CORE_OBJS) $(TEST_OBJS)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $^ -o $@

# -MMD -MP emits .d header-dependency files next to each object so editing a
# header (e.g. changing the Npc class layout) recompiles every dependent
# object instead of leaving stale, ABI-mismatched ones behind.
$(BUILD)/core_%.o: ../src/core/%.cpp | $(BUILD)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(INCLUDES) -MMD -MP -c $< -o $@

$(BUILD)/%.o: %.cpp | $(BUILD)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(INCLUDES) -MMD -MP -c $< -o $@

-include $(wildcard $(BUILD)/*.d)

$(BUILD):
	mkdir -p $(BUILD)

clean:
	rm -rf $(BUILD)

Let me scope the classifier to asterisk segments only — plain speech is never chargeable.

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of the topic:

## Fixed Timestep vs Variable Delta Time

A fixed delta time game loop breaks up elapsed time into smaller chunks and applies changes iteratively, allowing predictable and controlled movement. In contrast, the variable delta time game loop progresses the game in terms of time elapsed instead of frames.

However, variable game loops introduce unpredictability in time between frames, which often leads to unexpected gameplay.

## The "Spiral of Death"

The spiral of death occurs when your physics simulation can't keep up with the steps it's asked to take—if it takes Y seconds of real time to simulate X seconds of physics where Y > X, the simulation falls behind over time.

The accumulator grows, you run more steps to catch up which takes longer, putting you further behind, until the game freezes and stops responding.

## Best Practice Solutions

You need to ensure it takes significantly less than X seconds of real time to update X seconds of physics simulation, allowing your physics engine to "catch up" from temporary spikes.

A sanity check can be added to the update loop to limit the number of update steps executed, with a panic function to handle edge cases.

If the game falls behind by more than a quarter second, accepting the slowdown rather than crashing (showing slow motion instead) is preferable to an unresponsive window.

This project is a **hand-rolled engine** — variable timestep, vsync-capped, with that clamp — so I can teach the real thing from their own loop. Writing the lesson:

input.content:
Lesson 0002
0%

Game Engines & the Game Loop

cpp_game_with_llm_npcs · lesson 0002 · builds on 0001 (how to run & develop)
Why this matters for your project: you didn't import Unity or Unreal — you built a small game engine by hand. The thing that ties your renderer, your NPCs, your traffic, and your collision together into a running game is one loop in main.cpp. Understanding it as "an engine" is what lets you add the next system (birds? weather? a day/night cycle?) without guessing where it goes.
poll input → update(dt) → render → repeat ↺

1 What a game engine actually is

A game engine is the reusable machinery that sits beneath a specific game. It is not the game's story, levels, or rules — it's the substrate that makes any game of its kind possible. Strip away the LLM NPCs and the city, and what remains is engine:

Engine subsystemIts jobIn your repo
Game loopRun forever: read input, advance the world, draw itmain.cpp while(window.isOpen())
RendererTurn world state into pixelsRenderer3D
World / entitiesHold and simulate the things in the worldWorld, Npc, Traffic
CollisionStop things passing through each otherCity::resolveMovement
InputTranslate device events into intentInputMap, KeyBindings
TimeMeasure how much real time a frame tooksf::Clock frameClock

Commercial engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot) bundle these plus an editor, an asset pipeline, and a physics library. Yours is hand-rolled on SFML (window/input) + OpenGL (drawing): smaller, fully yours, no editor — but the same anatomy. Knowing the anatomy is the transferable skill.

2 The loop, in 12 lines

Every real-time game is this shape. The three phases never blur together: gather input, advance the simulation by the elapsed time, then draw a snapshot.

// The universal real-time game loop.
while (running) {
    float dt = clock.restart();        // (A) TIME: real seconds since last frame

    for (Event e : pollEvents())     // (B) INPUT: drain the OS event queue
        handle(e);

    world.update(dt);                 // (C) UPDATE: advance state by dt — the simulation

    renderer.draw(world);             // (D) RENDER: read state, paint pixels (changes nothing)
    window.display();                // (E) PRESENT: show the finished frame
}

The subtle star is dt. Multiply every movement by it (pos += speed * dt) and your game runs the same real-world speed whether the machine renders 30 or 144 frames per second. Forget it (pos += speed) and the game literally runs faster on faster computers.

3 Your actual loop, walked through

src/app/main.cpp 
327  sf::Clock frameClock;
328  while (window.isOpen()) {                          // the loop runs until the window closes
330      while (window.pollEvent(event)) { ... }         // (B) INPUT: keys, mouse, close, focus
        ...
406      const float dt = std::min(0.03f, frameClock.restart().asSeconds());  // (A) TIME
        ...
408      if (mode == AppMode::Playing) { ... move the player by dt ... }   // (C) UPDATE: you
382      for (Npc& npc : world.npcs()) npc.update(dt, camera.position, city);  // (C) UPDATE: NPCs
        traffic.update(dt, camera.position);                  // (C) UPDATE: cars
        ...
544      renderer.beginFrame(window, camera);                // (D) RENDER begins
545      renderer.drawCity(world.city());
        ... drawNpc(...) for each NPC, drawCar(...) for each car ...
617      window.display();                                  // (E) PRESENT the frame
  }

Three things worth noticing in your code:

  • Update and render are strictly separate. npc.update(dt,…) changes where an NPC is; drawNpc(…) only reads that position and paints it. The renderer never decides an arrest or moves a car — it's a camera, not a brain. That separation is why your whole core/ library can be unit-tested with no window at all.
  • dt drives the simulation. Cars (kNpcWander * dt), the walk-cycle phase, mood/gesture timers — all scale by dt, so the city moves at a consistent speed regardless of frame rate.
  • That std::min(0.03f, …) is a safety clamp. If the game stalls (you opened the pause menu, the OS hitched, the window lost focus), the next frame's real dt could be seconds. Feeding that raw into update would teleport every car a city-block and let the player tunnel through a wall. Clamping to 0.03 s (~33 ms) caps the biggest step the world can take — the game briefly runs in slow-motion instead of exploding.

The engine/platform boundary is real and visible here: everything that updates lives in the SFML-free src/core/ library; everything that draws or talks to the OS lives in src/app/ (main.cpp, Renderer3D). That line is why your tests build without SFML at all.

4 Often confused with…

Update vs. Render

Both run every frame, so they feel like one thing. They are not.

Update mutates the world by dt (move NPCs, advance timers, resolve collisions). Render only reads the world and draws it — it must change nothing.

Keep them separate and you can test update logic headlessly and swap the renderer freely. Blur them (game logic inside drawNpc) and the world only advances when it's visible — a classic bug.

Variable vs. Fixed timestep

Your loop uses a variable timestep: each frame advances by however much real time passed (clamped to 0.03 s), capped near 60 FPS by vsync. Simple, and fine for this game.

A fixed timestep instead advances the simulation in constant slices (say 1/60 s), running the update 0, 1, or several times per frame from an accumulator. It's what physics-heavy or networked games use because identical steps are deterministic and stable.

The danger a fixed loop must guard against is the spiral of death: if simulating one step takes longer than the step represents, you queue ever more steps and freeze. Your variable+clamp approach sidesteps it by simply taking one bounded step per frame.

And: engine vs. game. The engine is the loop, renderer, world model, and collision — reusable for any city game. The game is the specific content: LLM personas, the arrest rules, the downtown map. You could keep the engine and build a totally different game on it.

5 Practice — instant feedback

Options are shuffled on every open; there's no "always the first one." Click to answer.

In this game's loop, what is dt?

  • Real seconds elapsed since the previous frame, used to scale movement.
  • A fixed 1/60 s applied every frame regardless of timing.
  • A running count of frames rendered this session.
  • How long the LLM took to reply this turn.

Why is dt wrapped in std::min(0.03f, …)?

  • To force the game to run at exactly 30 FPS.
  • To cap the simulation step after a stall so nothing teleports or tunnels.
  • To make the NPCs move faster.
  • To round dt and avoid floating-point error.

Which line is doing the render step, not the update step?

  • npc.update(dt, camera.position, city)
  • traffic.update(dt, camera.position)
  • renderer.drawCar(pos, heading, colorId)
  • city.resolveMovement(from, to, r)

There's no Unity or Unreal here. In what sense is this still a game engine?

  • It isn't — only software with a visual editor is an engine.
  • It provides the reusable machinery (loop, renderer, world, input, collision) beneath the content.
  • It only becomes an engine once it ships to players.
  • It's just a script, not an engine at all.

Where does the engine/platform boundary live in this repo?

  • Between the SFML-free core/ library and the app/ layer that needs SFML/OpenGL.
  • Nowhere — every file includes SFML.
  • Renderer3D holds the rules; main.cpp only draws.
  • Between header files and source files.

Score: 0 / 5

6 Check your understanding (scenarios)

Scenario 1. You alt-tab away for 8 seconds, then return. The next frame's raw elapsed time is ~8 s. Without the clamp, what happens to the cars and the player — and why does the clamp fix it?

Each car would move speed × 8 units in one step — hundreds of units, leaping across (and through) the map; collision, which only checks the start and end of a step, could be skipped entirely, so the player could tunnel through a wall. std::min(0.03f, dt) caps that one step to ~33 ms of movement, so the world advances a normal amount and just appears to have paused.

Scenario 2. You want to add flocking birds. Which loop phases must you touch, and which stays exactly as-is?

Add a Birds system in core/ with a birds.update(dt, …) call in the UPDATE phase, and a drawBird(…) call in the RENDER phase. INPUT, TIME, and PRESENT are untouched — that's the payoff of a clean loop: new systems plug into two well-known slots.

Scenario 3. Why is it deliberate that Renderer3D contains no game rules — that it can't, say, decide an arrest?

Because render must be a pure read of world state. Keeping rules out of it means the simulation (in core/) is testable without a GPU, the renderer can be rewritten or replaced without touching gameplay, and the world advances identically whether or not anything is on screen.

## What's in it

A lesson on **game engines through the lens of your own code** — because you didn't import Unity, you *built* a micro-engine, and the thing tying it all together is one loop in `main.cpp`.

# Plan: Law fix, weapons, money & shops, and car↔pedestrian physics

## Context

Four interlocking requests after the "bigger, livelier city" work shipped:

1. **BUG — cops re-arrest forever.** After an arrest + release, police keep hunting
   the player. Cause: armed-violence (and `call_police`) triggers a **manhunt**
   that mobilizes *every* officer via `commandArrest()`, but on capture only the
   *catching* officer stands down (`commandReturnHome()`); the rest stay in
   `Arrest` and immediately re-catch the player at the release spot.
2. **Weapons** the player can carry and use on NPCs.
3. **Cars must affect NPCs** — pedestrians shouldn't obliviously walk in front of
   (or through) cars; treat them like real people.
4. **Money + a bank + shops** — withdraw infinite cash at a bank, see money in the
   HUD, buy things from shopkeepers.

These connect: the bank gives money → money buys weapons from shops → weapons used
on NPCs knock them down and trip the existing law system → cars and weapons share
one "knocked-down" state.

**Locked decisions (from Q&A):**
- Weapons: **fists + bat + pistol.** Number keys 1/2/3 select (only if owned),
  left-click attacks. Fists/bat = short frontal melee; pistol = hitscan along the
  camera ray. Infinite ammo for now.
- On attack (weapon **or** car): NPC is **knocked down and stays down** — an
  incapacitated body that stops wandering/talking but is **never deleted**. This is
  critical: deletion would shift the `world.npcs()` indices that `pendingRoutes`,
  `wasCaught`, and `session.npcIndex()` depend on. A downed flag keeps indices stable.

**Constraints (CLAUDE.md):** all new logic is SFML-free core with doctest tests;
renderer is eyeballed. Feature branch `7-weapons-money-and-mayhem`, incremental
`type(scope): description` commits, build + `make -C tests test` green after each,
inline review before each commit. No push (user's call).

---

## Phase 1 — Fix re-arrest after release  `fix(law): stand down all police on arrest`

In the capture handler in `src/app/main.cpp` (the `caughtNow && !wasCaught[i] &&
npc.persona().police` branch): instead of only the catcher's
`npc.commandReturnHome()`, loop **every** police officer and `commandReturnHome()`
them, and set `manhuntActive = false`. The crime is answered the instant they catch
you, so the whole pursuit stands down; `commandReturnHome()` also clears each cop's
`caughtPlayer_` latch, which prevents a same-frame double-trigger. The release reset
(`playerCharge = None`, `manhuntActive = false`) stays.

Files: `src/app/main.cpp`. Verified by play (main-loop wiring; `commandReturnHome`
itself is already unit-tested).

## Phase 2 — Money, a bank, and shops  `feat(economy): money, a bank, and buying from shops`

- **New core `PlayerState.hpp/.cpp`** (SFML-free, tested): `int money`, the set of
  owned weapons + current selection, and a `WeaponKind { Fists, Bat, Pistol }` enum.
  Methods: `withdraw(int)`, `bool buy(const ShopItem&)` (deduct + mark owned only
  when affordable and not already owned), `owns(WeaponKind)`, `select(WeaponKind)`.
  A small static catalog (`{id, label, price, WeaponKind}`): Bat, Pistol.
- **`City` gets a bank** (`makeDowntown`): a small solid "City Bank" landmark near
  the plaza spawn; proximity uses its footprint center. Tag which shop sells the
  weapon catalog — the **hardware store** (`Jensen Hardware`) sells bat + pistol.
- **`Action::Interact`** (default `"E"`): add to `KeyBindings` enum + the
  positional name/label/default arrays. Context-sensitive in `main.cpp`: near the
  bank → `withdraw(+500)`; near a catalog shopkeeper → toggle a **shop overlay**
  (a simple HUD list of items/prices drawn like `drawCenteredHudText`; number keys
  buy, shows "owned"/"can't afford"). HUD always shows `$<money>`.
- Tests: `tests/test_player_state.cpp` (withdraw adds; buy deducts only when
  affordable; no double-own; selection requires ownership).

Files: new `src/core/PlayerState.{hpp,cpp}`; `src/core/City.cpp`;
`src/core/KeyBindings.{hpp,cpp}`; `src/app/main.cpp`; `CMakeLists.txt`.

## Phase 3 — Weapons & the knocked-down state  `feat(combat): carry and use weapons; NPCs can be knocked down`

- **Downed state on `Npc`** (shared infra): `bool downed_`, `void knockDown()`,
  `bool isDowned()`. `update()` early-returns when downed (no wander/turn/behavior).
  Talk targeting skips downed NPCs. The renderer draws a downed figure collapsed
  (rotate flat / drop to the ground) instead of standing.
- **Firing** (`main.cpp`, Playing mode): left-click (`MouseButtonPressed`, Left)
  uses the current weapon; `1/2/3` select an owned weapon. Melee (fists/bat) downs
  the nearest NPC within a short range + frontal cone; pistol is a hitscan that
  downs the nearest NPC near the camera ray within range. On a hit:
  `npc.knockDown()` **and** `escalateCharge(...)` — bat/fists → `Assault`, pistol →
  `ArmedViolence` (reuses the existing charge/manhunt system, so a gunshot
  deterministically triggers the manhunt). This makes weapons a real in-world way
  to commit the crimes the law already understands.
- **Target selection is logic** → extract `pickTargetInCone(eye, yawDeg, range,
  coneDeg, positions)` into core (`Combat.hpp`) and unit-test it; reuse for melee
  and (narrow cone) the pistol.
- **Feedback**: HUD shows the equipped weapon (`[3] Pistol`); a brief muzzle/hit
  flash on fire; a simple 2D corner viewmodel (overlay pass) so the player sees what
  they hold. Infinite ammo.
- Tests: `tests/test_combat.cpp` (cone/range target picking); knock-down behavior in
  `tests/test_npc_behavior.cpp` (downed NPC stops moving and isn't a talk target).

Files: `src/core/Npc.{hpp,cpp}`, new `src/core/Combat.hpp` (+`.cpp` if needed),
`src/app/main.cpp`, `src/app/Renderer3D.cpp` (downed pose + viewmodel),
`CMakeLists.txt`.

## Phase 4 — Cars affect pedestrians  `feat(traffic): cars yield to and can knock down pedestrians`

- **`Traffic::update` gains pedestrian positions**: `update(dt, playerPos, const
  std::vector<Vec3>& people)` — cars brake for people with the same forward
  look-ahead they already use for the player, so they **stop for pedestrians**
  instead of plowing through (the "treat like real people" part).
- **`main.cpp`**: build the people list each frame; after each `npc.update`, if a
  **moving** car overlaps the NPC (`circleHitsVehicle` + a speed threshold) →
  `npc.knockDown()` (reuses Phase-3 state); if a **stopped** car overlaps them,
  block that NPC's step (revert to the pre-update position via a small guarded
  `Npc` setter) so they don't walk through a parked car.
- Tests: extend `tests/test_traffic.cpp` — a car brakes for a person ahead in its
  lane (people-list variant of the existing player-brake test).

Files: `src/core/Traffic.{hpp,cpp}`, `src/app/main.cpp`, `tests/test_traffic.cpp`.

---

## Out of scope
No ammo economy/reloading, no player health/damage (NPCs can't hurt the player
yet), no NPC path-planning around cars (cars yielding + contact-knockdown covers
it), no selling/looting, no persistent save. Money is intentionally infinite via the
bank.

## Risks / notes
- The fixed `world.npcs()` index invariant is load-bearing — the downed state is a
  flag precisely to avoid deletion. Verify arrest/jail still works after NPCs are
  downed.
- `pickTargetInCone` aim feel (range/cone, pistol angular threshold) is tuned in
  named constants; I can't screenshot the GL window, so you verify aim/feedback and
  I tune.

## Verification (each phase)
- `cmake --build build -j` clean; `make -C tests test` green (suite grows with
  test_player_state, test_combat, traffic additions).
- Play-test: get arrested for `*shoots*`/gunfire, serve time, confirm cops **stand
  down** and don't re-arrest at the door; withdraw at the bank and watch `$` rise;
  buy the bat + pistol at the hardware store; punch/shoot a pedestrian and see them
  drop + the law respond (assault vs. armed-violence manhunt); walk a pedestrian
  toward traffic and confirm cars brake, and that a moving car knocks a pedestrian
  down rather than passing through.
- Inline review before each commit; offer `/code-review` at the end.

# Plan: Law fix, weapons, money & shops, and car↔pedestrian physics

## Context

Four interlocking requests after the "bigger, livelier city" work shipped:

1. **BUG — cops re-arrest forever.** After an arrest + release, police keep hunting
   the player. Cause: armed-violence (and `call_police`) triggers a **manhunt**
   that mobilizes *every* officer via `commandArrest()`, but on capture only the
   *catching* officer stands down (`commandReturnHome()`); the rest stay in
   `Arrest` and immediately re-catch the player at the release spot.
2. **Weapons** the player can carry and use on NPCs.
3. **Cars must affect NPCs** — pedestrians shouldn't obliviously walk in front of
   (or through) cars; treat them like real people.
4. **Money + a bank + shops** — withdraw infinite cash at a bank, see money in the
   HUD, buy things from shopkeepers.

These connect: the bank gives money → money buys weapons from shops → weapons used
on NPCs knock them down and trip the existing law system → cars and weapons share
one "knocked-down" state.

**Locked decisions (from Q&A):**
- Weapons: **fists + bat + pistol.** Number keys 1/2/3 select (only if owned),
  left-click attacks. Fists/bat = short frontal melee; pistol = hitscan along the
  camera ray. Infinite ammo for now.
- On attack (weapon **or** car): NPC is **knocked down and stays down** — an
  incapacitated body that stops wandering/talking but is **never deleted**. This is
  critical: deletion would shift the `world.npcs()` indices that `pendingRoutes`,
  `wasCaught`, and `session.npcIndex()` depend on. A downed flag keeps indices stable.

**Constraints (CLAUDE.md):** all new logic is SFML-free core with doctest tests;
renderer is eyeballed. Feature branch `7-weapons-money-and-mayhem`, incremental
`type(scope): description` commits, build + `make -C tests test` green after each,
inline review before each commit. No push (user's call).

---

## Phase 1 — Fix re-arrest after release  `fix(law): stand down all police on arrest`

In the capture handler in `src/app/main.cpp` (the `caughtNow && !wasCaught[i] &&
npc.persona().police` branch): instead of only the catcher's
`npc.commandReturnHome()`, loop **every** police officer and `commandReturnHome()`
them, and set `manhuntActive = false`. The crime is answered the instant they catch
you, so the whole pursuit stands down; `commandReturnHome()` also clears each cop's
`caughtPlayer_` latch, which prevents a same-frame double-trigger. The release reset
(`playerCharge = None`, `manhuntActive = false`) stays.

Files: `src/app/main.cpp`. Verified by play (main-loop wiring; `commandReturnHome`
itself is already unit-tested).

## Phase 2 — Money, a bank, and shops  `feat(economy): money, a bank, and buying from shops`

- **New core `PlayerState.hpp/.cpp`** (SFML-free, tested): `int money`, the set of
  owned weapons + current selection, and a `WeaponKind { Fists, Bat, Pistol }` enum.
  Methods: `withdraw(int)`, `bool buy(const ShopItem&)` (deduct + mark owned only
  when affordable and not already owned), `owns(WeaponKind)`, `select(WeaponKind)`.
  A small static catalog (`{id, label, price, WeaponKind}`): Bat, Pistol.

- **`Action::Interact`** (default `"E"`): add to `KeyBindings` enum + the
  positional name/label/default arrays. Context-sensitive in `main.cpp`: near the
  bank → `withdraw(+500)`; near a catalog shopkeeper → toggle a **shop overlay**
  (a simple HUD list of items/prices drawn like `drawCenteredHudText`; number keys
  buy, shows "owned"/"can't afford"). HUD always shows `$<money>`.
- Tests: `tests/test_player_state.cpp` (withdraw adds; buy deducts only when
  affordable; no double-own; selection requires ownership).

Files: new `src/core/PlayerState.{hpp,cpp}`; `src/core/City.cpp`;
`src/core/KeyBindings.{hpp,cpp}`; `src/app/main.cpp`; `CMakeLists.txt`.

## Phase 3 — Weapons & the knocked-down state  `feat(combat): carry and use weapons; NPCs can be knocked down`

- **Downed state on `Npc`** (shared infra): `bool downed_`, `void knockDown()`,
  `bool isDowned()`. `update()` early-returns when downed (no wander/turn/behavior).
  Talk targeting skips downed NPCs. The renderer draws a downed figure collapsed

- **Firing** (`main.cpp`, Playing mode): left-click (`MouseButtonPressed`, Left)
  uses the current weapon; `1/2/3` select an owned weapon. Melee (fists/bat) downs
  the nearest NPC within a short range + frontal cone; pistol is a hitscan that
  downs the nearest NPC near the camera ray within range. On a hit:
  `npc.knockDown()` **and** `escalateCharge(...)` — bat/fists → `Assault`, pistol →
  `ArmedViolence` (reuses the existing charge/manhunt system, so a gunshot

- Tests: `tests/test_combat.cpp` (cone/range target picking); knock-down behavior in
  `tests/test_npc_behavior.cpp` (downed NPC stops moving and isn't a talk target).

Files: `src/core/Npc.{hpp,cpp}`, new `src/core/Combat.hpp` (+`.cpp` if needed),

- **`Traffic::update` gains pedestrian positions**: `update(dt, playerPos, const
  std::vector<Vec3>& people)` — cars brake for people with the same forward
  look-ahead they already use for the player, so they **stop for pedestrians**
  instead of plowing through (the "treat like real people" part).
- **`main.cpp`**: build the people list each frame; after each `npc.update`, if a

  `npc.knockDown()` (reuses Phase-3 state); if a **stopped** car overlaps them,
  block that NPC's step (revert to the pre-update position via a small guarded
  `Npc` setter) so they don't walk through a parked car.
- Tests: extend `tests/test_traffic.cpp` — a car brakes for a person ahead in its
  lane (people-list variant of the existing player-brake test).

Files: `src/core/Traffic.{hpp,cpp}`, `src/app/main.cpp`, `tests/test_traffic.cpp`.

---

## Out of scope
No ammo economy/reloading, no player health/damage (NPCs can't hurt the player
yet), no NPC path-planning around cars (cars yielding + contact-knockdown covers
it), no selling/looting, no persistent save. Money is intentionally infinite via the
bank.

## Risks / notes
- The fixed `world.npcs()` index invariant is load-bearing — the downed state is a
  flag precisely to avoid deletion. Verify arrest/jail still works after NPCs are
  downed.
- `pickTargetInCone` aim feel (range/cone, pistol angular threshold) is tuned in
  named constants; I can't screenshot the GL window, so you verify aim/feedback and
  I tune.

## Verification (each phase)
- `cmake --build build -j` clean; `make -C tests test` green (suite grows with
  test_player_state, test_combat, traffic additions).
- Play-test: get arrested for `*shoots*`/gunfire, serve time, confirm cops **stand
  down** and don't re-arrest at the door; withdraw at the bank and watch `$` rise;
  buy the bat + pistol at the hardware store; punch/shoot a pedestrian and see them
  drop + the law respond (assault vs. armed-violence manhunt); walk a pedestrian
  toward traffic and confirm cars brake, and that a moving car knocks a pedestrian
  down rather than passing through.
- Inline review before each commit; offer `/code-review` at the end.

# Plan: Law fix, weapons, money & shops, and car↔pedestrian physics

## Context

Four interlocking requests after the "bigger, livelier city" work shipped:

1. **BUG — cops re-arrest forever.** After an arrest + release, police keep hunting
   the player. Cause: armed-violence (and `call_police`) triggers a **manhunt**
   that mobilizes *every* officer via `commandArrest()`, but on capture only the
   *catching* officer stands down (`commandReturnHome()`); the rest stay in
   `Arrest` and immediately re-catch the player at the release spot.
2. **Weapons** the player can carry and use on NPCs.
3. **Cars must affect NPCs** — pedestrians shouldn't obliviously walk in front of
   (or through) cars; treat them like real people.
4. **Money + a bank + shops** — withdraw infinite cash at a bank, see money in the
   HUD, buy things from shopkeepers.

These connect: the bank gives money → money buys weapons from shops → weapons used
on NPCs knock them down and trip the existing law system → cars and weapons share
one "knocked-down" state.

**Locked decisions (from Q&A):**
- Weapons: **fists + bat + pistol.** Number keys 1/2/3 select (only if owned),
  left-click attacks. Fists/bat = short frontal melee; pistol = hitscan along the
  camera ray. Infinite ammo for now.
- On attack (weapon **or** car): NPC is **knocked down and stays down** — an
  incapacitated body that stops wandering/talking but is **never deleted**. This is
  critical: deletion would shift the `world.npcs()` indices that `pendingRoutes`,
  `wasCaught`, and `session.npcIndex()` depend on. A downed flag keeps indices stable.

**Constraints (CLAUDE.md):** all new logic is SFML-free core with doctest tests;
renderer is eyeballed. Feature branch `7-weapons-money-and-mayhem`, incremental

inline review before each commit. No push (user's call).

you, so the whole pursuit stands down; `commandReturnHome()` also clears each cop's
`caughtPlayer_` latch, which prevents a same-frame double-trigger. The release reset

find_package(OpenGL QUIET)

)

    target_link_libraries(llm_npc_core PUBLIC ws2_32)

# Plan: Law fix, weapons, money & shops, and car↔pedestrian physics

## Context

Four interlocking requests after the "bigger, livelier city" work shipped:

1. **BUG — cops re-arrest forever.** After an arrest + release, police keep hunting
   the player. Cause: armed-violence (and `call_police`) triggers a **manhunt**
   that mobilizes *every* officer via `commandArrest()`, but on capture only the
   *catching* officer stands down (`commandReturnHome()`); the rest stay in
   `Arrest` and immediately re-catch the player at the release spot.
2. **Weapons** the player can carry and use on NPCs.
3. **Cars must affect NPCs** — pedestrians shouldn't obliviously walk in front of
   (or through) cars; treat them like real people.
4. **Money + a bank + shops** — withdraw infinite cash at a bank, see money in the
   HUD, buy things from shopkeepers.

These connect: the bank gives money → money buys weapons from shops → weapons used
on NPCs knock them down and trip the existing law system → cars and weapons share
one "knocked-down" state.

**Locked decisions (from Q&A):**
- Weapons: **fists + bat + pistol.** Number keys 1/2/3 select (only if owned),
  left-click attacks. Fists/bat = short frontal melee; pistol = hitscan along the
  camera ray. Infinite ammo for now.
- On attack (weapon **or** car): NPC is **knocked down and stays down** — an
  incapacitated body that stops wandering/talking but is **never deleted**. This is
  critical: deletion would shift the `world.npcs()` indices that `pendingRoutes`,
  `wasCaught`, and `session.npcIndex()` depend on. A downed flag keeps indices stable.

**Constraints (CLAUDE.md):** all new logic is SFML-free core with doctest tests;
renderer is eyeballed. Feature branch `7-weapons-money-and-mayhem`, incremental
`type(scope): description` commits, build + `make -C tests test` green after each,
inline review before each commit. No push (user's call).

---

## Phase 1 — Fix re-arrest after release  `fix(law): stand down all police on arrest`

In the capture handler in `src/app/main.cpp` (the `caughtNow && !wasCaught[i] &&
npc.persona().police` branch): instead of only the catcher's
`npc.commandReturnHome()`, loop **every** police officer and `commandReturnHome()`
them, and set `manhuntActive = false`. The crime is answered the instant they catch
you, so the whole pursuit stands down; `commandReturnHome()` also clears each cop's
`caughtPlayer_` latch, which prevents a same-frame double-trigger. The release reset
(`playerCharge = None`, `manhuntActive = false`) stays.

Files: `src/app/main.cpp`. Verified by play (main-loop wiring; `commandReturnHome`
itself is already unit-tested).

## Phase 2 — Money, a bank, and shops  `feat(economy): money, a bank, and buying from shops`

- **New core `PlayerState.hpp/.cpp`** (SFML-free, tested): `int money`, the set of
  owned weapons + current selection, and a `WeaponKind { Fists, Bat, Pistol }` enum.
  Methods: `withdraw(int)`, `bool buy(const ShopItem&)` (deduct + mark owned only
  when affordable and not already owned), `owns(WeaponKind)`, `select(WeaponKind)`.
  A small static catalog (`{id, label, price, WeaponKind}`): Bat, Pistol.
- **`City` gets a bank** (`makeDowntown`): a small solid "City Bank" landmark near
  the plaza spawn; proximity uses its footprint center. Tag which shop sells the
  weapon catalog — the **hardware store** (`Jensen Hardware`) sells bat + pistol.
- **`Action::Interact`** (default `"E"`): add to `KeyBindings` enum + the
  positional name/label/default arrays. Context-sensitive in `main.cpp`: near the
  bank → `withdraw(+500)`; near a catalog shopkeeper → toggle a **shop overlay**
  (a simple HUD list of items/prices drawn like `drawCenteredHudText`; number keys
  buy, shows "owned"/"can't afford"). HUD always shows `$<money>`.
- Tests: `tests/test_player_state.cpp` (withdraw adds; buy deducts only when
  affordable; no double-own; selection requires ownership).

Files: new `src/core/PlayerState.{hpp,cpp}`; `src/core/City.cpp`;
`src/core/KeyBindings.{hpp,cpp}`; `src/app/main.cpp`; `CMakeLists.txt`.

## Phase 3 — Weapons & the knocked-down state  `feat(combat): carry and use weapons; NPCs can be knocked down`

- **Downed state on `Npc`** (shared infra): `bool downed_`, `void knockDown()`,
  `bool isDowned()`. `update()` early-returns when downed (no wander/turn/behavior).
  Talk targeting skips downed NPCs. The renderer draws a downed figure collapsed
  (rotate flat / drop to the ground) instead of standing.
- **Firing** (`main.cpp`, Playing mode): left-click (`MouseButtonPressed`, Left)
  uses the current weapon; `1/2/3` select an owned weapon. Melee (fists/bat) downs
  the nearest NPC within a short range + frontal cone; pistol is a hitscan that
  downs the nearest NPC near the camera ray within range. On a hit:
  `npc.knockDown()` **and** `escalateCharge(...)` — bat/fists → `Assault`, pistol →
  `ArmedViolence` (reuses the existing charge/manhunt system, so a gunshot
  deterministically triggers the manhunt). This makes weapons a real in-world way
  to commit the crimes the law already understands.
- **Target selection is logic** → extract `pickTargetInCone(eye, yawDeg, range,
  coneDeg, positions)` into core (`Combat.hpp`) and unit-test it; reuse for melee
  and (narrow cone) the pistol.
- **Feedback**: HUD shows the equipped weapon (`[3] Pistol`); a brief muzzle/hit
  flash on fire; a simple 2D corner viewmodel (overlay pass) so the player sees what
  they hold. Infinite ammo.
- Tests: `tests/test_combat.cpp` (cone/range target picking); knock-down behavior in
  `tests/test_npc_behavior.cpp` (downed NPC stops moving and isn't a talk target).

Files: `src/core/Npc.{hpp,cpp}`, new `src/core/Combat.hpp` (+`.cpp` if needed),
`src/app/main.cpp`, `src/app/Renderer3D.cpp` (downed pose + viewmodel),
`CMakeLists.txt`.

## Phase 4 — Cars affect pedestrians  `feat(traffic): cars yield to and can knock down pedestrians`

- **`Traffic::update` gains pedestrian positions**: `update(dt, playerPos, const
  std::vector<Vec3>& people)` — cars brake for people with the same forward
  look-ahead they already use for the player, so they **stop for pedestrians**
  instead of plowing through (the "treat like real people" part).
- **`main.cpp`**: build the people list each frame; after each `npc.update`, if a
  **moving** car overlaps the NPC (`circleHitsVehicle` + a speed threshold) →
  `npc.knockDown()` (reuses Phase-3 state); if a **stopped** car overlaps them,
  block that NPC's step (revert to the pre-update position via a small guarded
  `Npc` setter) so they don't walk through a parked car.
- Tests: extend `tests/test_traffic.cpp` — a car brakes for a person ahead in its
  lane (people-list variant of the existing player-brake test).

Files: `src/core/Traffic.{hpp,cpp}`, `src/app/main.cpp`, `tests/test_traffic.cpp`.

---

## Out of scope
No ammo economy/reloading, no player health/damage (NPCs can't hurt the player
yet), no NPC path-planning around cars (cars yielding + contact-knockdown covers
it), no selling/looting, no persistent save. Money is intentionally infinite via the
bank.

## Risks / notes
- The fixed `world.npcs()` index invariant is load-bearing — the downed state is a
  flag precisely to avoid deletion. Verify arrest/jail still works after NPCs are
  downed.
- `pickTargetInCone` aim feel (range/cone, pistol angular threshold) is tuned in
  named constants; I can't screenshot the GL window, so you verify aim/feedback and
  I tune.

## Verification (each phase)
- `cmake --build build -j` clean; `make -C tests test` green (suite grows with
  test_player_state, test_combat, traffic additions).
- Play-test: get arrested for `*shoots*`/gunfire, serve time, confirm cops **stand
  down** and don't re-arrest at the door; withdraw at the bank and watch `$` rise;
  buy the bat + pistol at the hardware store; punch/shoot a pedestrian and see them
  drop + the law respond (assault vs. armed-violence manhunt); walk a pedestrian
  toward traffic and confirm cars brake, and that a moving car knocks a pedestrian
  down rather than passing through.
- Inline review before each commit; offer `/code-review` at the end.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Linux launcher: verifies Ollama is reachable, builds, and runs the game.
# Run from anywhere; this script cds to its own directory.
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

HOST="${OLLAMA_HOST:-localhost}"
PORT="${OLLAMA_PORT:-11434}"

if ! curl -fsS --max-time 2 "http://${HOST}:${PORT}/api/tags" >/dev/null; then
    echo "Ollama not reachable at ${HOST}:${PORT}." >&2
    echo "Start it with:  ollama serve   (and pull a model: ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct)" >&2
    exit 1
fi

# On macOS, sfml@2 is keg-only and not in the default prefix.
CMAKE_PREFIX=""
if [[ -d /opt/homebrew/opt/sfml@2 ]]; then
    CMAKE_PREFIX="-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/homebrew/opt/sfml@2"
elif [[ -d /usr/local/opt/sfml@2 ]]; then
    CMAKE_PREFIX="-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/usr/local/opt/sfml@2"
fi

cmake -S . -B build $CMAKE_PREFIX
cmake --build build -j

exec ./build/cpp_game_with_llm_npcs

# LLM NPC City

A small first-person 3D city where every inhabitant is a live LLM character.
Walk the streets, find the baker, the cop, the busker, the hot-dog vendor —
press `T` and talk to them about anything. Each NPC has their own personality,
their own knowledge of the city (and pointed ignorance of everything else),
and remembers your conversation.

Powered locally by [Ollama](https://ollama.com) — no cloud, no API key.

## Quick start (Windows)

1. **Install Ollama** from <https://ollama.com/download>, then pull the model:

   ```
   ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
   ```

2. **Install MSYS2** from <https://www.msys2.org> and, in the *UCRT64* shell:

   ```
   pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml
   ```

3. **Double-click `run.bat`** (or run `./run.ps1`). It checks Ollama is up,
   builds, and launches the game.

## Playing

- `WASD` to walk, mouse to look around.
- Walk up to anyone: `[T] Talk to <name>` appears — press `T`.
- Type, press `Enter`, and watch the reply stream in live. `Escape` to leave.
- `Escape` opens the pause menu: resume, quit, or **rebind every key with the
  mouse** (changes save instantly).

Full reference: [docs/CONTROLS.md](docs/CONTROLS.md).

## Meet the city

Ten residents, each with their own patch of downtown:

| Who | Where |
|-----|-------|
| Marge Holloway, baker | Marge's Bakery, north-west |
| Officer Dana Brooks | outside the police station |
| Theo Park, barista | Bean There Coffee |
| Ms. Adaeze Obi, librarian | the library steps |
| Hal Jensen, hardware man | Jensen Hardware |
| Gus Romano, hot-dog vendor | the cart, dead center of the plaza |
| Ray Okafor, taxi driver | idling by his cab, east of the plaza |
| Yuki Tanaka, tourist | photographing the fountain |
| Benny "Strings" Malone, busker | the park's street corner |
| Mr. Albert Whitfield, retired teacher | the park bench |

They know each other — ask Gus about the squeaky cart wheel and someone at
the hardware store may have opinions.

## Configuration

- `config/llm.cfg` — model, host/port, temperature, `keep_alive` (latency).
  Any model you have pulled in Ollama works; smaller = snappier.
- `config/keybindings.cfg` — key bindings (also editable in-game).
- `personas/*.persona` — the characters themselves. Edit freely; the file
  format is documented in [docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md).

## Development

Architecture, headless test workflow, and the latency playbook live in
[docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md). Short version:

```sh
make -C tests test      # full offline unit-test suite, no SFML required
```

12	// A persona plus its placement in the city, loaded from personas/<id>.persona.
13	struct LoadedPersona {
14	    std::string id;         // filename stem, e.g. "baker"
15	    Persona persona;        // identity rendered into the system prompt
16	    Vec3 position;          // world position on the ground plane (y = 0)
17	    float facingDeg = 0.f;  // initial facing, degrees around +y (0 = +z)
18	    std::string spotId;     // landmark tag, e.g. "bakery" or "park"
19	};
20	
21	// Result of parsing one persona definition.
22	struct PersonaParseResult {
23	    bool ok = false;
24	    LoadedPersona value;
25	    std::string error;  // human-readable reason when !ok
26	};
27	
28	// Parses one persona definition. Format: a key=value header, then an optional
29	// '---' line followed by free-form extra system-prompt directives:
30	//
31	//   name = Marge Holloway        (required)
32	//   role = bakery owner
33	//   traits = warm, gossipy       (comma-separated)
34	//   style = 1-3 short sentences
35	//   knowledge = Knows the neighborhood; nothing of world news.
36	//   spot = bakery
37	//   position = -40, 28           (x, z world coordinates)
38	//   facing = 180                 (degrees)
39	//   ---
40	//   Everything after the --- line is passed to the model verbatim.
41	//
42	// Header lines are taken literally (no comment stripping) so persona text can
43	// contain any character except a leading 'key =' shape.
44	PersonaParseResult parsePersonaText(const std::string& text, const std::string& id);
45	
46	// Parses a single .persona file; the persona id is the filename stem.
47	PersonaParseResult parsePersonaFile(const std::filesystem::path& path);

50	// roster order. Files that fail to parse are skipped; their error messages
51	// are appended to `errors` when it is non-null.
52	std::vector<LoadedPersona> loadAllPersonas(const std::filesystem::path& dir,
53	                                           std::vector<std::string>* errors = nullptr);

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

find_package(Threads REQUIRED)
# Game executable needs SFML+OpenGL; QUIET so the dev container can still
# configure CMake and build the core library + tests without them.
find_package(SFML 2.6 COMPONENTS graphics window system QUIET)
find_package(OpenGL QUIET)

# Core: SFML-free game logic shared with the unit tests.
add_library(llm_npc_core STATIC
    src/core/City.cpp
    src/core/Combat.cpp
    src/core/Config.cpp
    src/core/DialogueSession.cpp
    src/core/KeyBindings.cpp
    src/core/LlmClient.cpp
    src/core/Npc.cpp
    src/core/Offense.cpp
    src/core/PersonaFactory.cpp
    src/core/PersonaLoader.cpp
    src/core/PlayerState.cpp
    src/core/Traffic.cpp
    src/core/World.cpp
)
target_include_directories(llm_npc_core PUBLIC
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/core
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/external
)
target_link_libraries(llm_npc_core PUBLIC Threads::Threads)
if(WIN32)
    # httplib needs winsock when built with MinGW.
    target_link_libraries(llm_npc_core PUBLIC ws2_32)
endif()

if(SFML_FOUND AND OPENGL_FOUND)
    add_executable(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
        src/app/main.cpp
        src/app/DialogUI.cpp
        src/app/InputMap.cpp
        src/app/Menu.cpp
        src/app/Renderer3D.cpp
    )
    target_include_directories(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/app
    )
    target_link_libraries(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
        PRIVATE
            llm_npc_core
            sfml-graphics
            sfml-window
            sfml-system
            OpenGL::GL
    )
    if(APPLE)
        # Mouse-look uses CoreGraphics cursor warping directly; see main.cpp.
        target_link_libraries(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs PRIVATE
            "-framework ApplicationServices")
    endif()
else()
    message(STATUS "SFML or OpenGL not found; building core library only "
                   "(use tests/Makefile for the test suite)")
endif()

content.text:
I have a thorough picture of the LLM layer now. Key facts grounding the plan:

- **`LlmClient`** (one worker thread, `submit`/`drainDeltas`/`drainReplies`) is hardwired to Ollama: `processOne()` builds an `/api/chat` body and `parseOllamaChunk()` parses Ollama's NDJSON. Everything provider-specific lives in those two spots.
- **Config** is a tiny `key=value` reader (`config/llm.cfg` → `LlmConfig`); adding keys is trivial.
- **Launch scripts** (`run.sh`/`run.ps1`/`run.bat`) only *check* Ollama is up (`curl /api/tags`) and bail if not — they don't start it.
- Cloud APIs are **HTTPS-only**, and the vendored `httplib.h` needs OpenSSL to do HTTPS — that's the one real new dependency this direction implies.

Let me research current pricing/streaming formats so the cost model and provider plan are grounded.

## Key Findings:

**OpenRouter Overview:**
OpenRouter is a unified API gateway that routes requests to dozens of AI models — including Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, DeepSeek, Mistral, Llama, and many others — through a single endpoint.

**OpenAI Compatibility:**
OpenRouter's API is fully OpenAI-compatible. Just change the base URL to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 and use your OpenRouter API key. OpenRouter exposes both an OpenAI-compatible API (/api/v1) and an Anthropic-compatible API. This is what makes it possible to point Claude Code at OpenRouter — Claude Code speaks Anthropic's API format, and OpenRouter can receive it.

**Streaming Support:**
OpenRouter supports streaming responses, function calling, and context management with access to multiple model providers through a single API. The API also supports streaming.

**Model Access:**
OpenRouter provides access to 315+ Models through one API Key: Access Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Llama, Grok, and hundreds more through a single endpoint. Switch models by changing one parameter — no code changes needed.

**Model Identifiers:**
OpenRouter model identifiers use the provider/model format (e.g., openai/gpt-4o, anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514, google/gemini-pro).

# Streaming Chat Completion Request

Based on the provided documentation, here's what you need to know:

**Endpoint:** `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions`

**Required Headers:**
- `Authorization: Bearer <OPENROUTER_API_KEY>`
- `Content-Type: application/json`
- Optional: `HTTP-Referer` and `X-OpenRouter-Title` for app attribution

**Request Body Structure:**
The documentation shows the standard chat completion format with a `model` and `messages` array. To enable streaming, you would add `"stream": true` to the JSON payload (following OpenAI API conventions, though not explicitly shown in the excerpts above).

**Streaming Response Format:**
The documentation states the API "supports [streaming](/docs/api/reference/streaming)" but doesn't provide the exact SSE format details in this quickstart page. The content references that "You can also use the OpenAI SDK" as a drop-in replacement, suggesting compatibility with OpenAI's streaming format (Server-Sent Events with `data:` prefixed JSON lines, including `[DONE]` signaling), but the specific response line format isn't documented in the material provided.

**Recommendation:** Consult the full API reference or streaming documentation linked in the page for exact SSE response specifications.

## Ollama OpenAI Compatible Endpoint

Ollama has built-in compatibility with the OpenAI Chat Completions API, making it possible to use more tooling and applications with Ollama locally. Supported endpoints include /v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings, and /v1/models.

To use the `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint, you can invoke it using the same OpenAI format and change the hostname to http://localhost:11434, with example curl commands available in the documentation.

## Ollama CLI Commands for Models

For managing models via CLI:

- **List installed models**: Use `ollama list` to list all the available models you have installed

- **Pull models**: Use `ollama pull <model name>` to pull a model from the Ollama repository, and in some instances, you might need to specify which version you want to download, for example, 8B, 70B, 405B, etc.

- **List via API**: You can also fetch a list of models and their details using `curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags`

The search results show that Ollama supports tag-based versioning for models, allowing you to specify specific versions when pulling and listing models.

content.text:
I now have everything I need — pricing, the OpenAI-compatible wire format, and confirmation that **Ollama, OpenRouter, OpenAI, and Gemini all speak the same `/v1/chat/completions` shape**. That means one OpenAI-compatible backend covers local *and* cloud; the only real fork is HTTP (local) vs HTTPS (cloud, which needs OpenSSL in the build).

Two decisions genuinely change what I build, so let me get them before finalizing the plan.

questions.question: How far should I take this on the new branch right now? (Talking to cloud LLMs requires HTTPS, which means adding OpenSSL to the C++ build — a genuinely new dependency, and the trickiest part on Windows.)

options.label: Local now + cloud-ready
options.description: One-click launch (auto-starts Ollama) + in-game picker for your installed local models, refactor the LLM layer into a pluggable backend interface so a cloud backend is a drop-in, and write the full Character.ai-in-3D roadmap. Zero new deps; works everywhere today. Cloud goes live the moment you add OpenSSL + a key.
options.preview:
NOW (no new deps):
  ./run.command  -> starts Ollama, pulls model, builds, runs
  Pause menu -> [ Model: qwen2.5:3b v ]  (lists ollama models)
  LlmClient -> LlmBackend interface
        |- OllamaBackend (works today)
        '- OpenAiBackend (compiled, dormant until OpenSSL+key)
  docs/VISION.md  (roadmap + cost model)

options.label: Go cloud now (add OpenSSL)
options.description: Everything in the first option PLUS a working cloud backend wired to OpenRouter, so you can talk to Claude / GPT / Gemini NPCs today. Requires installing OpenSSL and putting in an API key; more build setup, especially on Windows.
options.preview:
NOW (adds OpenSSL):
  config/llm.cfg -> provider = openrouter
  config/secrets.cfg -> api_key (gitignored)
  Talk to an NPC -> answered by claude-haiku-4.5
  Switch model by editing one string
  + everything from 'Local now + cloud-ready'

options.label: Plans / docs only
options.description: Don't touch code yet. Just deliver the research, architecture design, cost model, and staged roadmap as a doc; you decide when to build. Lowest risk, nothing to test in-game.
options.preview:
NOW:
  docs/VISION.md only
  - provider architecture
  - per-message cost tables
  - staged roadmap to the product
  (no code changes)

-> no markup, more code to maintain

# Plain-make test runner for the SFML-free core library.
#
# The dev container has g++/make but no cmake or SFML, so this Makefile is the
# primary way to build and run unit tests there. It compiles every
# src/core/*.cpp plus every tests/test_*.cpp into one doctest binary.
#
#   make -C tests test     # build + run all tests
#   make -C tests clean    # remove build artifacts

CXX      ?= g++
CXXFLAGS ?= -std=c++17 -g -O0 -pthread -Wall -Wextra
INCLUDES := -I../src/core -I../external -I.

BUILD  := build
TARGET := $(BUILD)/run_tests

CORE_SRCS := $(wildcard ../src/core/*.cpp)
TEST_SRCS := $(wildcard test_*.cpp)

CORE_OBJS := $(patsubst ../src/core/%.cpp,$(BUILD)/core_%.o,$(CORE_SRCS))
TEST_OBJS := $(patsubst %.cpp,$(BUILD)/%.o,$(TEST_SRCS))

.PHONY: test build clean

test: $(TARGET)
	./$(TARGET)

build: $(TARGET)

$(TARGET): $(CORE_OBJS) $(TEST_OBJS)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $^ -o $@

# -MMD -MP emits .d header-dependency files next to each object so editing a
# header (e.g. changing the Npc class layout) recompiles every dependent
# object instead of leaving stale, ABI-mismatched ones behind.
$(BUILD)/core_%.o: ../src/core/%.cpp | $(BUILD)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(INCLUDES) -MMD -MP -c $< -o $@

$(BUILD)/%.o: %.cpp | $(BUILD)
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(INCLUDES) -MMD -MP -c $< -o $@

tests/build/
