def main() -> None:
    token = os.environ.get("GH_TOKEN") or os.environ.get("GITHUB_TOKEN")
    username = os.environ.get("GITHUB_USERNAME")
    if not token or not username:
        raise SystemExit("Set GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_USERNAME in your shell config first.")

    gh = Github(token)
    repo = gh.get_repo(os.environ.get("GITHUB_REPO") or REPO_SLUG)
    print(f"Planning issues for: {repo.full_name}")

    existing_titles = set()
    for issue in repo.get_issues(state="open"):
        if not issue.pull_request:
            existing_titles.add(issue.title.lower())
    print(f"Existing open issues: {len(existing_titles)}")

    # Overnight workflow labels (idempotent).
    labels = [
        ("ready-for-ai", "0075ca", "Scoped and clear — safe for overnight AI run"),
        ("ai-in-progress", "e4e669", "Claude is currently working on this"),
        ("ai-completed", "0e8a16", "AI finished — awaiting human review"),
        ("ai-blocked", "d93f0b", "AI attempted but could not complete"),
        ("needs-human", "cc317c", "Requires a human decision before work starts"),
    ]
    for name, color, description in labels:
        try:
            repo.create_label(name=name, color=color, description=description)
            print(f"Created label: {name}")
        except GithubException as e:
            if e.status == 422:
                print(f"Label exists (skipped): {name}")
            else:
                raise

    # Milestone (reuse if a rerun already made it).
    milestone = None
    for m in repo.get_milestones(state="open"):
        if m.title == MILESTONE_TITLE:
            milestone = m
            print(f"Milestone exists (reusing): #{m.number}")
            break
    if milestone is None:
        milestone = repo.create_milestone(title=MILESTONE_TITLE, description=MILESTONE_DESC)
        print(f"Created milestone: {milestone.title} (#{milestone.number})")

    created = []
    for spec in SPECS:
        if spec["title"].lower() in existing_titles:
            print(f"Skipping (exists): {spec['title']}")
            continue
        body = ISSUE_TEMPLATE.format(**{k: spec[k] for k in
                                        ("what", "where", "verify", "constraints",
                                         "economy_note", "slug", "concept")})
        issue = repo.create_issue(
            title=spec["title"],
            body=body,
            labels=["ready-for-ai"],
            assignees=[username],
            milestone=milestone,
        )
        issue.edit(body=body.replace("feature/issue-N-", f"feature/issue-{issue.number}-"))
        print(f"  Created #{issue.number}: {spec['title']}")
        print(f"  Concept: {spec['concept']}")
        created.append({"number": issue.number, "title": spec["title"],
                        "concept": spec["concept"], "url": issue.html_url})

    print("\n=== Tonight's ready-for-ai queue ===")
    label = repo.get_label("ready-for-ai")
    count = 0
    for issue in repo.get_issues(state="open", labels=[label]):
        if issue.pull_request:
            continue
        print(f"  #{issue.number:3} {issue.title}")
        print(f"       URL: {issue.html_url}")
        count += 1
    print(f"\nTotal: {count} issues queued")

    summary = (
        f"# Issue Planning Summary\n"
        f"Date: {datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')}\n"
        f"Repo: {repo.full_name}\n"
        f"Focus: adding multiplayer\n\n"
        f"## Issues Created Tonight\n"
    )
    for i in created:
        summary += (f"- #{i['number']}: {i['title']}\n"
                    f"  Concept: {i['concept']}\n  URL: {i['url']}\n\n")
    summary += (
        "\n## What Was NOT Planned\n"
        "- Phase B (headless cpp_game_server target, deploy-aws-server skill): plan\n"
        "  defers it until an AWS instance exists; free-tier RAM vs local Ollama is\n"
        "  an open question in the plan.\n"
        "- NAT traversal/UPnP, persistence, >4 players, player chat: out of scope\n"
        "  per .claude/plans/multiplayer-and-aws-deploy.md.\n"
        "- The unpushed 8-pluggable-llm-and-one-click branch is unrelated to this\n"
        "  milestone and was not turned into issues.\n"
    )
    Path(".claude/memory/planning-session.md").write_text(summary)
    print("\nPlan saved to .claude/memory/planning-session.md")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text:
You are running an overnight autonomous development session on this
repository. Use the overnight-coordinator agent to manage the full session.
You have full permission to read, write, commit, push, and open draft PRs.
You do NOT have permission to merge to main or close PRs after opening them.

## SETUP (run once at session start)

```bash
# 1. Ensure we are on main and up to date
git checkout main
git pull

# 2. Rebuild the knowledge graph so you navigate current code, not stale code
# (only if graphify is installed — skip silently if not)
graphify update . --force 2>/dev/null || echo "graphify not installed — skipping"

# 3. Check for a prior checkpoint (resume if interrupted)
cat .claude/memory/checkpoint.md 2>/dev/null || echo "No checkpoint — starting fresh"

# 4. Read tonight's issues
gh issue list --label "ready-for-ai" --json number,title,body,labels \
  --order created --limit 20
```

If a checkpoint exists and shows IN PROGRESS or FAILED stages, resume
from there rather than starting over.

Write the session start to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
# Checkpoint
Session started: [timestamp]
Goal: Work through all ready-for-ai issues
Status: IN PROGRESS
Issues to process: [list from gh output]
Issues completed: []
Issues failed: []
Issues skipped: []
```

---

## FOR EACH ISSUE (in number order, lowest first)

### A. READ AND ASSESS

```bash
gh issue view [N] --comments
```

Ask: Is this issue clear enough to attempt autonomously?

**Blockers that cause a SKIP:**
- Requires a design decision not documented in the issue
- Depends on another issue that isn't complete yet
- Requires credentials, API keys, or external resources not available
- Scope is too vague to produce a verifiable result

If blocked, label and move on — do NOT guess at intent:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "needs-human" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Skipped overnight: [specific reason]. Please clarify before re-queuing."
```

### B. ORIENT

Invoke the git-historian agent:
"Use the git-historian agent to understand the code area this issue will touch."

This surfaces hot files, recent decisions, and things NOT to redo.
Read .claude/memory/history-brief.md after it completes.

### C. MARK IN PROGRESS

```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "ai-in-progress" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Starting overnight implementation. Planning now."
```

### D. BRANCH

```bash
git checkout main
git checkout -b feature/issue-[N]
```

### E. PLAN

Use /plan-feature [concept from issue title] and wait for a plan.
Save the plan to .claude/plans/issue-[N].md

Do not implement until you have a written plan.

### F. IMPLEMENT

Use the appropriate specialist agents for this repo (see repo-specific
section below). Follow the plan. Write complete code — no placeholders.

If you hit a problem after 2 attempts on the same sticking point, SKIP
the issue and mark it ai-blocked. Do not spiral.

### G. TEST

Run the project's test suite. The exact commands are in the repo-specific
section below. Tests MUST pass before committing.

If tests fail after 2 fix attempts: skip, mark blocked, move on.
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --remove-label "ai-in-progress" --add-label "ai-blocked"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Blocked: tests failing after 2 attempts. [describe failure]. Needs human attention."
git checkout main
git branch -D feature/issue-[N]
```

### H. COMMIT AND PUSH

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "fix(#[N]): [issue title, shortened]"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### I. OPEN DRAFT PR

Generate the PR description using the /mr-description command, then:

```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "fix(#[N]): [issue title]" \
  --body "[output from /mr-description]" \
  --base main \
  --head feature/issue-[N] \
  --draft
```

Label the issue complete and close it with a reference to the PR:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] \
  --remove-label "ai-in-progress" \
  --add-label "ai-completed"
gh issue close [N] \
  --comment "Implemented. Draft PR open for review — see above."
```

### J. GENERATE LEARNING MATERIALS

**Identify the primary concept:**
Ask yourself: "What is the single most important technical concept a
developer would need to understand to maintain or extend this change?"

Guidelines:
- Choose the concept, not the feature name
  ("triple-channel SCPI addressing" not "E3631A support")
- Should be teachable in one lesson
- Should have testable recall in a drill
- Should introduce vocabulary worth learning

Then generate all three artifacts. In overnight/automated context:
- Generate the HTML files fully
- Skip in-chat interactive knowledge checks (no user present)
- Make the HTML content thorough — it is the only output
- Update PROGRESS.md with what was covered

```
/teach [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/drill-me [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/drills/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/terms [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/vocab/NNNN-[concept].html
and updates docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md

Commit the learning materials on the same feature branch:
```bash
git add docs/learning/
git commit -m "docs(learning): add lesson, drill and vocab for [concept] (from issue #[N])"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### K. UPDATE CHECKPOINT

Append to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
Issue #[N]: [COMPLETED | FAILED | SKIPPED]
  Branch: feature/issue-[N]
  PR: #[PR number if opened]
  Concept taught: [concept]
  Learning files: lessons/NNNN-x.html, drills/NNNN-x.html, vocab/NNNN-x.html
  Notes: [anything notable]
```

Return to main: `git checkout main`

---

## END OF ALL ISSUES

### 1. Rebuild the learning index

```
/index
```

Commit:
```bash
git add docs/learning/index.html
git commit -m "docs(learning): rebuild index after overnight run $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

### 2. Write the morning report

Write OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md to the repo root:

```markdown
# Overnight Build Report
Date: [date]

git add src/core/LlmClient.cpp tests/test_llm_client.cpp && git commit -m "fix(llm): take the queue mutex before signalling worker shutdown

The destructor set stop_ and notified without holding requestMutex_, so
the notify could land between the worker evaluating its wait predicate
(false) and blocking on the condition variable — a lost wakeup that left
join() hanging forever. Surfaced as a once-in-a-few-runs suite hang
during multiplayer flake checks. Regression test: 200 construct/destroy
cycles, which hit exactly the destructor-vs-wait-entry window.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>" && git add src/core/NetSocket.hpp src/core/NetServer.hpp src/core/NetServer.cpp src/core/NetClient.hpp src/core/NetClient.cpp tests/test_net_loopback.cpp && git commit -m "feat(net): NetServer and NetClient with join handshake and world snapshots

NetServer accepts up to kMaxPlayers-1 remote players (version + join-code
+ capacity checks in the handshake), applies PlayerInput, and broadcasts
WorldSnapshots at snapshotHz. Thread contract: server threads touch only
sockets and internal queues — the host loop publishes poses in and drains
chat events out, so World/LlmClient stay single-threaded as in solo play.
NetClient connects with a 4s timeout, drains via poll() (LlmClient's
drainReplies shape). NetSocket.hpp carries the winsock/POSIX shims; on
macOS SIGPIPE is suppressed per-socket (SO_NOSIGPIPE). Five loopback
tests live (join, movement, unreachable, session-full, version
mismatch); suite green 8x consecutively.

project(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)

set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

find_package(Threads REQUIRED)
# Game executable needs SFML+OpenGL; QUIET so the dev container can still
# configure CMake and build the core library + tests without them.
find_package(SFML 2.6 COMPONENTS graphics window system QUIET)
find_package(OpenGL QUIET)

# Core: SFML-free game logic shared with the unit tests.
add_library(llm_npc_core STATIC
    src/core/City.cpp
    src/core/Config.cpp
    src/core/DialogueSession.cpp
    src/core/KeyBindings.cpp
    src/core/LlmClient.cpp
    src/core/NetClient.cpp
    src/core/NetFraming.cpp
    src/core/NetMessage.cpp
    src/core/NetServer.cpp
    src/core/Npc.cpp
    src/core/PersonaLoader.cpp
    src/core/World.cpp
)
target_include_directories(llm_npc_core PUBLIC
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/core
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/external
)
target_link_libraries(llm_npc_core PUBLIC Threads::Threads)
if(WIN32)
    # httplib needs winsock when built with MinGW.
    target_link_libraries(llm_npc_core PUBLIC ws2_32)
endif()

if(SFML_FOUND AND OPENGL_FOUND)
    add_executable(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
        src/app/main.cpp
        src/app/DialogUI.cpp
        src/app/InputMap.cpp
        src/app/Menu.cpp
        src/app/Renderer3D.cpp
    )
    target_include_directories(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/app
    )
    target_link_libraries(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs
        PRIVATE
            llm_npc_core
            sfml-graphics
            sfml-window
            sfml-system
            OpenGL::GL
    )
    if(APPLE)
        # Mouse-look uses CoreGraphics cursor warping directly; see main.cpp.
        target_link_libraries(cpp_game_with_llm_npcs PRIVATE
            "-framework ApplicationServices")
    endif()
else()
    message(STATUS "SFML or OpenGL not found; building core library only "
                   "(use tests/Makefile for the test suite)")
endif()

# LLM NPC City

A small first-person 3D city where every inhabitant is a live LLM character.
Walk the streets, find the baker, the cop, the busker, the hot-dog vendor —
press `T` and talk to them about anything. Each NPC has their own personality,
their own knowledge of the city (and pointed ignorance of everything else),
and remembers your conversation.

Powered locally by [Ollama](https://ollama.com) — no cloud, no API key.

## Quick start (Windows)

1. **Install Ollama** from <https://ollama.com/download>, then pull the model:

   ```
   ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
   ```

2. **Install MSYS2** from <https://www.msys2.org> and, in the *UCRT64* shell:

   ```
   pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml
   ```

3. **Double-click `run.bat`** (or run `./run.ps1`). It checks Ollama is up,
   builds, and launches the game.

## Playing

- `WASD` to walk, mouse to look around.
- Walk up to anyone: `[T] Talk to <name>` appears — press `T`.
- Type, press `Enter`, and watch the reply stream in live. `Escape` to leave.
- `Escape` opens the pause menu: resume, quit, or **rebind every key with the
  mouse** (changes save instantly).

Full reference: [docs/CONTROLS.md](docs/CONTROLS.md).

## Meet the city

Ten residents, each with their own patch of downtown:

| Who | Where |
|-----|-------|
| Marge Holloway, baker | Marge's Bakery, north-west |
| Officer Dana Brooks | outside the police station |
| Theo Park, barista | Bean There Coffee |
| Ms. Adaeze Obi, librarian | the library steps |
| Hal Jensen, hardware man | Jensen Hardware |
| Gus Romano, hot-dog vendor | the cart, dead center of the plaza |
| Ray Okafor, taxi driver | idling by his cab, east of the plaza |
| Yuki Tanaka, tourist | photographing the fountain |
| Benny "Strings" Malone, busker | the park's street corner |
| Mr. Albert Whitfield, retired teacher | the park bench |

They know each other — ask Gus about the squeaky cart wheel and someone at
the hardware store may have opinions.

## Configuration

- `config/llm.cfg` — model, host/port, temperature, `keep_alive` (latency).
  Any model you have pulled in Ollama works; smaller = snappier.
- `config/keybindings.cfg` — key bindings (also editable in-game).
- `personas/*.persona` — the characters themselves. Edit freely; the file
  format is documented in [docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md).

## Development

Architecture, headless test workflow, and the latency playbook live in
[docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md). Short version:

```sh
make -C tests test      # full offline unit-test suite, no SFML required
```

3:## Architecture: core / app split
21:### Core modules
23:| Module            | Responsibility |
25:| `LlmClient`       | One worker thread for all NPCs. Streams Ollama `/api/chat` (NDJSON); main thread polls `drainDeltas()` / `drainReplies()` per frame. `warmUp()` preloads the model; `keep_alive` keeps it resident. |
26:| `StreamAssembler` | Reassembles NDJSON lines from arbitrary TCP chunk boundaries; `parseOllamaChunk` maps one line to delta/done/error. |
27:| `Persona`         | Static NPC identity, rendered into the system prompt. |
28:| `PersonaLoader`   | Parses `personas/*.persona` (key=value header, `---`, free-form directives) including world placement. |
29:| `Npc`             | Per-NPC chat history (bounded), pending-request tracking, world placement. History only grows on successful replies. |
30:| `City`            | Building AABBs + circle collision with axis-separated slide (`resolveMovement`). |
31:| `World`           | City + NPC roster; `nearestNpcWithin` drives the talk prompt. |
32:| `DialogueSession` | Roaming → Talking → WaitingReply → Streaming state machine; routes streamed deltas by request id. |
33:| `KeyBindings`     | Action → key-name map with swap-on-conflict rebinding and file persistence. Names are translated to SFML codes only in `src/app/InputMap`. |
34:| `Config`          | Tiny key=value reader + `llm.cfg` loader. |

## Multiplayer (2-4 friends)

One player hosts; up to three more walk the same city and talk to the same
NPCs — one shared brain per character, so the baker remembers what your
friend told her.

**Hosting:** `Escape` → **Multiplayer** → **Host on port 40605**. Your machine
runs the world and the LLM; nobody else needs Ollama. Tell your friends your
IP address (`ipconfig` / `ifconfig`, e.g. `192.168.1.20`).

**Joining:** `Escape` → **Multiplayer** → click the address field, type
`<host-ip>:40605`, press `Enter`. Connection problems show up right there —
wrong address, full session (4 players max), or mismatched game versions.

What to expect in a session:

- Everyone sees everyone walk around, plus each NPC's live position and mood.
- NPC conversations are private to read, public in effect: if your friend
  angers Officer Brooks, you'll see her scowl.
- An NPC answers one person at a time; a second question waits its turn.
- Only the host's world persists — when the host quits, the session ends.

**Beyond your LAN:** the internet can't reach your living room uninvited.
Either forward TCP port 40605 on the host's router, or skip router config
entirely with [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com)/ZeroTier (both make a
private network where your friends use the host's Tailscale IP). The game
does not do NAT punching itself.

# LLM NPC City

A small first-person 3D city where every inhabitant is a live LLM character.
Walk the streets, find the baker, the cop, the busker, the hot-dog vendor —
press `T` and talk to them about anything. Each NPC has their own personality,
their own knowledge of the city (and pointed ignorance of everything else),
and remembers your conversation.

Powered locally by [Ollama](https://ollama.com) — no cloud, no API key.

## Quick start (Windows)

1. **Install Ollama** from <https://ollama.com/download>, then pull the model:

   ```
   ollama pull qwen2.5:3b-instruct
   ```

2. **Install MSYS2** from <https://www.msys2.org> and, in the *UCRT64* shell:

   ```
   pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sfml
   ```

3. **Double-click `run.bat`** (or run `./run.ps1`). It checks Ollama is up,
   builds, and launches the game.

## Playing

- `WASD` to walk, mouse to look around.
- Walk up to anyone: `[T] Talk to <name>` appears — press `T`.
- Type, press `Enter`, and watch the reply stream in live. `Escape` to leave.
- `Escape` opens the pause menu: resume, quit, or **rebind every key with the
  mouse** (changes save instantly).

Full reference: [docs/CONTROLS.md](docs/CONTROLS.md).

## Meet the city

Ten residents, each with their own patch of downtown:

| Who | Where |
|-----|-------|
| Marge Holloway, baker | Marge's Bakery, north-west |
| Officer Dana Brooks | outside the police station |
| Theo Park, barista | Bean There Coffee |
| Ms. Adaeze Obi, librarian | the library steps |
| Hal Jensen, hardware man | Jensen Hardware |
| Gus Romano, hot-dog vendor | the cart, dead center of the plaza |
| Ray Okafor, taxi driver | idling by his cab, east of the plaza |
| Yuki Tanaka, tourist | photographing the fountain |
| Benny "Strings" Malone, busker | the park's street corner |
| Mr. Albert Whitfield, retired teacher | the park bench |

They know each other — ask Gus about the squeaky cart wheel and someone at
the hardware store may have opinions.

## Configuration

- `config/llm.cfg` — model, host/port, temperature, `keep_alive` (latency).
  Any model you have pulled in Ollama works; smaller = snappier.
- `config/keybindings.cfg` — key bindings (also editable in-game).
- `personas/*.persona` — the characters themselves. Edit freely; the file
  format is documented in [docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md).

## Development

Architecture, headless test workflow, and the latency playbook live in
[docs/DEVELOPER.md](docs/DEVELOPER.md). Short version:

```sh
make -C tests test      # full offline unit-test suite, no SFML required
```

  first-person camera, and `worldToScreen` for SFML nameplates.

# Developer Guide

## Architecture: core / app split

The codebase is split so that all game logic builds and tests on a headless
machine, while graphics stay isolated:

```
src/core/   SFML-free, GL-free. Everything here is unit-tested.
src/app/    SFML + OpenGL. Only builds where graphics libs exist (Windows).
external/   Vendored single-header deps: httplib, nlohmann/json, doctest.
tests/      doctest suites + a plain-make runner for cmake-less containers.
personas/   One .persona file per NPC (identity + world placement).
config/     llm.cfg (model/host/latency) and keybindings.cfg.
```

CMake builds the `llm_npc_core` static library unconditionally; the game
executable is added only when `SFML_FOUND AND OPENGL_FOUND`. Keep it that
way: **nothing in `src/core/` may include SFML or OpenGL headers.**

### Core modules

| Module            | Responsibility |
|-------------------|----------------|
| `LlmClient`       | One worker thread for all NPCs. Streams Ollama `/api/chat` (NDJSON); main thread polls `drainDeltas()` / `drainReplies()` per frame. `warmUp()` preloads the model; `keep_alive` keeps it resident. |
| `StreamAssembler` | Reassembles NDJSON lines from arbitrary TCP chunk boundaries; `parseOllamaChunk` maps one line to delta/done/error. |
| `Persona`         | Static NPC identity, rendered into the system prompt. |
| `PersonaLoader`   | Parses `personas/*.persona` (key=value header, `---`, free-form directives) including world placement. |
| `Npc`             | Per-NPC chat history (bounded), pending-request tracking, world placement. History only grows on successful replies. |
| `City`            | Building AABBs + circle collision with axis-separated slide (`resolveMovement`). |
| `World`           | City + NPC roster; `nearestNpcWithin` drives the talk prompt. |
| `DialogueSession` | Roaming → Talking → WaitingReply → Streaming state machine; routes streamed deltas by request id. |
| `KeyBindings`     | Action → key-name map with swap-on-conflict rebinding and file persistence. Names are translated to SFML codes only in `src/app/InputMap`. |
| `Config`          | Tiny key=value reader + `llm.cfg` loader. |

### App modules

- `Renderer3D` — legacy GL 2.1 immediate mode, procedural textures, the
  first-person camera, and `worldToScreen` for SFML nameplates.
- `main.cpp` — mode machine (Playing / Dialogue / Menu) and the frame loop:
  GL 3D pass → `pushGLStates()` → SFML overlay → `popGLStates()` → `display()`.
  Always restore that order; mixing raw GL with SFML drawing outside the
  push/pop pair corrupts state.
- `DialogUI` — chat overlay with live streaming line; `swallowNextTextEntered()`
  keeps the talk key's character out of the input box.
- `Menu` — mouse-driven pause menu and key rebinding.
- `InputMap` — portable key-name ↔ `sf::Keyboard::Key` table.

## Building and testing

### Container / Linux (no SFML needed)

```sh
make -C tests test          # builds core + all unit tests with g++, runs them
```

The make runner is the primary gate: run it before every commit. It compiles
`src/core/*.cpp` + `tests/test_*.cpp` with `-Wall -Wextra -pthread`.

Tests run fully offline: `tests/FakeOllama.hpp` spins an in-process
`httplib::Server` on a random port that speaks the Ollama streaming protocol,
including error modes and chunk boundaries that split JSON lines mid-token.

Live end-to-end tests (real Ollama on localhost) are opt-in:

```sh
OLLAMA_LIVE=1 make -C tests test            # uses qwen2.5:3b-instruct
OLLAMA_TEST_MODEL=llama3.2:1b OLLAMA_LIVE=1 make -C tests test
```

### Windows (full game)

```bat
run.bat        # double-clickable: checks MSYS2 + Ollama, cmake, build, play
```

or the equivalent `run.ps1`. Requires MSYS2 UCRT64 with `mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-{gcc,cmake,sfml}` and an Ollama install with the model pulled.

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles" && cmake --build build -j
ctest --test-dir build        # same doctest suites via cmake
```

## Latency playbook

Findings applied from the sibling games and the original companion demo:

1. **Stream replies** (`"stream": true`): first words render ~10x sooner than
   waiting for the full completion.
2. **`keep_alive=10m`** (config/llm.cfg): the model stays in RAM between
   conversations; without it every chat pays a multi-second reload.
3. **`warmUp()` at boot**: an empty-messages request forces the load while
   the player is still walking around.
4. **One worker thread, non-blocking drains**: the render loop never waits on
   the network; 60 FPS is independent of Ollama health.
5. Small default model (`qwen2.5:3b-instruct`) — swap via `config/llm.cfg`.

## Adding an NPC

1. Create `personas/<id>.persona` (see existing files; `name` is required,
   `position`/`facing`/`spot` place them in the world).
2. Pick a free spot — `tests/test_world.cpp` has a placement-sanity pattern;
   NPCs must not stand inside a building AABB.
3. That's it: the roster is whatever `personas/` contains, sorted by filename.
   Palette color comes from roster order (`Renderer3D::kNpcPalettes`).

## Conventions

- Commits: `type(scope): description`, small (2-3 files), pushed to the
  feature branch — never to main.
- Every public function carries a doc comment; no TODOs in committed code.
- New core logic requires doctest coverage in the same or the following
  commit.

- `Menu` — mouse-driven pause menu, key rebinding, and the Multiplayer
  host/join page (callbacks injected from `main.cpp` via `MultiplayerHooks`,
  so the menu never sees networking types).
- `InputMap` — portable key-name ↔ `sf::Keyboard::Key` table.

### Multiplayer at a glance

One process hosts: its `World` and `LlmClient` stay the single source of
truth, exactly as in solo play. `NetServer` fans state out at ~12 Hz
(`WorldSnapshot`: player poses + NPC pose/mood/behavior) and joined clients
send `PlayerInput` up. Remote NPC chat rides `ChatOpen`/`ChatLine` up and
`ChatDelta`/`ChatReply` back down to the asker only, with
`NpcSpeechBubble`/`NpcMoodUpdate` broadcast so bystanders see effects.

Wire format: every frame is `[4-byte big-endian length][JSON object]`, and
every JSON object carries a `"type"` tag. Bump `kNetProtocolVersion`
(NetMessage.hpp) whenever the format changes incompatibly — the handshake
refuses mismatched builds instead of desyncing.

Thread rule that keeps this safe: **no NetServer/NetClient thread ever
touches `World`, `Npc`, or `LlmClient`.** Game state crosses the boundary
only through value snapshots (`publishNpcPoses`) and drained queues
(`drainChatEvents`, `poll`), all pumped by the host/client main loop.
`tests/test_net_loopback.cpp` runs the full stack — server, clients, router,
FakeOllama — over 127.0.0.1 with no real network or Ollama:

```sh
make -C tests test    # includes framing, protocol, and loopback suites
```

Both machines should run the same build and the same `personas/` roster
(clients label NPC nameplates from their local persona files).

| `NetSocket`       | Header-only winsock/POSIX shims: `sendAll`, recv timeouts, `SO_NOSIGPIPE` on macOS. |
| `NetServer`       | Authoritative host. Threads: accept → per-connection reader (handshake: version, join code, `kMaxPlayers`) → tick (snapshot broadcast + connection reaping). Its threads touch only sockets and queues; the host loop feeds `setHostPose`/`publishNpcPoses` in and drains `drainChatEvents()` out, so `World`/`LlmClient` stay single-threaded. |
| `NetClient`       | Joining side: `connect` (4s timeout + handshake), reader thread → `poll()` drain on the main loop (the `drainReplies` shape). Never simulates; renders what snapshots say. |
| `HostChatRouter`  | Host-loop glue routing remote NPC chat: per-NPC queues serialize concurrent askers, deltas/replies return to the requesting player only, `NpcSpeechBubble`/`NpcMoodUpdate` broadcast to all. |

### App modules

- `Renderer3D` — legacy GL 2.1 immediate mode, procedural textures, the
  first-person camera, and `worldToScreen` for SFML nameplates.
- `main.cpp` — mode machine (Playing / Dialogue / Menu) and the frame loop:
  GL 3D pass → `pushGLStates()` → SFML overlay → `popGLStates()` → `display()`.
  Always restore that order; mixing raw GL with SFML drawing outside the
  push/pop pair corrupts state.
- `DialogUI` — chat overlay with live streaming line; `swallowNextTextEntered()`
  keeps the talk key's character out of the input box.
- `Menu` — mouse-driven pause menu and key rebinding.
- `InputMap` — portable key-name ↔ `sf::Keyboard::Key` table.

## Building and testing

### Container / Linux (no SFML needed)

```sh
make -C tests test          # builds core + all unit tests with g++, runs them
```

The make runner is the primary gate: run it before every commit. It compiles
`src/core/*.cpp` + `tests/test_*.cpp` with `-Wall -Wextra -pthread`.

Tests run fully offline: `tests/FakeOllama.hpp` spins an in-process
`httplib::Server` on a random port that speaks the Ollama streaming protocol,
including error modes and chunk boundaries that split JSON lines mid-token.

Live end-to-end tests (real Ollama on localhost) are opt-in:

```sh
OLLAMA_LIVE=1 make -C tests test            # uses qwen2.5:3b-instruct
OLLAMA_TEST_MODEL=llama3.2:1b OLLAMA_LIVE=1 make -C tests test
```

### Windows (full game)

```bat
run.bat        # double-clickable: checks MSYS2 + Ollama, cmake, build, play
```

or the equivalent `run.ps1`. Requires MSYS2 UCRT64 with `mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-{gcc,cmake,sfml}` and an Ollama install with the model pulled.

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles" && cmake --build build -j
ctest --test-dir build        # same doctest suites via cmake
```

## Latency playbook

Findings applied from the sibling games and the original companion demo:

1. **Stream replies** (`"stream": true`): first words render ~10x sooner than
   waiting for the full completion.
2. **`keep_alive=10m`** (config/llm.cfg): the model stays in RAM between
   conversations; without it every chat pays a multi-second reload.
3. **`warmUp()` at boot**: an empty-messages request forces the load while
   the player is still walking around.
4. **One worker thread, non-blocking drains**: the render loop never waits on
   the network; 60 FPS is independent of Ollama health.
5. Small default model (`qwen2.5:3b-instruct`) — swap via `config/llm.cfg`.

## Adding an NPC

1. Create `personas/<id>.persona` (see existing files; `name` is required,
   `position`/`facing`/`spot` place them in the world).
2. Pick a free spot — `tests/test_world.cpp` has a placement-sanity pattern;
   NPCs must not stand inside a building AABB.
3. That's it: the roster is whatever `personas/` contains, sorted by filename.
   Palette color comes from roster order (`Renderer3D::kNpcPalettes`).

## Conventions

- Commits: `type(scope): description`, small (2-3 files), pushed to the
  feature branch — never to main.
- Every public function carries a doc comment; no TODOs in committed code.
- New core logic requires doctest coverage in the same or the following
  commit.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Create the multiplayer milestone, labels, 7 issues, and stacked draft PRs
for the branches pushed overnight on bjl14710/cpp_game_with_llm_npcs."""
import os
import sys

from github import Github, GithubException

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from create_multiplayer_issues import (ISSUE_TEMPLATE, MILESTONE_DESC,
                                       MILESTONE_TITLE, REPO_SLUG, SPECS)

USERNAME = os.environ.get("GITHUB_USERNAME", "bjl14710")

# spec index -> the branch that implemented it (None = folded elsewhere).
BRANCH_FOR_SPEC = {
    0: "feature/issue-1-net-protocol-framing",
    1: "feature/issue-2-netserver-snapshots",
    2: "feature/issue-2-netserver-snapshots",  # client landed with server
    3: "feature/issue-4-server-npc-chat",
    4: "feature/issue-5-menu-host-join",

    6: "feature/issue-7-docs-multiplayer",
}

# (head, base, title, body-intro, spec indexes it closes)
PR_CHAIN = [
    ("feature/multiplayer-scaffold", "main",
     "chore(net): scaffold multiplayer core modules and test stubs",
     "Skeletons and skipped doctest stubs for the shared-world multiplayer v1 "
     "(plan: `.claude/plans/multiplayer-and-aws-deploy.md`). No behavior "
     "change; every stub is `doctest::skip()` so the suite stays green.\n\n"
     "**Merge order: 1 of 6** — merge this first; the stack re-targets "
     "automatically.",
     []),
    ("feature/issue-1-net-protocol-framing", "feature/multiplayer-scaffold",
     "feat(net): message protocol and length-prefixed framing",
     "`FrameAssembler` (4-byte big-endian length prefix, 1 MiB cap, "
     "connection-drop on violation) and the `NetMessage` JSON codec "
     "(type-tagged envelope, nullopt on garbage, Vec3/pose helpers). "
     "All 11 framing/protocol stubs are now live tests.\n\n"
     "**Merge order: 2 of 6.**",
     [0]),
    ("feature/issue-2-netserver-snapshots", "feature/issue-1-net-protocol-framing",
     "feat(net): NetServer and NetClient with join handshake and world snapshots",
     "The authoritative host (accept/reader/tick threads, version + join-code "
     "+ capacity handshake, snapshot broadcast) and the joining client "
     "(timeout connect, poll() drain). Thread contract: server threads touch "
     "only sockets/queues — World and LlmClient stay single-threaded.\n\n"
     "**Also fixes a pre-existing deadlock**: `LlmClient::~LlmClient` set "
     "`stop_` and notified without the queue mutex — a lost wakeup that hung "
     "`join()` about once per few suite runs (caught by tonight's flake "
     "checks; regression test included: 200 construct/destroy cycles).\n\n"
     "Five loopback tests live (join, movement, unreachable, session-full, "
     "version mismatch); suite green 8x consecutively.\n\n"
     "**Merge order: 3 of 6.**",
     [1, 2]),
    ("feature/issue-4-server-npc-chat", "feature/issue-2-netserver-snapshots",
     "feat(net): route NPC dialogue through the server with mood/speech broadcast",
     "`HostChatRouter` (host-main-loop glue): remote ChatLines queue per-NPC "
     "and serialize through the one shared Npc/LlmClient path — same NPC, "
     "same memory, for every player. Deltas/replies go only to the asker; "
     "`NpcSpeechBubble`/`NpcMoodUpdate` broadcast to everyone. LLM failures "
     "reach just the requester; a mid-conversation disconnect drops only that "

     "other; walk around and chat with the same NPC from both.\n\n"

]


def main() -> None:
    token = os.environ.get("GH_TOKEN") or os.environ.get("GITHUB_TOKEN")
    if not token:
        raise SystemExit("GH_TOKEN not set")
    gh = Github(token)
    repo = gh.get_repo(REPO_SLUG)
    print(f"Syncing: {repo.full_name}")

    for name, color, description in LABELS:
        try:
            repo.create_label(name=name, color=color, description=description)
            print(f"label created: {name}")
        except GithubException as e:
            if e.status != 422:
                raise
            print(f"label exists: {name}")

    milestone = None
    for m in repo.get_milestones(state="open"):
        if m.title == MILESTONE_TITLE:
            milestone = m
            break
    if milestone is None:
        milestone = repo.create_milestone(title=MILESTONE_TITLE, description=MILESTONE_DESC)
    print(f"milestone: #{milestone.number} {milestone.title}")

    existing_titles = {}
    for issue in repo.get_issues(state="all"):
        if not issue.pull_request:
            existing_titles[issue.title.lower()] = issue

    issue_numbers = {}  # spec index -> issue number
    for idx, spec in enumerate(SPECS):
        if spec["title"].lower() in existing_titles:
            issue_numbers[idx] = existing_titles[spec["title"].lower()].number
            print(f"issue exists: #{issue_numbers[idx]} {spec['title']}")
            continue
        body = ISSUE_TEMPLATE.format(**{k: spec[k] for k in
                                        ("what", "where", "verify", "constraints",
                                         "economy_note", "slug", "concept")})
        issue = repo.create_issue(title=spec["title"], body=body,
                                  labels=["ai-completed"], assignees=[USERNAME],
                                  milestone=milestone)
        branch = BRANCH_FOR_SPEC.get(idx)
        real_branch = branch if branch else "feature/issue-2-netserver-snapshots + feature/issue-4-server-npc-chat"
        issue.edit(body=body.replace("feature/issue-N-" + spec["slug"], real_branch))
        issue_numbers[idx] = issue.number
        print(f"issue created: #{issue.number} {spec['title']}")

    existing_pr_heads = {pr.head.ref: pr for pr in repo.get_pulls(state="open")}
    created_prs = []
    for head, base, title, intro, closes in PR_CHAIN:
        if head in existing_pr_heads:
            print(f"PR exists for {head}: #{existing_pr_heads[head].number}")
            created_prs.append(existing_pr_heads[head])
            continue
        body = intro + "\n\n**Testing:** `make -C tests test` — 96 cases, 0 failed, "
        body += "repeated runs clean (threaded loopback suites flake-checked).\n"
        if closes:
            body += "\n" + "\n".join(f"Closes #{issue_numbers[i]}" for i in closes) + "\n"
        body += "\n---\n\U0001F916 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\n"
        try:
            pr = repo.create_pull(title=title, body=body, head=head, base=base, draft=True)
        except GithubException as e:
            if e.status == 422 and any("draft" in str(err).lower()
                                       for err in (e.data or {}).get("errors", [])):
                pr = repo.create_pull(title=title, body=body, head=head, base=base)
            else:
                raise
        created_prs.append(pr)
        print(f"PR created: #{pr.number} {title} ({head} -> {base})")

    for idx, num in issue_numbers.items():
        branch = BRANCH_FOR_SPEC.get(idx)
        pr_link = next((f"#{pr.number}" for pr in created_prs if branch and pr.head.ref == branch),
                       "#" + str(created_prs[3].number) + " and #" + str(created_prs[2].number))
        issue = repo.get_issue(num)
        if not any("Implemented overnight" in (c.body or "") for c in issue.get_comments()):
            issue.create_comment(f"Implemented overnight. Draft PR: {pr_link}\n"
                                 f"Merge the PR stack bottom-up (scaffold first); "
                                 f"this issue closes automatically when its PR merges.")

    print("\n=== Draft PR stack (merge top to bottom) ===")
    for pr in created_prs:
        print(f"  #{pr.number} {pr.title}\n      {pr.html_url}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Lesson 0008 · Multiplayer networking · from feat(net): message protocol and length-prefixed framing

Length-Prefixed Framing over TCP

Why FrameAssembler exists, and why "just send the JSON" doesn't work.

The problem: TCP is a byte stream, not a message service

TCP guarantees bytes arrive in order and uncorrupted — but it says nothing about where one write ends and the next begins. If the host sends {"type":"Welcome"} and then {"type":"WorldSnapshot",...}, the client's recv() might return both glued together, or the first half of one, or three bytes of a length header. Anything.

Every "works on my machine, breaks over Wi-Fi" protocol bug starts with code that assumes one send() equals one recv(). It never reliably does.

Two classic fixes

StrategyHowWhere this repo uses it
Delimiter framingEnd every message with a byte that can't appear inside it (e.g. \n)StreamAssembler — Ollama's NDJSON stream, one JSON object per line
Length-prefixed framingSend the payload size first, then exactly that many bytesFrameAssembler (src/core/NetFraming.hpp) — all multiplayer traffic

Delimiters are great when the sender guarantees the delimiter never appears in a message (NDJSON promises exactly that). For our own protocol we chose a 4-byte big-endian length prefix: no escaping rules, O(1) "do I have a full message yet?" checks, and binary-safe if we ever move off JSON.

The wire format

[ 4 bytes: payload length, big-endian ][ length bytes: JSON payload ]
[ 00 00 00 11 ][ {"type":"ChatOpen"} ]

Big-endian (network byte order) is the convention every internet protocol uses for multi-byte integers — both peers must agree, and x86/ARM CPUs are little-endian, so the code converts explicitly with shifts rather than casting an int's raw bytes:

frame.push_back(static_cast<char>((len >> 24) & 0xFF));  // most significant first
frame.push_back(static_cast<char>((len >> 16) & 0xFF));
frame.push_back(static_cast<char>((len >> 8) & 0xFF));
frame.push_back(static_cast<char>(len & 0xFF));

Reassembly: the accumulate-and-peel loop

bool FrameAssembler::feed(bytes, onFrame) {
    buffer_.append(bytes);                    // whatever recv() gave us
    while (buffer_.size() >= 4) {             // enough for a prefix?
        uint32_t declared = readPrefix(buffer_);
        if (declared > kMaxFrameBytes) return false;   // see below
        if (buffer_.size() < 4 + declared) return true; // wait for more
        onFrame(buffer_.substr(4, declared)); // complete frame!
        buffer_.erase(0, 4 + declared);       // peel and repeat
    }
    return true;
}

Bytes can arrive split anywhere — mid-prefix, mid-payload — and multiple frames can arrive in one read. The loop handles both: it buffers until a whole frame exists, emits it, and keeps going. tests/test_net_framing.cpp feeds a frame one byte at a time to prove it.

The poisoned-prefix problem

If a prefix is corrupt (or hostile) and declares a 3 GB payload, a naive reader allocates 3 GB and waits forever. Worse: once you mistrust one prefix, you can never find the next frame boundary again — the stream is unrecoverable.

That's why feed() returns false when the declared length exceeds kMaxFrameBytes (1 MiB — generous, since a 4-player snapshot is a few KB), and why the caller's only correct response is to drop the connection. There is no "skip this frame": without trusting the length, you don't know where it ends.

Contrast: StreamAssembler vs FrameAssembler

The two classes are siblings — same feed/callback shape, different boundary rule:

  • StreamAssembler::feed() scans for \n; unbounded line length (trusts Ollama).
  • FrameAssembler::feed() reads a declared size; bounded, endian-explicit, drop-on-violation (trusts nobody).
Design takeaway: when you control both ends of a socket, a length prefix is almost always the simplest robust choice. Reach for delimiters only when a protocol you don't control already promises them.

Lesson 0009 · Multiplayer networking · from feat(net): NetServer and NetClient

Server-Authoritative Replication and the Thread Contract

How four players share one world without sharing one crash.

Who owns the truth?

In a networked game, some machine must be the referee. Two players both think they reached the hot-dog cart first — whose claim wins? This game answers the way most multiplayer games do: the host is authoritative. The host's World, its NPC positions, moods, and conversation histories are the only real ones. Clients hold a replica: a copy that's a few dozen milliseconds stale, refreshed ~12 times a second by WorldSnapshot broadcasts.

DirectionMessageContent
client → hostPlayerInputmy position + facing this frame
host → allWorldSnapshotevery player pose + every NPC pose/mood/behavior

Joined clients stop simulating entirely — main.cpp skips npc.update() when joined and renders straight from the last snapshot. A replica that also simulates drifts from the authority; then you need reconciliation machinery. Not simulating is the simplest correct thing.

The three server threads

accept thread    one blocking accept() loop; spawns a reader per connection
reader threads   one per client: recv → FrameAssembler → decodeMessage → apply
tick thread      every 1/12 s: build snapshot, broadcast, reap dead connections

Each blocking concern gets its own thread so nothing can starve anything else: a client that stalls mid-handshake only stalls its own reader. Shutdown is the subtle part — a blocked recv() doesn't return just because you set a flag. The trick used throughout NetServer/NetClient: shutdown(fd, SHUT_RDWR) forces the blocked call to return, then join() the thread, then close(fd). Closing before joining risks the kernel recycling the fd number while the old thread still uses it.

The thread contract (the load-bearing decision)

No network thread ever touches World, Npc, or LlmClient. Game state crosses the boundary only as values through mutex-guarded queues, pumped by the host's main loop.
// host main loop, once per frame:
netServer->setHostPose(camera.position, camera.yawDeg);   // value in
netServer->publishNpcPoses(posesCopiedFromWorld);          // values in
chatRouter->update();   // drains drainChatEvents() — events out

Why so strict? The alternative is the tick thread reading world.npcs()[i].position() while the render loop writes it — a data race, which in C++ is undefined behavior even when it "mostly works". Locking World instead would leak mutexes into every system that touches NPCs, including solo play. The publish/drain contract keeps all game logic single-threaded — exactly as it was before multiplayer existed — which is why the solo code path didn't change.

This is the same pattern LlmClient already used: its worker thread never touches NPCs either; the main loop drains drainDeltas()/drainReplies(). Multiplayer just applied the house pattern to a second subsystem.

The handshake: reject early, reject loudly

  1. Client connects and sends JoinRequest {version, name, code}.
  2. Server checks, in order: protocol version (mismatched builds get told to update, not left to desync), join code, capacity (lowest free id 1..3; none free → "session full").
  3. Welcome {accepted, playerId} or Welcome {accepted:false, reason}.
The version check is the cheapest insurance in the protocol: one int compared once per join, versus hours of debugging why your friend's older build renders everyone at the origin.

Where the ids live

The host is always player 0. Remote ids (1-3) are assigned at handshake and reused after a disconnect — the session-full test proves a slot frees up when someone leaves. NPCs are identified by roster index, which is safe because this codebase never deletes NPCs (an existing invariant the wire protocol now depends on).

Lesson 0010 · Multiplayer networking · from feat(net): route NPC dialogue through the server

Request-Id Routing: One LLM, Many Askers

How HostChatRouter gives four players one shared NPC brain without crossing anyone's wires.

The fan-in / fan-out problem

All NPC replies stream out of a single LlmClient as anonymous-looking ChatDelta{id, text} fragments. In solo play, "who is this for?" had one easy answer: the open dialogue. With remote players, one stream now serves:

  • the host's own conversation (rendered in the local DialogUI),
  • player 2 chatting with the baker (goes over player 2's socket only),
  • player 3 chatting with the cop (player 3's socket only).

The routing key already existed: LlmClient::submit() returns a unique, monotonically increasing request id, and every delta and reply carries it. The router just remembers who each id belongs to:

uint64_t id = npc.ask(line.text);          // submit through the SHARED path
inflight_[id] = {line.playerId, npcIndex}; // claim the id for that player

The host's frame loop drains the LLM queues exactly once, offering each item to the router first. Consumed means "that was a remote player's"; declined falls through to the existing solo handling, untouched:

for (auto& d : client.drainDeltas()) {
    if (chatRouter && chatRouter->routeDelta(d)) continue;  // remote → socket
    if (session.deltaArrived(d.id, d.text))                 // mine → DialogUI
        dialog.appendStreamingDelta(d.text);
}
This boolean consume-or-pass shape is how you extend a single-consumer queue to two consumers without rewriting either: the new consumer gets first refusal, the old code cannot tell anything changed.

An Npc tracks exactly one pending request (pendingId_), so two simultaneous questions to the same NPC would clobber each other. The router enforces one-at-a-time per NPC with a queue:

// pumpNpc(): if (!npc.waiting()) submit the front line

npc.waiting() covers anyone's in-flight question — including the host's — so host and guests can't interleave a conversation turn. When a reply resolves, the router pumps that NPC's queue again: the next asker gets their turn, in order. Different NPCs don't queue on each other (the single LlmClient worker serializes actual HTTP calls, but that's an implementation detail the router doesn't depend on).

On a successful reply the router does three sends with different audiences:

  1. ChatReply → the asker only (their transcript).
  2. NpcSpeechBubble → everyone (bystanders see the NPC speak).
  3. NpcMoodUpdate → everyone (faces update on all screens).

Failures are the asymmetric case: an "Ollama unreachable" error goes to the requesting player only. Broadcasting errors would tell every player about a problem only one of them can act on.

Note the shared-memory consequence: npc.onReplyArrived() appends to the one true history no matter who asked. Tell the baker your name, and she knows it when your friend talks to her — that's the "same NPC for everyone" feature, implemented by not duplicating state.

Disconnects: drop the route, keep the world

If a player leaves mid-reply, the reply still resolves against the NPC (history stays consistent), but sendToPlayer() returns false and the payload evaporates. Nothing else notices. The loopback test proves the next player can immediately use the same NPC — the failure of one client is never allowed to wedge shared state.

Lesson 0011 · Concurrency · from fix(llm): take the queue mutex before signalling worker shutdown

Condition Variables and the Lost Wakeup

A real bug from this codebase: the game's test suite hung roughly one run in five, and the fix was two lines of lock scope.

The crime scene

LlmClient runs one worker thread that sleeps on a condition variable until there's a request (or shutdown). The destructor looked reasonable:

// BUGGY — as it was before the fix
LlmClient::~LlmClient() {
    stop_.store(true);          // stop_ is a std::atomic<bool>
    requestCv_.notify_all();
    if (worker_.joinable()) worker_.join();   // hung here, forever
}

// worker side
std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);
requestCv_.wait(lock, [this] { return stop_.load() || !requests_.empty(); });

stop_ is atomic, so no data race. notify_all() is called after the store. What could possibly go wrong?

The interleaving that kills it

worker thread                          destructor thread
─────────────────────────────          ─────────────────────────────
locks requestMutex_
evaluates predicate → false
                                       stop_.store(true)
                                       requestCv_.notify_all()   ← nobody is waiting yet!
blocks on the CV (releasing mutex)
...sleeps forever — the notify already happened

wait(lock, pred) is a loop: check predicate → if false, atomically release-and-block. The atomicity protects against wakeups while blocking — but there is a gap between evaluating the predicate and starting to block. A notification delivered in that gap hits no waiter and vanishes. That is the lost wakeup. The worker then sleeps waiting for a notify that will never come again, and join() waits for the worker: deadlock.

Atomics are the trap here. Because stop_ is atomic, the code compiles cleanly, passes TSan's data-race checks, and works 99% of the time. Atomicity of the flag does nothing to order the flag-write against the waiter's evaluate-then-block sequence.

The fix: write the predicate state under the mutex

LlmClient::~LlmClient() {
    {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(requestMutex_);
        stop_.store(true);              // now serialized with the wait
    }
    requestCv_.notify_all();
    if (worker_.joinable()) worker_.join();
}

Why does holding the mutex close the gap? The worker evaluates its predicate while holding requestMutex_. If the destructor must also hold that mutex to flip stop_, only two orderings exist:

  1. Destructor gets the mutex first → worker's predicate check happens after, sees stop_ == true, never blocks.
  2. Worker gets the mutex first → it is fully blocked on the CV (the release-and-block is atomic) before the destructor can take the mutex — so the notify finds a waiter.

The gap is gone by construction. Note that notify_all() itself may stay outside the lock — it's the predicate state change that must be inside.

The rule to remember

Any write that makes a condition-variable predicate become true must happen while holding the same mutex the waiter uses — even if the write is atomic. (Corollary: enqueue() in this same file was already correct: it pushes to the queue under the mutex, then notifies.)

How it was caught, and how it's kept dead

Multiplayer's loopback tests run the whole suite more often and construct more threaded objects; a routine 5×-run flake check hung on run 3. sample <pid> on the stuck process showed one thread in ~LlmClient → join() and the worker in condition_variable::wait — the two-line stack trace is the diagnosis.

The regression test exploits the race window directly: constructing and immediately destroying LlmClient 200 times hits the destructor-vs-wait-entry timing over and over. Pre-fix it hangs the suite within a few runs; post-fix it's deterministic. You can't unit-test a race into impossibility, but you can make the odds of missing it astronomically small.

Lesson 0012 · Testing · from tests/test_net_loopback.cpp

Deterministic Tests for Threaded Socket Code

The loopback suite spins up a real server, real clients, and a fake LLM — and passes every time. Here's the discipline that makes that possible.

Test the real stack, fake the boundary

tests/test_net_loopback.cpp does not mock NetServer or NetClient — it runs both over 127.0.0.1, because the threading and framing are the things under test. What it fakes is the external boundary: FakeOllama plays the LLM (canned streamed replies, error modes like Http500). The rule of thumb:

Fake what you don't own (Ollama's HTTP API). Run what you do own (your sockets, your threads, your router) for real — on the loopback interface, where the network is fast and private.

Two tricks make real sockets test-friendly:

  • Port 0: asking the OS to bind "any free port" (then reading it back with getsockname) means parallel test runs never collide on a hardcoded port.
  • The fixture mirrors production wiring: ChatLoopback::hostFrame() is the same three-line pump main.cpp runs per frame. If the fixture wiring diverges from the game's, the tests verify a program nobody ships.

Never sleep and hope

The cardinal sin of async testing:

client.sendInput(...);
std::this_thread::sleep_for(200ms);          // "should be enough"  ← flake factory
CHECK(snapshotArrived());

Too short on a loaded CI machine → false failure. Long enough to be safe → the suite crawls. The loopback suite's replacement is predicate polling with a deadline:

bool eventually(predicate, pump, deadline = 3000ms) {
    auto end = now() + deadline;
    while (now() < end) {
        if (pump) pump();          // drive the host frame / drain clients
        if (predicate()) return true;   // succeed the instant it's true
        sleep_for(5ms);
    }
    return false;                  // honest failure with a bounded wait
}

Fast when the system is fast (usually a few milliseconds), honest when it hangs (bounded, reports failure). The pump parameter matters: shared-NPC chat needs the host loop to keep draining queues while we wait, exactly like the real game loop would.

Force the ugly interleavings

Concurrency bugs live in orderings that "never happen" on a fast machine. Good suites force them:

  • FakeOllama serves responses in 7-byte chunks so JSON always splits mid-token across TCP reads — the framing gets no easy days.
  • The framing test feeds a wire frame one byte at a time.
  • The ordering test waits until the NPC is busy with player A's question before sending player B's — making the queue-contention path deterministic instead of accidental.
  • The regression test for the LlmClient deadlock constructs and destroys the client 200 times — hammering the exact destructor-vs-wait window.

Flake checks: run it again. And again.

One green run of threaded code proves little — the schedule you got is one of millions. Tonight's protocol was for i in 1..8: ./run_tests after each networking change, and it paid for itself immediately: run 3 of the first batch hung, exposing a pre-existing lost-wakeup deadlock in LlmClient's destructor (see lesson 0011) that had nothing to do with the new code — the new tests just rolled the dice more often.

When a threaded test hangs, don't kill it — autopsy it first: sample <pid> (macOS) or gdb -p (Linux) shows every thread's stack. A deadlock diagnosis is usually two stack traces: who is waiting, and who was supposed to wake them.

Lesson 0012 · Testing · from tests/test_net_loopback.cpp

Deterministic Tests for Threaded Socket Code

The loopback suite spins up a real server, real clients, and a fake LLM — and passes every time. Here's the discipline that makes that possible.

Test the real stack, fake the boundary

tests/test_net_loopback.cpp does not mock NetServer or NetClient — it runs both over 127.0.0.1, because the threading and framing are the things under test. What it fakes is the external boundary: FakeOllama plays the LLM (canned streamed replies, error modes like Http500). The rule of thumb:

Fake what you don't own (Ollama's HTTP API). Run what you do own (your sockets, your threads, your router) for real — on the loopback interface, where the network is fast and private.

Two tricks make real sockets test-friendly:

  • Port 0: asking the OS to bind "any free port" (then reading it back with getsockname) means parallel test runs never collide on a hardcoded port.
  • The fixture mirrors production wiring: ChatLoopback::hostFrame() is the same three-line pump main.cpp runs per frame. If the fixture wiring diverges from the game's, the tests verify a program nobody ships.

Never sleep and hope

The cardinal sin of async testing:

client.sendInput(...);
std::this_thread::sleep_for(200ms);          // "should be enough"  ← flake factory
CHECK(snapshotArrived());

Too short on a loaded CI machine → false failure. Long enough to be safe → the suite crawls. The loopback suite's replacement is predicate polling with a deadline:

bool eventually(predicate, pump, deadline = 3000ms) {
    auto end = now() + deadline;
    while (now() < end) {
        if (pump) pump();          // drive the host frame / drain clients
        if (predicate()) return true;   // succeed the instant it's true
        sleep_for(5ms);
    }
    return false;                  // honest failure with a bounded wait
}

Fast when the system is fast (usually a few milliseconds), honest when it hangs (bounded, reports failure). The pump parameter matters: shared-NPC chat needs the host loop to keep draining queues while we wait, exactly like the real game loop would.

Force the ugly interleavings

Concurrency bugs live in orderings that "never happen" on a fast machine. Good suites force them:

  • FakeOllama serves responses in 7-byte chunks so JSON always splits mid-token across TCP reads — the framing gets no easy days.
  • The framing test feeds a wire frame one byte at a time.
  • The ordering test waits until the NPC is busy with player A's question before sending player B's — making the queue-contention path deterministic instead of accidental.
  • The regression test for the LlmClient deadlock constructs and destroys the client 200 times — hammering the exact destructor-vs-wait window.

Flake checks: run it again. And again.

One green run of threaded code proves little — the schedule you got is one of millions. Lesson 0013 · Networking basics · from docs(multiplayer): hosting and joining guide

NAT, Port Forwarding, and Why "Send Me Your IP" Isn't Enough

Hosting works instantly on your LAN and mysteriously not for a friend across town. The reason is the router in your closet.

Private vs public addresses

Your machine's address (from ifconfig/ipconfig) is almost certainly something like 192.168.1.20 — a private address. Whole ranges (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x) are reserved for home/office LANs and are not routable on the internet; millions of homes reuse the same numbers. Your household shares one public IP, held by the router.

NAT: the reason outbound works and inbound doesn't

Network Address Translation is the router rewriting your traffic: when you connect out, it swaps your private source address for its public one and remembers the mapping so replies find their way back. That memory is keyed by connections you initiated. An unsolicited inbound connection — say, a friend's game client dialing your public IP on port 40605 — matches no mapping, so the router drops it. That asymmetry is why browsing works everywhere but hosting needs setup.

Three ways in

ApproachHowTrade-off
Port forwardingRouter config: "TCP 40605 → 192.168.1.20". Friends use your public IP.Free, standard; needs router admin access, exposes the port to the whole internet
Overlay VPN (Tailscale, ZeroTier)Every machine joins a private virtual network and gets a stable address (e.g. 100.x.y.z); friends join your "tailnet" and use thatZero router config, encrypted, invite-only; everyone installs an app
Relay / NAT punchingA third-party server brokers or relays the connection (what commercial games do)Someone must run that infrastructure — out of scope for v1
For "me and three friends", the overlay VPN is usually the best answer: no router menus, no open ports, and the game needs zero code changes — the host's Tailscale IP goes in the same join box as a LAN address.

Why the game itself stays out of it

NAT traversal (STUN/TURN/ICE, UPnP) is a deep well of protocol work that mostly exists so strangers can connect without configuring anything. This game's v1 scope is friends who can coordinate ("install Tailscale" fits in one text message), so the engineering budget went into the game instead. The README says so explicitly — documenting a limitation honestly beats half-implementing a solution.

Debugging "can't connect" in this game

  1. Same machine? 127.0.0.1:40605 must work — if not, the host isn't up (check the Multiplayer page status line).
  2. Same LAN? Use the host's 192.168.x.x. Failure here is usually the OS firewall prompting the host to allow the app, or club Wi-Fi isolating clients.
  3. Across the internet? You need one of the three approaches above — a plain public IP will time out, and the game will say so via its 4-second connect timeout rather than hanging.

input.content:
Drill 0008 · pairs with lesson 0008

Length-Prefixed Framing

1. The server calls send() twice: a Welcome, then a snapshot. What may the client's first recv() return?

TCP preserves byte order and integrity, never write boundaries. Framing exists to rebuild boundaries.

2. Why does FrameAssembler use a length prefix while StreamAssembler uses newlines?

Delimiters fit protocols that already guarantee them; a length prefix is the default when you own both ends.

3. A frame arrives whose 4-byte prefix declares 900 MB. The correct response is…

"Skip" requires knowing where the frame ends — which is exactly the number you don't trust. feed() returns false; the caller disconnects.

4. Why encode the prefix with shifts (len >> 24…) instead of memcpy-ing the uint32_t?

Copying raw int bytes ships your CPU's endianness; two same-endian peers would work by luck, mixed peers would read garbage lengths.

5. Written recall — no peeking:

Sketch feed()'s loop: what are the two "not yet" cases and the one "emit" case?

Reference answerAppend bytes to the buffer. Loop: (a) fewer than 4 bytes → return, wait for the prefix; (b) prefix read but buffer < 4+length → return, wait for payload; (c) full frame present → emit payload via callback, erase 4+length bytes, repeat. Oversized prefix → return false (drop connection).

Drill 0009 · pairs with lesson 0009

Server-Authoritative Replication

1. A joined client's copy of NPC positions is…

Clients don't simulate at all — the cheapest way to never diverge from the authority is to never compute your own answer.

2. Why does NetServer spawn one reader thread per connection instead of one loop over all sockets?

At 4 players, thread-per-connection is the simplest correct design; poll/epoll multiplexing earns its complexity at hundreds of sockets.

3. The tick thread needs NPC positions for snapshots. How does it get them?

The thread contract: game state crosses into networking only as values through guarded queues. World stays single-threaded; solo play is untouched.

4. Correct shutdown order for a thread blocked in recv():

shutdown() forces the blocked recv to return; join() guarantees the thread is done touching the fd; only then is close() safe (an early close risks the kernel recycling the fd number under the still-running thread). A flag alone never wakes a blocked syscall.

5. Written recall:

Why does the handshake carry kNetProtocolVersion, and what happens on mismatch?

Reference answerDifferent builds may speak different wire formats. The server compares the client's version to its own at JoinRequest time and answers a refusal Welcome with a human-readable reason ("update the game") instead of accepting a peer that would silently desync. One int compared once per join buys away a whole class of bugs.

input.content:
Drill 0010 · pairs with lesson 0010

Request-Id Routing

1. Player 2 asks the baker a question. What key tells the host the resulting stream belongs to player 2?

Deltas arrive on the host's LLM queue, not a socket. The unique submit id is claimed at ask-time: inflight_[id] = {playerId, npcIndex}.

2. In the host loop, routeDelta() returning false means…

Consume-or-pass: new consumer gets first refusal, old code path can't tell multiplayer exists. Disconnected players are handled inside routeDelta (sendToPlayer fails silently), which still returns true.

3. Two players message the same NPC at nearly the same time. What guarantees neither reply is lost or interleaved?

The worker serializes HTTP calls, but Npc tracks only ONE pendingId_ — a second ask() would clobber the first. The per-NPC queue is what protects Npc's single-pending invariant.

4. Why do NpcSpeechBubble/NpcMoodUpdate broadcast to everyone while the error case goes only to the asker?

Audience follows meaning: shared consequences broadcast, private outcomes route to their owner.

5. Written recall:

A player disconnects while their reply is streaming. Walk through what happens to (a) the stream, (b) the NPC's history, (c) the next player who asks that NPC.

Reference answer(a) routeDelta/routeReply still fire, but sendToPlayer() finds no live connection and returns false — the payload evaporates. (b) npc.onReplyArrived() still runs, so history/mood update consistently (the world doesn't fork). (c) The router pumps that NPC's queue as usual; the NPC is free and answers normally — one client's death never wedges shared state.

input.content:
Drill 0011 · pairs with lesson 0011

The Lost Wakeup

1. stop_ is a std::atomic<bool>. Why wasn't that enough to make stop_.store(true); cv.notify_all(); safe?

The waiter checks the predicate (false), and before it blocks, the store+notify both happen. The notify finds nobody; the waiter then sleeps forever.

2. The fix takes requestMutex_ around stop_.store(true). Which two orderings does that leave possible?

wait(lock, pred) evaluates pred under the mutex and releases-and-blocks atomically. Forcing the writer through the same mutex means it can't run between those two steps.

3. Must notify_all() itself be inside the lock?

Once the store is serialized with the wait, the waiter either never blocks or is already blocked when notify fires.

4. Why did this bug survive months of test runs, then show up during multiplayer work?

Rare races are found by frequency, not by cleverness — which is why the flake-check habit (run the suite 5-8x after threading changes) exists.

5. Written recall:

State the general rule that prevents lost wakeups, and explain how the regression test makes this bug reproducible.

Reference answerRule: any write that makes a CV predicate true must happen while holding the mutex the waiter uses — even if the write is atomic. Test: construct and destroy LlmClient 200 times in a loop; each cycle races the destructor against the worker's first wait-entry, so pre-fix the suite hangs within a few runs while post-fix it's deterministic.

Drill 0013 · pairs with lesson 0013

NAT and Port Forwarding

1. Your friend across town tries your 192.168.1.20:40605 and times out. Why was this doomed from the start?

Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) exist precisely so every home can reuse them behind one public IP.

2. Why does outbound traffic (browsing) work from behind NAT while inbound hosting doesn't?

The router only knows where to deliver packets for flows it has already seen leave.

3. What does the port-forward rule "TCP 40605 → 192.168.1.20" actually tell the router?

It's precisely the missing table entry NAT can't infer on its own, scoped to one port and one host.

4. Why is Tailscale/ZeroTier usually the better recommendation for a 4-friend game night?

A forwarded port is open to the whole internet and needs router admin access; an overlay network is private by construction and installs like an app.

Reference answer1) 127.0.0.1:port on the host's own machine — isolates "is the server even running/bound". 2) The host's 192.168.x.x from another machine on the same Wi-Fi — isolates OS firewall prompts and AP client isolation. 3) Across the internet — requires port forwarding or an overlay VPN; a bare public IP will hit the game's 4s connect timeout.

Vocab 0008 · Multiplayer networking · covers lessons 0008-0013

Multiplayer Networking — Terms

Framing

Rebuilding message boundaries on top of a byte stream that has none. In this repo: FrameAssembler (length prefix, multiplayer) and StreamAssembler (newlines, Ollama NDJSON).

Contrast: a datagram protocol (UDP) has built-in message boundaries but no delivery/order guarantees.

Length prefix

A fixed-size integer sent before each payload declaring its size — here 4 bytes, big-endian, capped at kMaxFrameBytes (1 MiB). A corrupt prefix is unrecoverable: the only safe response is dropping the connection.

Usage: "The snapshot is one length-prefixed JSON frame."

Network byte order (big-endian)

The convention that multi-byte integers on the wire send their most significant byte first. x86/ARM CPUs are little-endian in memory, so conversion must be explicit (shifts, or htonl).

Server-authoritative

Architecture where one node (our host) owns the true game state and clients render replicas of it. Prevents divergence and cheating by construction; costs one round trip of latency on interactions.

Contrast: lockstep (all peers simulate identically from shared inputs) and client-authoritative (each client owns its own state — trivially cheatable).

Replica / replication

A client's read-only copy of authoritative state, refreshed by WorldSnapshot broadcasts (~12 Hz here). Joined clients skip npc.update() entirely — a replica that simulates drifts.

Snapshot broadcast

Periodically sending the full (or delta-compressed) world state to every client. Full snapshots are simpler and fine at this scale: 4 players + ~43 NPC poses is a few KB at 12 Hz.

Handshake

The first exchange on a new connection that establishes identity and compatibility before any real traffic: JoinRequest {version, name, code} → Welcome {accepted, playerId | reason}. Rejects version mismatches, wrong join codes, and full sessions loudly.

Protocol version

An integer (kNetProtocolVersion) bumped whenever the wire format changes incompatibly. Compared in the handshake so mismatched builds get a clear refusal instead of a silent desync.

Thread contract (publish/drain)

This codebase's rule: network threads touch only sockets and internal queues; game state crosses the boundary as values (publishNpcPoses) in and drained events (drainChatEvents, poll()) out, pumped by the main loop. Keeps World/LlmClient single-threaded.

Contrast: shared-state locking, where every system that touches NPCs must know about mutexes.

Request-id routing

Correlating streamed results back to their requester via the unique id LlmClient::submit() returns: inflight_[id] = {playerId, npcIndex}. The consume-or-pass drain (routeDelta returns false → it's the host's own) extends the queue to two consumers without touching solo code.

Lost wakeup

A condition-variable deadlock where the notify lands between the waiter's predicate check (false) and its block — hitting no waiter, gone forever. Prevented by writing predicate state under the waiter's mutex, even if the write is atomic. Found and fixed in LlmClient::~LlmClient tonight.

shutdown-join-close

The safe teardown order for a socket with a blocked reader thread: shutdown() unblocks the recv(), join() proves the thread is done with the fd, then close(). Closing first risks the kernel recycling the fd under a live thread.

Predicate polling (vs sleep-and-hope)

Async test waiting done right: re-check a condition every few ms under a deadline, pumping the event loop between checks (eventually() in the loopback tests). Fast when things work, honest when they hang.

NAT (Network Address Translation)

The router rewriting private↔public addresses, keyed by outbound connections. Explains why browsing works everywhere but hosting needs a port forward or an overlay VPN (Tailscale/ZeroTier).

Loopback (127.0.0.1)

The virtual network interface that never leaves the machine — real sockets, real threads, zero external dependencies. Where the whole multiplayer stack is integration-tested (with port 0 = "OS picks a free port").

Date: 2026-07-05
Session: overnight multiplayer build (plan: `.claude/plans/multiplayer-and-aws-deploy.md`)
Issues attempted: 7 (all planned multiplayer tickets)

## Summary
Shared-world multiplayer v1 is fully implemented, tested, documented, and open
for review as a 7-PR stack: 2-4 players over TCP, one authoritative host, shared
NPCs with consistent memory and mood, host/join from the pause menu. Along the
way the flake checks exposed and fixed a pre-existing lost-wakeup deadlock in
`LlmClient`'s destructor. The suite went from 75 to 96 test cases, all green
across repeated runs.

## Completed ✅
| Issue | Title | Branch | PR | Concept Taught |
|-------|-------|--------|----|----------------|
| — | scaffold (skeletons + skipped stubs) | feature/multiplayer-scaffold | #28 | — |

| #24 | server-routed NPC chat | feature/issue-4-server-npc-chat | #31 | Request-id routing (0010) |
| #25 | Menu host/join + app modes | feature/issue-5-menu-host-join | #32 | — (UI wiring; no lesson, too thin a concept) |
| #26 | loopback fixture | folded into #30/#31 | #30, #31 | Deterministic threaded-socket testing (0012) |
| #27 | multiplayer docs | feature/issue-7-docs-multiplayer | #33 | NAT & port forwarding (0013) |
| bonus | LlmClient destructor deadlock fix | on #30's branch | #30 | Lost wakeup / condition variables (0011) |
| — | learning materials | feature/learning-multiplayer | #34 | all of the above |

## Failed ❌
None.

## Skipped ⏭
None. (Phase B — headless AWS server build + deploy skill — was excluded from
this milestone by the plan itself.)

## Learning Materials Created
| Concept | Lesson | Drill | Vocab |
|---------|--------|-------|-------|
| Length-prefixed framing over TCP | 0008 ✅ | 0008 ✅ | 0008 (shared) ✅ |
| Server-authoritative replication + thread contract | 0009 ✅ | 0009 ✅ | ✅ |
| Request-id routing of shared streams | 0010 ✅ | 0010 ✅ | ✅ |
| Condition variables & the lost wakeup | 0011 ✅ | 0011 ✅ | ✅ |
| Deterministic tests for threaded sockets | 0012 ✅ | 0012 ✅ | ✅ |
| NAT, port forwarding, overlay VPNs | 0013 ✅ | 0013 ✅ | ✅ |

`docs/learning/index.html` links everything (on PR #34). One consolidated vocab
page covers all six concepts instead of six near-empty pages.

## Test Status
`make -C tests test`: **96 cases, 699 assertions, 0 failed, 1 skipped**
(the deliberate live-Ollama test). Threaded loopback suites flake-checked:
8 consecutive green runs after the deadlock fix (which the flake check itself
caught — the suite hung on run 3 before it).

## Suggested First Move
Open **PR #30** and read the `fix(llm)` commit first — it's the one change that
touches pre-existing behavior (the destructor deadlock). Then merge the stack
top-down: #28 → #29 → #30 → #31 → #32 → #33 → #34. GitHub re-targets each PR
automatically as its base merges. Before merging #32, do the one manual check
the machines can't: run two instances, host in one, join `127.0.0.1:40605` in
the other.

## Draft PRs Awaiting Review
- #28 scaffold — skeletons and skipped test stubs (merge first)
- #29 protocol + framing — 11 unit tests
- #30 NetServer/NetClient + **LlmClient deadlock fix** — 5 loopback tests
- #31 server-routed NPC chat — 4 loopback tests
- #32 pause-menu host/join + app modes — needs your eyeball test
- #33 README/DEVELOPER multiplayer docs
- #34 learning materials (lessons/drills/vocab/index)

  nature; each PR bases on the previous so every diff reviews clean.

  integration-tested together; #26's fixture landed with them and #31.
- **This report and `.claude/memory/checkpoint.md` are left uncommitted** —
  your CLAUDE.md forbids pushing to main, and the report is a morning-read
  artifact, not repo history.
