# Plan: One-click launch, pluggable LLM backends (cloud-ready), in-game model picker, and a product roadmap

## Context

Today the game only talks to a local Ollama server, hardwired in `LlmClient`, and
the launch scripts merely *check* Ollama is up and bail if it isn't. The user wants
three things, plus a long-horizon vision:

1. **One-click launch** — `open`/double-click/`./` that starts the LLM server *and*
   the game together.
2. **Pluggable models you can add later** — pick among installed models in-game; add
   more without code changes.
3. **Smarter characters via cloud APIs** (Claude / GPT / Gemini), cheaply — to test
   now and possibly sell later.
4. **Future product**: "Character.ai in a 3D world" — players create characters with
   one LLM (e.g. Gemini) and converse with them via another (e.g. Claude/GPT), sold
   with token costs passed through.

**Locked decisions (from Q&A):**
- **Scope = "Local now + cloud-ready" (no new required deps).** Ship one-click launch
  + in-game model picker for installed Ollama models, **refactor `LlmClient` into a
  pluggable backend interface** so a cloud backend is a drop-in, and write the full
  roadmap doc. Cloud goes live the moment OpenSSL + a key are added — no rewrite.
- **Cloud routing = OpenRouter.** One OpenAI-compatible endpoint
  (`https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions`), one key, 315+ models (Claude,
  GPT, Gemini, …); switch model by a config string.

**Key technical findings (research):**
- **Ollama, OpenRouter, OpenAI, and Gemini all speak the same OpenAI
  `/v1/chat/completions` shape.** Ollama exposes it at `localhost:11434/v1`. So *one*
  OpenAI-compatible backend covers local **and** cloud — the only fork is HTTP (local)
  vs HTTPS (cloud → needs OpenSSL). This lets us **test the cloud code path locally
  against Ollama's `/v1` with zero new deps.**
- OpenAI SSE stream: lines `data: {json}` where text is `choices[0].delta.content`,
  terminated by `data: [DONE]`; errors arrive as a non-200 body or `{"error":...}`.
- httplib does HTTPS only when compiled with `CPPHTTPLIB_OPENSSL_SUPPORT` + OpenSSL.
- Launcher hooks: `ollama serve` (start), `GET /api/tags` (list installed),
  `ollama pull <model>` (install).

**Branch:** new `8-pluggable-llm-and-one-click`, branched from current HEAD
(`7-weapons-money-and-mayhem`) since the work is sequential and builds on the latest
game. Incremental `type(scope): description` commits; build + `make -C tests test`
green after each; inline review before each commit; no push (user's call).

**Constraints (CLAUDE.md):** all new logic is SFML-free `src/core/` with doctest
tests; renderer/Menu visuals eyeballed; **no committed secrets**; OpenSSL stays
*optional* (auto-detected, never required).

---

## Phase 1 — One-click launch  `chore(launch): auto-start Ollama and add a double-clickable launcher`

Harden the existing launchers so they bring the whole stack up; add a Finder-friendly
entry point.

- **`run.sh`** (macOS/Linux): when provider is local and the server isn't reachable,
  start it (`ollama serve` backgrounded, log to a temp file) and poll
  `http://HOST:PORT/api/tags` until ready (~20 s timeout). Read `model` from
  `config/llm.cfg`; if it's absent from `ollama list`, `ollama pull <model>`. Then the
  existing cmake build + run. Keep the install hint if the `ollama` binary is missing.
  Skip auto-start when `provider` is a cloud one.
- **`run.command`** (new, macOS): double-clickable wrapper that `cd`s to its dir and
  `exec ./run.sh`; marked executable. Satisfies "open / one click".
- **`run.ps1` / `run.bat`** (Windows): same — `Start-Process ollama serve` if not
  reachable, pull the model if missing, then build + run.

Files: `run.sh`, new `run.command`, `run.ps1`, `run.bat`. Verified by launch.

## Phase 2 — Pluggable LLM backend + config + secrets  `refactor(llm): pluggable backend interface with an OpenAI-compatible cloud path`

Split `LlmClient` into **threading/queue glue (unchanged)** + a swappable **backend**
that owns the HTTP + parse. The worker thread, `submit`/`drainDeltas`/`drainReplies`/
`busy()` and the public API stay identical.

- **New `src/core/LlmBackend.hpp`** — interface:
  `BackendResult chat(const BackendRequest&, const std::function<void(const std::string& delta)>& onDelta)`,
  plus `std::vector<std::string> listModels()`, `setModel`, `model()`. `BackendRequest`
  carries systemPrompt/history/userMessage/internal; `BackendResult{ok,content,error}`.
- **`src/core/OllamaBackend.{hpp,cpp}`** — the *existing* `processOne` body
  (`/api/chat` NDJSON + `parseOllamaChunk`) moved verbatim behind the interface;
  `listModels()` reads `GET /api/tags`. This is the default — behavior-identical today.
- **`src/core/OpenAiBackend.{hpp,cpp}`** — POST `{base_url}/chat/completions`,
  `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, `stream:true`; parse SSE via a new
  **`src/core/OpenAiChunk.hpp`** (`parseOpenAiChunk` → `{delta,done,error}`,
  header-only and unit-testable like `parseOllamaChunk`). Works over **http** (local
  Ollama `/v1`) with no SSL; over **https** only when built with OpenSSL — guarded by
  `#ifdef CPPHTTPLIB_OPENSSL_SUPPORT`, otherwise a clear "cloud needs an OpenSSL build"
  error and fall back to Ollama.
- **`LlmClient` change**: holds a `std::unique_ptr<LlmBackend>`; `processOne` builds a
  `BackendRequest`, calls `backend_->chat(...)` with an `onDelta` that pushes to the
  existing delta queue, maps the result to `ChatReply`. A factory
  `makeBackend(const LlmConfig&)` selects Ollama vs OpenAI-compatible by `provider`.
- **Config** (`LlmConfig` in `LlmClient.hpp` + `loadLlmConfig` in `Config.cpp`): add
  `provider` (default `ollama`), `base_url` (default derived; OpenRouter →
  `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`), `api_key_env` (default `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`). Key
  resolution order: env var named by `api_key_env` → `config/secrets.cfg` `api_key` →
  empty (cloud disabled with a clear message). **No key ever in version control.**
- **Secrets**: add `config/secrets.cfg` to `.gitignore`; ship
  `config/secrets.cfg.example`. (No `/secrets` dir is touched; this is the safe BYO-key
  pattern.)
- **CMake**: `find_package(OpenSSL QUIET)` — if present, add
  `CPPHTTPLIB_OPENSSL_SUPPORT` + link it (cloud "just works", no config change); if
  absent, builds exactly as today. **OpenSSL stays optional.** Add the new core `.cpp`
  files to the `llm_npc_core` source list (tests auto-glob them).
- **Tests**: extend `tests/test_stream.cpp` for `parseOpenAiChunk` (`data:` prefix,
  `[DONE]`, content delta, `{"error"}`, blank/`: keep-alive` lines); extend
  `tests/test_config.cpp` for the new keys + key-resolution precedence; add a
  `FakeBackend` (mirroring `tests/FakeOllama.hpp`) so `tests/test_llm_client.cpp`
  drives the queue/threading against a fake — no network.

Files: new `src/core/LlmBackend.hpp`, `OllamaBackend.{hpp,cpp}`,
`OpenAiBackend.{hpp,cpp}`, `OpenAiChunk.hpp`; modified `LlmClient.{hpp,cpp}`,
`Config.{hpp,cpp}`, `config/llm.cfg` (documented new keys), new
`config/secrets.cfg.example`, `.gitignore`, `CMakeLists.txt`, the three test files.

## Phase 3 — In-game model picker  `feat(llm): switch models from the pause menu`

- **Persist a single key without clobbering comments**: add `setKvValue(path, key,
  value)` to `Config.{hpp,cpp}` (rewrites only the matching line; mirrors `readKv`),
  used to save the chosen `model` back to `config/llm.cfg`.
- **Menu**: add a `Page::Model` (following the existing `Page`/`Hit`/`layout()`
  pattern in `Menu.{hpp,cpp}`) that lists clickable model names; clicking selects one.
  Inject the choices via small hooks from `main.cpp` (current model + list +
  `onSelect`) so Menu stays free of `LlmClient`.
- **main.cpp wiring**: fetch the installed-model list from `backend_->listModels()`
  (Ollama `/api/tags`); on select, `setModel` on the live client (next requests use it;
  in-flight finish on the old) and `setKvValue` to persist. Models are *added* out of
  band via `ollama pull` (launcher/CLI), which the picker then shows.

Files: `src/core/Config.{hpp,cpp}`, `src/app/Menu.{hpp,cpp}`, `src/app/main.cpp`,
`tests/test_config.cpp` (cover `setKvValue`).

## Phase 4 — Product roadmap doc  `docs(vision): Character.ai-in-3D architecture, cost model, and roadmap`

New **`docs/VISION.md`** (the "plan it out for the future" deliverable), grounded in
the research:

- **Vision & today** — the 3D shell where players populate a city with custom
  characters; what this branch already lays down (pluggable backends, one-click,
  picker).
- **Product architecture** — OpenRouter as the single gateway; **two LLM roles**:
  *Creation* (cheap one-shot, e.g. Gemini Flash-Lite: short description → a
  `.persona` file in the existing format → spawns an NPC, reusing `PersonaLoader` +
  `renderSystemPrompt`) and *Conversation* (streaming, e.g. Haiku / GPT-5-mini).
  In-game character-creator flow; shareable persona packs.
- **Cost model** (per-1M input/output, with a ~800-in/60-out NPC turn and prompt
  caching as the lever): Gemini 2.5 Flash $0.30/$2.50 ≈ **$0.0004/msg (~2,500/$)**;
  GPT-5 mini $0.125/$1.00 ≈ **$0.00016/msg (~6,000/$)**; Claude Haiku 4.5 $1/$5 ≈
  **$0.0011/msg (~900/$)**; character creation ≈ **<$0.0015 each**. → thousands of
  messages per dollar; BYO-key is trivially affordable, resale has margin.
- **Monetization** — (a) BYO-key (simplest, no key liability), (b) hosted
  credits/token packs (**requires a server-side proxy** so your key never ships in the
  client), (c) tiered free-local-Ollama + paid-cloud.
- **Staged roadmap** — A: this branch. B: cloud live + AI character creator. C: BYO-key
  product. D: hosted credits/proxy + persona marketplace. Each with scope + main risk.
- **Risks** — key security (never client-side for resale), content moderation of
  user-made characters, cloud latency vs local, cost runaway (budgets/rate limits),
  packaging/signing.
- **Sources** — the pricing/API links gathered during research.

Files: new `docs/VISION.md`; brief pointers added to `README.md` and
`docs/DEVELOPER.md`.

---

## Out of scope (now)
Adding OpenSSL as a *required* dep; a hosted billing/proxy backend; the in-game AI
character creator implementation (designed in VISION.md, built in a later phase);
per-provider native SDKs (OpenRouter covers all); content moderation; appearance
generation from text. The cloud backend ships **compiled but dormant** until a key +
OpenSSL build are present.

## Risks / notes
- The public `LlmClient` API and Ollama behavior must stay **byte-for-byte identical**
  after the refactor — `OllamaBackend` is the old code path moved, not rewritten;
  `test_llm_client`/`test_llm_live`/`test_stream` are the guardrail.
- Model switching mid-session affects only new requests (documented).
- Menu visuals and the SSE HTTP wiring are eyeballed (can't screenshot the GL window);
  you verify UI/latency, I tune.

## Verification
- `make -C tests test` green (new `parseOpenAiChunk`, config keys + `setKvValue`,
  `FakeBackend` client test).
- `cmake --build build -j` **without** OpenSSL → local behavior unchanged; `./run.sh`
  (or `run.command`) auto-starts Ollama, pulls the model if missing, builds, runs.
- **Cloud path, zero new deps**: set `provider=openai`,
  `base_url=http://localhost:11434/v1` → NPCs answered through the OpenAiBackend
  against Ollama (proves the cloud code path end to end).
- Pause menu → switch model → next reply uses it; choice persists in `config/llm.cfg`.
- **Later (user's step)**: install OpenSSL, set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`,
  `provider=openrouter`, `model=anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5` → real cloud NPC.
- Inline review before each commit; offer `/code-review` over the batch at the end.

skills.name: idea
skills.content:
You are turning "Expand" into a structured, actionable plan document.

This command has two phases:
- PHASE 1: Interrogate the idea until it is unambiguous
- PHASE 2: Produce the plan document

Do not skip to Phase 2 until Phase 1 is complete.

---

## PHASE 1 — INTERROGATE THE IDEA

Read the codebase first so your questions are grounded in reality:
```bash
find src/ lib/ app/ -type f 2>/dev/null | head -30
git log --oneline -10
cat CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null || true
```

Then ask clarifying questions — ONE at a time, wait for the answer,
then ask the next. Do not dump a list of questions all at once.
A question only gets asked if you genuinely cannot write a good plan
without knowing the answer.

Things worth asking about (pick the most important ones):

**Scope:**
- What does done look like? What can a user DO when this is complete?
- What is explicitly OUT of scope for this version?
- Is this a new feature, a change to existing behaviour, or a fix?

**Users and context:**
- Who uses this and in what situation?
- What do they have / know before they reach this feature?

**Technical constraints:**
- Does this touch existing code that other things depend on?
- Any performance, security, or compatibility requirements?
- Any third-party APIs or libraries involved?

**Edge cases:**
- What happens when the input is invalid or missing?
- What's the failure mode and how should it be handled?

**Priority:**
- Does this need to be done in a specific order relative to other work?
- Is there a simpler version that delivers most of the value?

Stop asking when you have enough to write a plan that could be handed
to a developer (or the overnight session) without them needing to ask
you anything.

---

## PHASE 2 — PRODUCE THE PLAN DOCUMENT

Save to `.claude/plans/[slug].md` where slug is a short dash-case
name derived from the idea. Example: "add weapon inventory" →
`.claude/plans/weapon-inventory.md`

The document structure:

```markdown
# Plan: [Feature Name]
Date: [date]
Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
Estimated complexity: S / M / L / XL

## The Idea (one paragraph)
[What this is, in plain language. Someone unfamiliar with the codebase
should understand this in 30 seconds.]

## Goal
[One sentence: what a user can DO when this is shipped that they
cannot do now.]

## Out of Scope (this version)
[Explicit list of things NOT included. This prevents scope creep
during implementation.]

## Affected Areas
[Files, modules, or systems this touches. Be specific.]
- `src/path/to/file.py` — [why it changes]
- `src/path/to/other.cpp` — [why it changes]
- New files needed: [list]

## Implementation Order
[Ordered steps. Each step should be independently committable.]

1. [Step 1 — what it produces]
2. [Step 2 — builds on step 1]
3. [Step 3 — etc.]

## Acceptance Criteria
[Testable conditions that define "done". Each one should be
verifiable by running a test or observing a specific behaviour.]

- [ ] [Given X, when Y, then Z]
- [ ] [Given X, when Y, then Z]
- [ ] Tests pass: [specific test file or command]

## Edge Cases and Error Handling
[What can go wrong and how each case is handled.]

| Situation | Expected behaviour |
|-----------|-------------------|
| [case] | [what happens] |

## Open Questions
[Anything still unresolved that will need a decision during implementation.
If there are none, write "None — plan is complete."]

## Suggested GitHub Issues
[If this plan should become overnight issues, list them here as a
starting point for /plan-github:]

1. [Issue title] — [one line scope]
2. [Issue title] — [one line scope]
3. [Issue title] — [one line scope]
```

---

## AFTER SAVING THE PLAN

Tell the user:
1. Where the plan was saved
2. How to turn it into GitHub issues:
   `/plan-github "[feature name]"` — or offer to run it now
3. How to start implementation immediately:
   `/develop [feature name]` — uses the plan as the spec
4. How to queue it for overnight:
   Add the suggested issues to GitHub, label ready-for-ai,
   then `bash ~/scripts/nightly.sh`

---

## TONE

Ask questions like a sharp senior engineer reviewing a spec —
direct, specific, not adversarial. The goal is to surface
assumptions before they become bugs, not to gatekeep.

If the idea is already clear enough to plan without questions,
say so briefly and go straight to the plan.

skills.name: overnight-session
skills.content:
You are running an overnight autonomous development session on this
repository. Use the overnight-coordinator agent to manage the full session.
You have full permission to read, write, commit, push, and open draft PRs.
You do NOT have permission to merge to main or close PRs after opening them.

## SETUP (run once at session start)

```bash
# 1. Ensure we are on main and up to date
git checkout main
git pull

# 2. Rebuild the knowledge graph so you navigate current code, not stale code
# (only if graphify is installed — skip silently if not)
graphify update . --force 2>/dev/null || echo "graphify not installed — skipping"

# 3. Check for a prior checkpoint (resume if interrupted)
cat .claude/memory/checkpoint.md 2>/dev/null || echo "No checkpoint — starting fresh"

# 4. Read tonight's issues
gh issue list --label "ready-for-ai" --json number,title,body,labels \
  --order created --limit 20
```

If a checkpoint exists and shows IN PROGRESS or FAILED stages, resume
from there rather than starting over.

Write the session start to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
# Checkpoint
Session started: [timestamp]
Goal: Work through all ready-for-ai issues
Status: IN PROGRESS
Issues to process: [list from gh output]
Issues completed: []
Issues failed: []
Issues skipped: []
```

---

## FOR EACH ISSUE (in number order, lowest first)

### A. READ AND ASSESS

```bash
gh issue view [N] --comments
```

Ask: Is this issue clear enough to attempt autonomously?

**Blockers that cause a SKIP:**
- Requires a design decision not documented in the issue
- Depends on another issue that isn't complete yet
- Requires credentials, API keys, or external resources not available
- Scope is too vague to produce a verifiable result

If blocked, label and move on — do NOT guess at intent:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "needs-human" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Skipped overnight: [specific reason]. Please clarify before re-queuing."
```

### B. ORIENT

Invoke the git-historian agent:
"Use the git-historian agent to understand the code area this issue will touch."

This surfaces hot files, recent decisions, and things NOT to redo.
Read .claude/memory/history-brief.md after it completes.

### C. MARK IN PROGRESS

```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "ai-in-progress" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Starting overnight implementation. Planning now."
```

### D. BRANCH

```bash
git checkout main
git checkout -b feature/issue-[N]
```

### E. PLAN

Use /plan-feature [concept from issue title] and wait for a plan.
Save the plan to .claude/plans/issue-[N].md

Do not implement until you have a written plan.

### F. IMPLEMENT

Use the appropriate specialist agents for this repo (see repo-specific
section below). Follow the plan. Write complete code — no placeholders.

If you hit a problem after 2 attempts on the same sticking point, SKIP
the issue and mark it ai-blocked. Do not spiral.

### G. TEST

Run the project's test suite. The exact commands are in the repo-specific
section below. Tests MUST pass before committing.

If tests fail after 2 fix attempts: skip, mark blocked, move on.
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --remove-label "ai-in-progress" --add-label "ai-blocked"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Blocked: tests failing after 2 attempts. [describe failure]. Needs human attention."
git checkout main
git branch -D feature/issue-[N]
```

### H. COMMIT AND PUSH

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "fix(#[N]): [issue title, shortened]"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### I. OPEN DRAFT PR

Generate the PR description using the /mr-description command, then:

```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "fix(#[N]): [issue title]" \
  --body "[output from /mr-description]" \
  --base main \
  --head feature/issue-[N] \
  --draft
```

Label the issue complete and close it with a reference to the PR:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] \
  --remove-label "ai-in-progress" \
  --add-label "ai-completed"
gh issue close [N] \
  --comment "Implemented. Draft PR open for review — see above."
```

### J. GENERATE LEARNING MATERIALS

**Identify the primary concept:**
Ask yourself: "What is the single most important technical concept a
developer would need to understand to maintain or extend this change?"

Guidelines:
- Choose the concept, not the feature name
  ("triple-channel SCPI addressing" not "E3631A support")
- Should be teachable in one lesson
- Should have testable recall in a drill
- Should introduce vocabulary worth learning

Then generate all three artifacts. In overnight/automated context:
- Generate the HTML files fully
- Skip in-chat interactive knowledge checks (no user present)
- Make the HTML content thorough — it is the only output
- Update PROGRESS.md with what was covered

```
/teach [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/drill-me [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/drills/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/terms [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/vocab/NNNN-[concept].html
and updates docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md

Commit the learning materials on the same feature branch:
```bash
git add docs/learning/
git commit -m "docs(learning): add lesson, drill and vocab for [concept] (from issue #[N])"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### K. UPDATE CHECKPOINT

Append to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
Issue #[N]: [COMPLETED | FAILED | SKIPPED]
  Branch: feature/issue-[N]
  PR: #[PR number if opened]
  Concept taught: [concept]
  Learning files: lessons/NNNN-x.html, drills/NNNN-x.html, vocab/NNNN-x.html
  Notes: [anything notable]
```

Return to main: `git checkout main`

---

## END OF ALL ISSUES

### 1. Rebuild the learning index

```
/index
```

Commit:
```bash
git add docs/learning/index.html
git commit -m "docs(learning): rebuild index after overnight run $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

### 2. Write the morning report

Write OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md to the repo root:

```markdown
# Overnight Build Report
Date: [date]
Session duration: [start] to [finish]
Issues attempted: [N]

## Summary
[2-3 sentences on what was accomplished overall]

## Completed ✅
| Issue | Title | Branch | PR | Concept Taught |
|-------|-------|--------|----|----------------|
| #N | [title] | feature/issue-N | #PR | [concept] |

## Failed ❌
| Issue | Title | Failure Reason |
|-------|-------|----------------|
| #N | [title] | [why — specific, actionable] |

## Skipped (needs human) ⏭
| Issue | Title | Reason |
|-------|-------|--------|
| #N | [title] | [what needs clarification] |

## Learning Materials Created
| Concept | Lesson | Drill | Vocab |
|---------|--------|-------|-------|
| [concept] | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Test Status
[overall pass/fail and any notable failures]

## Suggested First Move
[The single most useful thing to do when you open your laptop]

## Draft PRs Awaiting Review
[list with PR numbers and one-line description each]
```

Commit and push the report:
```bash
git add OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md .claude/memory/checkpoint.md
git commit -m "chore: overnight report $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

---

## LEARNING CONCEPT SELECTION — GENERAL GUIDANCE

These guidelines apply to all repos unless overridden in a repo-specific
overnight-session command.

Choose a concept that:
- Is non-obvious (skip things any developer already knows)
- Will appear again in this codebase (worth learning for maintainability)
- Can be explained in one lesson without splitting into prerequisite lessons
- Has clear vocabulary (terms worth adding to the glossary)
- Produces useful recall questions in a drill

Avoid:
- Concepts named after specific model numbers or vendor names
  ("E3631A" is not a concept; "triple-channel PSU SCPI addressing" is)
- Concepts so generic they produce a useless lesson
  ("adding a class" — skip this)
- Concepts already well-covered in the existing lesson library
  (check docs/learning/PROGRESS.md first)

---

## FAILURE HANDLING POLICY

This policy applies to the entire session.

**Never stop the run because one issue failed.**
**Never silently skip — always label and comment.**
**Never attempt a risky or irreversible action without a prior commit.**

If at any point the session hits a situation that is genuinely ambiguous,
dangerous, or requires a human decision not covered by the issue:
1. Stop work on that issue
2. Label it needs-human
3. Leave a detailed comment explaining exactly what decision is needed
4. Move to the next issue

The goal is to maximize completed work, not to force through stuck issues.

---

## NOTE ON AUTOMATED LEARNING GENERATION

In a live session, /teach, /drill-me, and /terms end with in-chat
knowledge checks. In overnight autonomous mode, skip the interactive
questions and put that energy into making the HTML content more thorough
instead. The HTML is the deliverable — the in-chat conversation is not.

skills.name: plan-github
skills.content:
Read .claude/skills/github/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/code-economy/SKILL.md
before doing anything. The GitHub skill covers auth and issue creation.
The code-economy skill defines what makes a good, reviewable change.

---

You are a backlog planning agent for a personal GitHub project.
Your job is to read the current project state and create well-formed
GitHub issues that the overnight session can work through autonomously.

Every issue you create must be:
- Self-contained (completable in one overnight session)
- Specific (clear acceptance criteria, not vague goals)
- Verifiable (a test to run or output to check)
- Code-economy compliant (won't produce bloated PRs)
- Labelled ready-for-ai and assigned to the repo owner

---

## STEP 1 — PREREQUISITES

```python
import os
from github import Github

# Verify auth
token = os.environ.get("GH_TOKEN")
username = os.environ.get("GITHUB_USERNAME")
if not token or not username:
    raise SystemExit(
        "Set GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_USERNAME in your shell config first."
    )

gh = Github(token)
repo = get_repo(gh)   # auto-detects from git remote
print(f"Planning issues for: {repo.full_name}")

# Read existing open issues to avoid duplicates
existing = list_issues(repo, state="open")
existing_titles = {i["title"].lower() for i in existing}
print(f"Existing open issues: {len(existing)}")
```

---

## STEP 2 — READ PROJECT CONTEXT

Read all of these before planning any issues:

**CLAUDE.md** — the project purpose, stack, rules, and current state.
This is the source of truth for what the project is trying to be.

**README.md** — user-facing description and roadmap if any.

**Current codebase:**
```bash
# What exists right now
find src/ lib/ app/ -type f 2>/dev/null | head -50 || \
  find . -name "*.py" -o -name "*.cpp" -o -name "*.ts" \
  | grep -v node_modules | grep -v build | head -50

# Where work is heading
git log --oneline -20

# Known gaps and TODOs
grep -rn "TODO\|FIXME\|HACK\|NotImplemented\|raise NotImplementedError" \
  src/ lib/ app/ 2>/dev/null | head -30

# Test coverage gaps (uncovered files)
pytest --co -q 2>/dev/null | head -30 || true
```

---

## STEP 3 — CREATE MILESTONE (GITHUB EQUIVALENT OF EPIC)

Group related issues under a milestone:

```python
def create_milestone(repo, title: str, description: str) -> int:
    """Create a GitHub milestone. Returns the milestone number."""
    milestone = repo.create_milestone(
        title=title,
        description=description
    )
    print(f"Created milestone: {milestone.title} (#{milestone.number})")
    return milestone.number
```

Create one milestone per theme of work. For "" focus, one milestone
is enough. For full project analysis, create 2-4 milestones.

Good milestone names:
- "SCPI Device Family — Oscilloscopes"
- "NPC Tier 1: Structured Output"
- "Data Pipeline — Market Data Ingestion"

---

## STEP 4 — CREATE ISSUES

For each issue, use this exact body template so the overnight session
has everything it needs:

```python
ISSUE_TEMPLATE = """## What to change
{what}

## Where it is
{where}

## How to verify it's done
{verify}

## Constraints
{constraints}

## Code economy note
{economy_note}

## Branch name
`feature/issue-{{number}}-{slug}`

## Concept for learning materials
{concept}
"""
```

The **concept** field is critical — it tells the overnight session what
to teach/drill after completing this issue. It must be:
- A technical concept, not a feature name
- Specific enough to produce a useful lesson
- Different from concepts already in docs/learning/PROGRESS.md

```python
def plan_and_create_issues(repo, milestone_number: int,
                           specs: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Create a batch of issues. Each spec is a dict with keys:
        title, what, where, verify, constraints, economy_note,
        slug, concept

    Returns list of created issue dicts with number and URL.
    """
    username = os.environ["GITHUB_USERNAME"]
    created = []

    # Ensure overnight labels exist
    create_overnight_labels(repo)

    milestone = repo.get_milestone(milestone_number)

    for spec in specs:
        # Skip if similar issue already exists
        if spec["title"].lower() in existing_titles:
            print(f"Skipping (exists): {spec['title']}")
            continue

        body = ISSUE_TEMPLATE.format(
            what=spec["what"],
            where=spec["where"],
            verify=spec["verify"],
            constraints=spec["constraints"],
            economy_note=spec["economy_note"],
            slug=spec["slug"],
            concept=spec["concept"],
            number="N"    # placeholder — updated after creation
        )

        issue = repo.create_issue(
            title=spec["title"],
            body=body,
            labels=["ready-for-ai"],
            assignees=[username],
            milestone=milestone
        )

        # Update branch name now that we have the number
        updated_body = body.replace(
            "feature/issue/N",
            f"feature/issue-{issue.number}"
        )
        issue.edit(body=updated_body)

        print(f"  Created #{issue.number}: {spec['title']}")
        print(f"  Concept: {spec['concept']}")
        created.append({
            "number":  issue.number,
            "title":   spec["title"],
            "concept": spec["concept"],
            "url":     issue.html_url
        })

    return created
```

---

## STEP 5 — ECONOMY NOTE GUIDANCE

Every issue should include an `economy_note` that pre-constrains the
implementation. This prevents the overnight session from over-building.

Good economy notes:
```
Use stdlib re for command pattern matching — no regex library needed.
Follow the existing BaseDevice pattern exactly — no new abstractions.
One new file maximum: src/devices/psu_e3631a.py plus its test file.
```

Bad economy notes (too vague):
```
Keep it simple.
Don't over-engineer.
```

The note should name the specific stdlib/pattern to use, or the
specific constraint on scope.

---

## STEP 6 — VERIFY THE QUEUE

After creating all issues:

```python
print("\n=== Tonight's ready-for-ai queue ===")
queue = list_issues(repo, label="ready-for-ai")
for issue in queue:
    print(f"  #{issue['number']:3} {issue['title']}")
    print(f"       URL: {issue['url']}")

print(f"\nTotal: {len(queue)} issues queued")
print("Run nightly-all.sh tonight to work through them.")
```

---

## STEP 7 — WRITE LOCAL PLAN SUMMARY

Save a planning summary locally (not committed):

```python
summary = f"""# Issue Planning Summary
Date: {datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')}
Repo: {repo.full_name}
Focus: {"" or "full project analysis"}

## Issues Created Tonight
"""
for issue in created_issues:
    summary += f"- #{issue['number']}: {issue['title']}\n"
    summary += f"  Concept: {issue['concept']}\n"
    summary += f"  URL: {issue['url']}\n\n"

summary += """
## What Was NOT Planned
[things seen in codebase not turned into issues and why]
"""

Path(".claude/memory/planning-session.md").write_text(summary)
print("\nPlan saved to .claude/memory/planning-session.md")
```

---

## CONCEPT SELECTION GUIDE

The `concept` field in each issue is what drives learning generation.
Choose well — this is what you'll study after the overnight session.

| Issue type | Good concept | Bad concept |
|------------|-------------|-------------|
| New SCPI device | "Multi-channel PSU channel selection in SCPI" | "E3631A support" |
| New Qt block | "Qt drag-and-drop hardware block pattern" | "New block" |
| Bug fix | "SCPI ErrorQueue per IEEE 488.2" | "Fixed a bug" |
| New NPC | "LLM character constraint and knowledge domain" | "Added blacksmith" |
| Backtest fix | "Lookahead bias in rolling feature windows" | "Fixed backtest" |
| Data pipeline | "Point-in-time market data and survivorship bias" | "Data ingestion" |

Before finalizing a concept, check docs/learning/PROGRESS.md to avoid
re-teaching something already well covered.

---

## RUNNING THIS COMMAND

```
/plan-github                        full project analysis
/plan-github "oscilloscope family"  focus on one area
/plan-github "phase 2"             focus on next milestone
```

Re-run after completing a milestone to plan the next set of work.
It reads existing open issues first and skips duplicates.

skills.name: scaffold
skills.content:
You are scaffolding the initial file structure for a planned feature.
This command bridges the gap between a plan document and actual files
on disk — creating skeletons, directories, config updates, and skill
files so the overnight session or /develop has something real to build on.

---

## STEP 1 — READ THE PLAN

```bash
# Find the plan document
ls .claude/plans/
cat .claude/plans/.md 2>/dev/null || \
  cat .claude/plans/$(echo "" | tr ' ' '-' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]').md 2>/dev/null || \
  echo "No plan found for '' — run /idea first"
```

If no plan exists, stop and tell the user to run `/idea` first.
The plan is the spec. Do not scaffold without it.

---

## STEP 2 — READ THE CODEBASE

```bash
# Understand what already exists before creating anything
find src/ lib/ app/ tests/ -type f 2>/dev/null | head -50
cat CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null | head -50 || true
git log --oneline -10
```

Use real class names, real import paths, and real conventions from
what you find — not generic placeholders.

---

## STEP 3 — DERIVE WHAT NEEDS TO BE CREATED

From the plan's "Affected Areas" and "Implementation Order" sections,
determine:

- New directories needed
- New source files (with correct imports and skeleton structure)
- New test files (matching the project's test conventions)
- Config file updates (pytest.ini, CMakeLists.txt, requirements.txt etc.)
- New skill files if the feature introduces patterns Claude needs
  to reference repeatedly (e.g. a new API, a new framework)
- Any one-time setup scripts (e.g. installing system packages)
- .gitignore additions for generated or temporary files

---

## STEP 4 — CREATE THE FILES

For each file derived in Step 3:

**Source files** — create with:
- Correct imports based on existing patterns in the project
- Class/function skeleton matching the plan's interface
- Docstrings explaining what each piece does and why
- TODO comments marking what the overnight session needs to fill in
- No placeholder names — use real names from the codebase

**Test files** — create with:
- Correct pytest conventions for this project
- One test function stub per acceptance criterion in the plan
- Each stub has a docstring explaining what it tests
- `pytest.mark.skip(reason="not implemented yet")` on each stub
  so the test suite runs clean before the feature is built

**Config updates** — update existing files rather than creating new ones
where possible. Add only what the plan requires.

**Skill files** — only if the feature introduces something Claude needs
to reference repeatedly. Write to `.claude/skills/<feature>/SKILL.md`.
Not every feature needs a skill — only ones with non-obvious APIs,
protocols, or patterns.

**Setup scripts** — only if the feature requires one-time environment
setup (installing system packages, external tools, etc.). Write to
`scripts/setup-<feature>.sh`. Make it idempotent — safe to run twice.

---

## STEP 5 — DO NOT CREATE

Things the scaffold should NOT create:

- Implementation code (that's for /develop or the overnight session)
- Golden/reference files (those are generated by running the tests)
- Database migrations (those need careful human review)
- Secrets or credentials
- Anything not mentioned in the plan

If the plan is unclear about something, leave a clear TODO comment
and note it in the summary rather than guessing.

---

## STEP 6 — UPDATE .gitignore

Add any paths that should never be committed:
```bash
# Examples based on feature type:
# Visual testing:   tests/visual/diffs/  tests/visual/actual/
# Build artifacts:  dist/  build/  *.pyc
# Generated files:  whatever the feature produces at runtime

grep -qF "<path>" .gitignore || echo "<path>" >> .gitignore
```

---

## STEP 7 — SUMMARY

After creating all files, print a clear summary:

```
Scaffold complete for: [feature name]
Plan: .claude/plans/[plan].md

Files created:
  [path]  ← [one line: what it is]
  [path]  ← [one line: what it is]
```

message.content:
Use the Opus model for this task specifically, not the default routing — this
is cross-cutting creative/design judgment across the whole project, which is
exactly the kind of work CLAUDE.md already reserves for Opus rather than Sonnet.

Goal: A full creative and game-feel audit of this project, producing a
prioritized, categorized backlog of design improvements — not code changes,
not one feature, a design document I can react to and then feed into /idea
one item at a time.

Do not interrogate me with clarifying questions before starting. I don't have
strong opinions yet on how this genre of game should look and feel — that's
the point of this audit. Read the actual codebase, any existing plan
documents, README, and git history to ground every recommendation in what
this project actually is, then use your own judgment about what "good" looks
like for a top-down, conversation-driven, LLM-NPC town game specifically —
not generic game-polish advice that could apply to anything.

Ground every recommendation in a real, named, findable source — a specific
game, a GDC talk, a published design framework, or a usability heuristic —
not generic best-practice phrasing. Web-search as needed rather than relying
only on your own training. Specifically:
- For game feel / "juice" critiques, ground in Steve Swink's Game Feel
  framework and/or the "Juice It or Lose It" GDC talk (Jonasson & Purho).
- For menu/UI/dialogue-flow critiques, ground in Nielsen Norman Group
  usability heuristics where applicable.
- For genre/pacing comparisons, name specific comparable games (e.g.
  Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing for town pacing, Oxenfree and Night in
  the Woods for dialogue-as-core-mechanic UX, Obra Dinn or Her Story if the
  investigation angle is relevant) and say concretely what they do that
  this project currently doesn't, not just that they're good examples.
Every recommendation should be able to answer "compared to what, and where
did that come from" — if you can't name a source, say the recommendation is
your own judgment call explicitly, rather than presenting it with the same
confidence as a sourced one.

Cover, as separate sections:
1. Visual style and art direction — cohesion, what's currently placeholder
   vs. intentional, what a stronger visual identity would look like given
   the existing size-contract and socket systems already in place.
2. Game feel / "juice" — feedback on player actions, animation weight,
   camera behavior, UI responsiveness — the small polish details that
   separate "functional" from "satisfying" in this genre.
3. UX and menu/dialogue flow — is the conversation interface actually
   pleasant to use repeatedly, given that talking to NPCs is the core loop
   here, not a side activity.
4. Pacing and progression — what makes a town worth continuing to explore
   past the first ten minutes; reference how other conversation-driven or
   town-sim games handle this, and name what you're drawing on.
5. Atmosphere and narrative texture — environmental storytelling,
   ambient detail, anything that makes the world feel authored rather than
   assembled.

For each recommendation: state what's true now, what you'd change, why it
matters specifically for THIS game (not a generic best-practice), and how
it's sized (S/M/L) so I can gauge effort before committing to it.

Be honest and specific rather than diplomatically vague — if something is
currently weak, say so plainly. I'd rather get a real assessment than a
softened one.

Output: save this as docs/design/GAME_FEEL_AUDIT.md, structured so each
recommendation could become its own /idea prompt later without further
scoping work. Do not implement anything — this is audit and recommendation
only.

30

Socket Contracts: Per-Part Attach Points vs Per-Pair Offsets

31

The character creator's core promise is "any combination of parts renders 32 correctly". Whether that promise scales depends entirely on where the 33 attachment knowledge lives.

34 35

The trap: per-pair offsets

36

The obvious first implementation is a table of hand-tuned offsets: 37 "round eyes on the blocky head sit at (0, 0.42, 0.38); on the round head at 38 (0, 0.40, 0.30)…" That table grows as parts × parts — adding 39 one head means re-tuning an offset against every eye and hair part, and a 40 missed pair ships as floating eyeballs.

41 42

The contract: each part describes only itself

43 
PartDef {
44	  id:        "head_round"
45	  localSize: (0.72, 0.72, 0.72)      // anchor at bottom-center
46	  sockets:   { eyes: (0, .40, .30),   // MY eye position, MY local space
47	               hair: (0, .64, 0) }
48	}
49	CategorySpec rows:  Head→Body via "head",  Eyes→Head via "eyes",  Hair→Head via "hair"
50

Assembly is a fold over the category specs: each part lands at 51 parent anchor + parent's declared socket. Knowledge is 52 parts + categories, not parts²: a wider head declares its 53 eye socket farther forward and every eye part inherits that placement for 54 free. Adding a category (a hat, a held item) is one spec row plus socket 55 entries on the parts that can carry it — no restructuring.

56 57

Where the size contract fits

58

The brief flagged the interaction. Resolution order is the whole answer: 59 sockets resolve in unscaled local space first, the assembly's total 60 height is measured, then one uniform scale takes the figure 61 to the same 1.8-unit character height contract the pack models use. Scale 62 per-part and sockets drift; scale once at the end and alignment is 63 invariant. Swapping the art style later means re-authoring parts — the 64 contract keeps world proportions fixed on top of everything else.

65 66

Guard rails that make it hold

67
    68
  • Style tags (round/blocky/any) gate combinations in the 69 validator, the picker, and the randomizer — one predicate 70 (styleCompatible), three call sites.
    • 71
  • Exhaustive test: every parts combination is assembled; 72 validity must equal pairwise style compatibility, all categories must place, 73 and the head must sit above the body's midpoint. The promise is checked at 74 the data level, not eyeballed per pair.
    • 75
  • Explicit "none": baldness is a real zero-size part, so 76 the assembly never has holes and the picker never needs a special case.
    • 77
78 79
The general shape. Whenever 80 "any A works with any B" is the requirement, make A and B each describe 81 themselves against a shared contract and derive the pairing — the moment 82 knowledge about a specific (A,B) pair appears anywhere, the combinatorial 83 promise is already broken.

Drill 0020 · pairs with lesson 0020
26

Drill: Socket Contracts

27 28

1. Adding a third head

29

Under per-pair offsets vs socket contracts: how many entries does a new 30 "head_oval" require in each scheme, with 3 eye parts and 4 hair parts in 31 the catalog?

32
Answer
33

Per-pair: 7 hand-tuned offsets (one per eye and hair part), each a 34 potential floating-eyeball bug. Socket contract: 1 PartDef with its own 35 eyes and hair sockets — every existing eye/hair 36 part snaps correctly with zero further edits.

37
38 39

2. Scale order

40

Why must the assembly resolve sockets BEFORE the character-height scale 41 is applied, rather than scaling each part to world size first?

42
Answer
43

Sockets are authored in each part's local space. Scaling parts 44 individually would move their sockets relative to differently-scaled 45 neighbors — alignment drifts. Resolving in unscaled local space and then 46 applying ONE uniform scale to the finished figure preserves every relative 47 placement and satisfies the 1.8-unit contract in a single step.

48
49 50

3. New category: hats

51

List the exact data changes to add a Hat category that sits on the 52 head, without touching assembly code.

53
Answer
54

(1) Add Hat to PartCategory and bump 55 kPartCategoryCount; (2) one CategorySpec row 56 {Hat, Head, "hat"}; (3) add a hat socket to each 57 head PartDef; (4) hat parts (including a zero-size "hat_none"). The 58 recursive assembly, validator, randomizer, and picker all pick it up from 59 the spec table.

60
61 62

4. Where's the one join between persona and look?

63
Answer
64

The spawn path (main.cpp startup + onCreate): it loads both records by 65 character_id, builds the Npc from the persona, and registers the look for 66 rendering. Storage, editing, and validation never touch both — enforced by 67 two separate SQLite tables rather than convention.

68
69 70

5. The exhaustive test's invariant

71

The combination test asserts assembled.ok == compatible. 72 Why is the equality (not just implication) important?

73
Answer
74

Both directions catch bugs: a compatible combo failing to assemble means 75 a missing socket (contract hole); an INcompatible combo assembling means 76 the style gate leaks and the picker could offer mixed-style characters. 77 The promise is "valid iff compatible", so the test asserts exactly that.

79

Lesson 0023 · Systems design · from PR #94 (#91, #93)

The Single Authoritative Source, and the Moonwalk Bug

Two of this milestone's fixes look unrelated — one is about where a bullet goes, the other about when a preview figure spins. They are the same lesson. Both are cases where a value was reconstructed next to its real source instead of derived from it, and the copy drifted.

The bug class: the moonwalk

The name comes from an earlier fix (#61): a character whose facing was computed in one place and whose movement was computed in another, so it slid backwards while appearing to walk forward — a moonwalk. The shape recurs whenever two consumers each derive "the same" quantity from raw inputs separately. They agree until one side changes its math, and then they silently disagree.

Case 1 — aim reconstructed from feet (#91)

The camera looked along yaw and pitch from eye height. The weapon built its own aim: yaw only, flat, spawned from the player's feet. Fire while looking up and the round left horizontally from the ground — the crosshair and the bullet were two different vectors that happened to share a yaw.

The fix is not "add pitch to the weapon too". That just makes two copies that agree today. The fix is one function both sides read:

// src/core/Math.hpp
inline Vec3 lookDirection(float yawDeg, float pitchDeg) {
    const float yr = degToRad(yawDeg), pr = degToRad(pitchDeg);
    const float cp = std::cos(pr);
    return normalize({std::sin(yr)*cp, std::sin(pr), std::cos(yr)*cp});
}
// the camera  (RaylibRenderer.cpp:141)
const Vec3 dir = lookDirection(pose.yawDeg, pose.pitchDeg);
// the weapon  (main.cpp:567)
world.playerAttack(lookDirection(player.yawDeg, player.pitchDeg));

Now the aim cannot drift from the crosshair, because there is no second aim to drift. A weapon added next year gets correct behavior for free — the bug is designed out, not patched over. Note kEyeHeight is shared the same way: camera and spawn origin both read the one constant.

Case 2 — a decision re-sampled every frame (#93)

The creator preview rotates when you drag it, but a click on a control button must not. The first cut asked each frame: "is the cursor over an interactive rect right now?" That re-derives the intent — drag vs click — from a value (cursor position) that moves during the very gesture it is trying to classify. A control-click flicked off its button mid-press spun the preview; a real drag that grazed a button stalled.

The intent is fixed at one instant — the press — so read it once and hold it:

if (IsMouseButtonPressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT))
    previewDragging = !menu.pointOverInteractive(GetMousePosition()); // latch
if (!IsMouseButtonDown(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT))
    previewDragging = false;                                          // release

This is the same move as #91 in the time dimension: the authoritative fact ("this gesture is a drag") is established once, at its source event, and every later frame reads that latch instead of recomputing an answer from data that has since moved on.

Deriving toward a target: shortestAngleDelta

When the preview is idle it eases back to front. "Face the camera" is derived every frame from one owned value (player.yawDeg + 180), never stored as a second copy that could go stale:

const float defaultYaw = player.yawDeg + 180.f;   // derived, not cached
previewYaw += shortestAngleDelta(previewYaw, defaultYaw)
            * (1.f - std::exp(-kPreviewEaseRate * dt));

shortestAngleDelta wraps the difference to [-180, 180] so the ease always takes the short way round instead of unwinding through 359°.

How to recognise it before it ships

SmellFix
Two sites compute "the same" value from raw inputsExtract one function; both call it
A per-frame test answers a question fixed at an earlier eventLatch the answer at that event; read the latch
A value is cached "for convenience" beside its ownerDerive it on read from the owner
The general shape. A quantity used in two places should have exactly one place that computes it — a shared function (space) or a latched event (time). The moment a second reconstruction exists, the two are only ever coincidentally equal, and coincidences expire.
The tell in review. If a bug fix adds a term to a copy so it matches the original "now", stop — you have made two copies agree, not made them one. Ask where the value is truly owned and have the other site derive from there.

Drill 0023 · pairs with lesson 0023

Drill: The Single Authoritative Source

1. Name the bug class

A character's facing is computed in one system and its movement in another, so it slides backward while animating a forward walk. What is this class of bug called in this codebase, and what is the one-line root cause?

Answer

The moonwalk (first fixed in #61). Root cause: two consumers each reconstruct "the same" quantity from raw inputs instead of deriving it from one shared source, so the copies drift apart.

2. Why not just add pitch to the weapon?

In #91 the weapon aimed yaw-only from the feet while the camera used yaw, pitch, and eye height. Why is "add pitch and eye height to the weapon's own aim code" the wrong fix even though it would look correct immediately?

Answer

It creates a second aim vector that merely agrees today. The next change to look math (or a new weapon) can desync it again. The real fix routes both camera and weapon through one lookDirection(yaw, pitch) so there is no second copy to drift — the bug is designed out, not patched.

3. Space vs time

#91 and #93 are the same principle applied along different axes. State the principle, and say what plays the role of "the one source" in each.

Answer

Principle: a value used in two places should be computed in exactly one place. #91 (space): the shared function lookDirection is the one source both camera and weapon read. #93 (time): the mouse-press event is the one moment the drag-vs-click decision is made; every later frame reads the latch instead of recomputing.

4. Spot the re-sampling bug

float rotateInput = 0.f;
if (IsMouseButtonDown(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) &&
    !menu.pointOverInteractive(GetMousePosition()))
    rotateInput += GetMouseDelta().x * kPreviewDragDegPerPx;

Why does this spin the preview on a control-click, and stall a legitimate drag? What single change fixes both?

Answer

It re-evaluates "over a control?" every frame using the moving cursor. A click that slips off its button mid-press stops reading as a control and spins the figure; a drag that grazes a button momentarily stops rotating. Fix: latch previewDragging once at IsMouseButtonPressed and hold it until the button releases.

5. Derive, don't cache

The idle ease targets player.yawDeg + 180.f recomputed every frame rather than stored once when idling begins. Give one concrete reason the derive-on-read version is safer.

Answer

If the player turns during the idle ease, a cached target would aim the preview at a stale "front" and it would settle facing the wrong way. Deriving from the live player.yawDeg each frame keeps "face the camera" correct as the owner changes — no second copy to invalidate.

6. Why shortestAngleDelta?

The ease uses shortestAngleDelta(previewYaw, defaultYaw) rather than defaultYaw - previewYaw. What goes wrong with the plain subtraction?

Answer

Plain subtraction can be up to ±360°, so the figure can unwind the long way round (e.g. spin 350° left instead of 10° right). shortestAngleDelta wraps the difference to [-180, 180] so the ease always takes the short arc.

7. Generalise it

You review a PR fixing a totals-mismatch bug: the cart shows one total, the invoice another. The diff copies the cart's discount formula into the invoice. What do you comment?

Answer

Same moonwalk shape. Two independently-computed totals that now agree will drift the next time either formula changes. Ask for one shared computeTotal() that both the cart and invoice call, so the number has a single authoritative source.

The ease uses shortestAngleDelta(previewYaw, defaultYaw) rather than defaultYaw - previewYaw. What goes wrong with the plain subtraction?

Answer

Plain subtraction can be up to ±360°, so the figure can unwind the long way round (e.g. spin 350° left instead of 10° right). shortestAngleDelta wraps the difference to [-180, 180] so the ease always takes the short arc.

7. Generalise it

You review a PR fixing a totals-mismatch bug: the cart shows one total, the invoice another. The diff copies the cart's discount formula into the invoice. What do you comment?

Answer

Same moonwalk shape. Two independently-computed totals that now agree will drift the next time either formula changes. Ask for one shared computeTotal() that both the cart and invoice call, so the number has a single authoritative source.

Vocab 0022 · pairs with lesson 0023

Vocab: The Single Authoritative Source

single authoritative source
The one place a quantity is computed or owned. Every other user derives from it rather than reconstructing its own copy, so the value cannot disagree with itself.
moonwalk bug
This codebase's name (from #61) for the failure where two consumers each rebuild "the same" value from raw inputs and drift apart — like a character sliding backward while animating a forward walk.
reconstruction
Recomputing a value beside its real source instead of reading the source. The seed of a moonwalk: two reconstructions are only ever coincidentally equal.
derived value
A value computed on demand from an owner (defaultYaw = player.yawDeg + 180). Contrast with a cached copy, which can go stale when the owner changes.
latch
Capturing a decision at the instant its inputs are meaningful (the mouse press) and holding it until a defined release, rather than re-deriving it each frame from data that has since moved.
sample-per-frame
Re-answering, every tick, a question that was actually settled at an earlier event. The time-domain form of reconstruction; the fix is to latch.
shortest angular delta
The signed difference between two angles wrapped to [-180°, 180°] (shortestAngleDelta), so an ease or turn always takes the short arc instead of unwinding the long way round.
designed-out bug
A defect removed by structure rather than patched by a guard — after #91 no weapon can mis-aim, because there is no second aim vector to be wrong.

# Overnight Build Report
Date: 2026-07-07 → 07-08 (session 5 — aim / styles / preview milestone)
Milestone #10 — three ready-for-ai issues, one stacked draft PR **#94**.

## Session 5 summary
Three independent fixes shipped as one atomic-commit-per-issue branch
(`feature/aim-styles-preview`, stacked on `feature/player-journal`) and a
single draft PR #94:

| Issue | Title | Commit |
|-------|-------|--------|
| #91 | fix(combat): aim the gun where the camera looks, from eye height | `c811e88` |
| #92 | feat(creator): more style-tagged character parts and palettes | `3ea616f` |
| #93 | feat(creator): player-driven preview rotation, idle return-to-front | `31b8c17` |
| — | fix(review): latch preview drag at press, cull grounded shots | `7be3057` |

**#91** — the weapon reconstructed a separate yaw-only, flat aim from the
player's feet, drifting from the camera's real 3D look (the *moonwalk* bug
class, cf. #61). Now one authoritative `lookDirection(yaw, pitch)` feeds both
camera and weapon, and shots leave from `kEyeHeight` along the full vector, so
new weapons can't reintroduce the drift.

**#92** — +2 parts per category and +3 palettes, additive within the existing
socket/style-tag size-contract, with renderer recipes. **Screenshot-verified**
in-engine.

**#93** — replaced the unconditional auto-spin with two states: drag/keys
rotate; after an idle timeout the figure eases back to face the camera
(`shortestAngleDelta` short-arc). No autonomous spin remains.

**Review fixes (`7be3057`)** — strict review found a real HIGH in #93: the
drag-vs-click gate was sampled per-frame against the live cursor, so a
control-click flicked off its rect spun the preview and a genuine drag grazing
a hit-rect stalled. The decision is now **latched once at press** and held
until release (a held drag also counts as active input, so the figure never
eases away under a grabbing cursor). Plus a #91 LOW: a missed *downward* shot —
newly possible now that aim follows pitch — kept travelling underground until
its lifetime expired; it's now retired once it passes below ground descending.

## Completed ✅
| Issue | Title | Branch | PR | Concept |
|-------|-------|--------|----|---------|
| #91 | gun aim from shared look vector | feature/aim-styles-preview | #94 | single authoritative source |
| #92 | more style-tagged parts & palettes | feature/aim-styles-preview | #94 | additive socket catalog |
| #93 | player-driven creator preview | feature/aim-styles-preview | #94 | latch-at-event vs sample-per-frame |

## Test status
`make -C tests test` green: **165 cases / 2343 assertions, 0 failed, 1 skipped**
(4 new aim tests, a `shortestAngleDelta` test, and the exhaustive
part-combination test extended to the new parts). Game target builds clean.

## Needs human verification
- **#91 in-game feel** — firing while mouse-looking and watching rounds land is
  interactive; the aim math is unit-tested but the felt behaviour is yours.
- **#93 entirely** — the creator preview only renders with the Creator page
  open, which a headless smoke run can't trigger. Drag feel, the idle
  return-to-front, and "no spin" need you to open the Creator page and try it.

## Learning materials (LOCAL-ONLY — not committed)
| Concept | Lesson | Drill | Vocab |
|---------|--------|-------|-------|
| single authoritative source / the moonwalk bug class | 0023 ✅ | 0023 ✅ | 0022 ✅ |

## Suggested first move
Open the Creator page and confirm #93's drag + idle-ease feel, then fire uphill
and downhill in-game to confirm #91. If both feel right, PR #94 is ready to
promote out of draft (into its `feature/player-journal` base, not main).

## Next work item (not started)
`shared-character-library` — plan authored at
`.claude/plans/shared-character-library.md`. Audit found NPCs render from
rigged glTF (`drawCharacter`) while created characters use primitive composites
(`drawCompositeCharacter`) — two pools, no shared assets, hence the
created-vs-roaming mismatch. Decision: make the composite CharacterParts pool
the single shared library and render NPCs from it. Not yet issues or code.

1	# Plan: One Shared Character Library — Unify NPCs and the Creator, Then Expand Hair
2	Date: 2026-07-08 (overnight, autonomous — decisions logged here + OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md)
3	Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
4	Estimated complexity: L
5	
6	## The Idea (one paragraph)
7	Roaming NPCs and player-created characters are drawn by two unrelated systems,
8	so a created character never looks native next to the townsfolk. NPCs render as
9	whole **rigged glTF KayKit models** (`drawCharacter`, 5 fixed adventurers);
10	creator characters render as **primitive-composite parts** from the
11	`CharacterParts` socket catalog (`drawCompositeCharacter`). They share no
12	assets, and KayKit's rigged models physically can't donate swappable
13	heads/hair/bodies — which is exactly why the composite system was built. This
14	plan makes the composite `CharacterParts` catalog the **single shared character
15	library**: every roaming NPC gets a composite look drawn from the same pool the
16	creator picks from, the rigged-model path is retired as the NPC source, and the
17	hair category is then expanded — so new hairstyles appear for NPCs and the
18	creator at once, and the two can literally use the same assets.
19	
20	## Goal
21	A character built in the creator and a townsperson are rendered by the same
22	parts library and look like they belong to the same world — and the creator
23	offers many more hairstyles, all shared with the NPCs.
24	
25	## Audit finding (step 1 — already confirmed; record in OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md first)
26	Established first-hand this session (while shipping #92, including side-by-side
27	screenshots of both):
28	- **NPCs are NOT part-based.** `main.cpp` NPC loop: `customLooks.find(i)` →
29	  `drawCompositeCharacter(...)`, **else** `drawCharacter(visual)`
30	  (`src/app/main.cpp:983-990`). `drawCharacter` uses a rigged glTF model chosen
31	  by index from five KayKit adventurers loaded in `Assets.cpp:170-172`
32	  (Barbarian/Knight/Mage/Rogue/Rogue_Hooded; Knight = police,
33	  `Assets.cpp:240,246`).
34	- **The creator is the only part-based system.** `CharacterParts.cpp` holds the
35	  socketed body/head/eyes/hair catalog + palettes; `drawCompositeCharacter`
36	  (`RaylibRenderer.cpp`) renders it from primitives.
37	- **So the mismatch is not "two pools, one smaller."** It is two different
38	  construction methods (whole rigged models vs primitive composites) that share
39	  nothing. The creator's pool can't include the KayKit models because they are
40	  not decomposable into parts.
41	- **The unification hook already exists:** any NPC with a `customLooks[i]` entry
42	  already renders as a composite. Unifying = give *every* NPC a look.
43	
44	## Decision (most-defensible pick — logged)
45	**Make the composite `CharacterParts` catalog the one shared library and render
46	every roaming NPC from it; retire rigged models as the NPC source.** This is the
47	only option that satisfies all five goals at once — one pool, creator as a
48	picker over it, NPCs native to it, and *more hairstyles* (rigged models can't
49	donate hair). It needs no new art pipeline because the composite NPC render path
50	already exists.
51	
52	**Trade-off (honest):** this retires the five rigged, textured, skeletally
53	animated KayKit adventurers as the NPC look. NPCs become primitive composites
54	with the existing procedural walk-bob and billboard mood faces — lower art
55	fidelity, higher cohesion + customization + hair variety. The user's stated
56	priority is explicitly cohesion ("literally the same assets… not two separate
57	art sources"), so cohesion wins.
58	
59	**Preserve NPC variety as the baseline (per the brief):** the current NPC "range"
60	is five distinct whole looks + a police variant. The composite pool already far
61	exceeds that combinatorially (4 bodies × 4 heads × 6 eyes × 8 hair × 8 palettes),
62	so each of the ten personas gets its **own distinct, authored** composite look,
63	and the police/armed NPCs keep a recognizable uniform look. Variety is matched
64	and then exceeded, never reduced.
65	
66	### Alternatives considered (logged, not chosen)
67	- **Match-but-keep-separate:** tune composites to resemble the KayKit style so
68	  they read as native, keeping rigged NPCs. Rejected: does not give "the same
69	  assets / one pool" the brief asks for, and still blocks shared hairstyles.
70	- **Source a CC0 *modular* character pack** (e.g. Quaternius modular /
71	  KayKit skeleton-style separable parts) and rebuild BOTH systems on it. This is
72	  the only path that keeps rigged fidelity AND unifies — but it is XL (new asset
73	  import, re-rigging, socket re-mapping) and may not drop in cleanly. Noted as
74	  the future upgrade if rigged fidelity later outweighs simplicity.
75	
76	## Out of Scope (this version)
77	- Sourcing/importing any new external art pack (the modular-pack alternative).
78	- Re-adding skeletal animation to composites (walk stays the procedural bob).
79	- Remote **player** rendering: fellow players still use `drawCharacter` (the
80	  rigged mesh) for now — a multiplayer edge; giving remote players composite
81	  looks is a logged follow-up, not this ticket.
82	- Deleting the rigged-model *loading* code in `Assets.cpp` (leave it dormant so
83	  remote players keep working and the path can be revived); only the **NPC
84	  dispatch** to it is retired.
85	- New part *categories* — still Body/Head/Eyes/Hair. Hair expansion is additive
86	  within the existing contract (as in #92).
87	
88	## Affected Areas
89	- `src/app/main.cpp` — the NPC render loop (`~968-991`): populate `customLooks[i]`
90	  for **every** NPC so all render via `drawCompositeCharacter`; the
91	  `else drawCharacter(visual)` branch stops being reached for NPCs. Look source:
92	  the persona's authored look, else a deterministic fallback.
93	- `src/core/PersonaLoader.{hpp,cpp}` — parse an optional `look = body, head,
94	  eyes, hair, palette` header key into `LoadedPersona` (a placement/appearance
95	  concern, like `position` — additive, an unknown-key today would error, so it
96	  must be registered). Extend `renderPersonaText` to round-trip it.
97	- `src/core/Persona*` / a small helper — a deterministic
98	  `lookForPersona(name)` = author-supplied look if present, else
99	  `randomizeLook(hash(name))`, so all ten personas (and any future procedural
100	  NPC) get distinct, valid, style-consistent looks with zero manual gaps.
101	- `personas/*.persona` — add an authored `look = …` line to each of the ten
102	  (baker motherly, cop uniform/cap, busker casual, etc.), so looks are
103	  intentional, not just hashed. Police/armed personas get a uniform-reading look.
104	- `src/core/CharacterParts.cpp` — expand the Hair category with N new
105	  style-tagged parts (and any palettes that suit them), additive within the
106	  socket/size contract.
107	- `src/app/RaylibRenderer.cpp` — bespoke `drawCompositeCharacter` recipes for the
108	  new hair parts (or documented generic-box fallback), as in #92.
109	- Tests: `tests/test_character_parts.cpp` (exhaustive combo test auto-covers new
110	  hair; add reachability), new `tests/test_persona_look.cpp` (persona `look`
111	  parse + round-trip + deterministic fallback validity), and update
112	  `tests/test_persona_roster.cpp` if it asserts anything about NPC models.
113	
114	## Implementation Order
115	1. **Record the audit finding in OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md** (the brief requires this
116	   before code): the two-systems finding above and the chosen direction.
117	2. **Persona `look` support** — add the optional `look` key to PersonaLoader +
118	   `LoadedPersona` + `renderPersonaText`, with a `lookForPersona(name)` helper
119	   (authored-or-deterministic). Unit-tested. *Independently committable.*
120	3. **Unify NPC rendering** — in main.cpp, assign every NPC a `CharacterLook` from
121	   step 2 and route all NPCs through `drawCompositeCharacter`; keep police/armed
122	   visually distinct. Rigged `drawCharacter` no longer dispatched for NPCs.
123	   *Independently committable.*
124	4. **Author the ten persona looks** — a distinct, in-character `look =` line per
125	   persona; verify variety ≥ the old five-model baseline. *Committable.*
126	5. **Expand hairstyles** — add the new style-tagged hair parts + recipes to the
127	   shared pool; both creator and NPCs pick them up. *Committable.*
128	6. **Visual QA** — side-by-side screenshot of a creator-built character next to
129	   roaming NPCs; confirm they read as one art source; attach the QA report to
130	   OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md. (Use the visual-qa subagent per the brief; if absent,
131	   the smoke-render + Read-PNG method used for #92.)
132	
133	## Acceptance Criteria
134	- [ ] OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md states the audit finding (two systems, chosen
135	      unification) before implementation.
136	- [ ] Every roaming NPC renders via `drawCompositeCharacter` from the shared
137	      `CharacterParts` pool — no NPC uses a rigged glTF model (verify: with the
138	      character models absent, NPCs still render as composites, not fallback
139	      markers).
140	- [ ] A `.persona` `look = body, head, eyes, hair, palette` line parses,
141	      round-trips through `renderPersonaText`, and drives that NPC's look; a
142	      persona with no `look` still gets a deterministic, valid, distinct look
143	      (`tests/test_persona_look.cpp`).
144	- [ ] All ten personas have distinct looks; police/armed read as uniformed;
145	      count of visually distinct NPC looks ≥ the previous five.
146	- [ ] The creator's part/palette pool is exactly the pool NPCs render from — the
147	      creator maintains no separate subset (same `partCatalog()`/`paletteCatalog()`).
148	- [ ] New hairstyles appear in both the creator picker and on NPCs; every
149	      style-compatible combination still assembles (`tests/test_character_parts.cpp`).
150	- [ ] `make -C tests test` green; game builds.
151	- [ ] Visual-QA side-by-side screenshot in OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md shows a
152	      creator-built character looking native beside roaming NPCs.
153	
154	## Edge Cases and Error Handling
155	| Situation | Expected behaviour |
156	|-----------|-------------------|
157	| Persona `look` names an unknown part/palette | Reject that look with a logged reason; fall back to the deterministic `lookForPersona(name)` so the NPC still spawns. |
158	| Persona has no `look` line | Deterministic `randomizeLook(hash(name))` — valid, style-consistent, stable across runs. |
159	| Two personas hash to similar looks | Authored `look` lines make the ten intentionally distinct; the hash fallback only covers unauthored/procedural NPCs. |
160	| Character models missing on disk | NPCs now render as composites regardless (composites are primitives, not loaded assets) — a strict improvement over today's marker-cylinder fallback. |
161	| Police/armed NPC | Authored uniform look (e.g. cap + cool/blue palette) so authority stays readable without the Knight model. |
162	| Remote players | Still rigged this version (out of scope); logged follow-up to give them composite looks too. |
163	| New hair part without a bespoke recipe | Generic declared-box fallback (documented in #92) — renders, never crashes. |
164	
165	## Open Questions
166	- **Fidelity vs cohesion is a genuine product call.** This plan retires the
167	  rigged NPC models to satisfy the "one shared library / same assets" goal. If
168	  keeping the rigged art matters more, the off-ramp is the modular-pack
169	  alternative (XL) — flagged here so it can be redirected before implementation.
170	  Otherwise: none — plan is complete.
171	
172	## Suggested GitHub Issues
173	1. **Persona `look` support + deterministic fallback** — optional `look` persona
174	   key parsed/round-tripped; `lookForPersona(name)` = authored-or-hashed. (Concept:
175	   *authored data with a deterministic derived fallback.*)
176	2. **Unify NPC rendering onto the shared composite parts library** — every NPC
177	   gets a CharacterLook and renders via `drawCompositeCharacter`; rigged models
178	   retired as the NPC source; police stays distinct. (Concept: *collapsing two
179	   render paths onto one shared asset library behind an existing dispatch hook.*)
180	3. **Author ten in-character persona looks** — a distinct look per townsperson,
181	   preserving/exceeding the old five-model variety. (Concept: *art-directing a
182	   cast within a constrained part system.*)
183	4. **Expand the shared hairstyle pool** — N new style-tagged hair parts + recipes,
184	   shared by creator and NPCs. (Concept: *additive style-tagged catalog growth in
185	   a single shared pool.*)
